					<description><![CDATA[The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has issued Public Clarification CTP011 on 15 July 2026, clarifying the requirements for transfer pricing adjustments under the Corporate Tax Law. It mandates that all transactions between Related Parties must adhere to the arm’s length standard, requiring a Taxable Person to adjust their Taxable Income if financial records do...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has issued <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1T5gqIisMXH62LhGxhxbAAx1rKkmG_IHh/view?usp=drive_link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Public Clarification CTP011</a> on 15 July 2026, clarifying the requirements for transfer pricing adjustments under the Corporate Tax Law.</p>
<p>It mandates that all transactions between Related Parties must adhere to the arm’s length standard, requiring a Taxable Person to adjust their Taxable Income if financial records do not reflect market-value pricing. While upward adjustments increase taxable income, downward adjustments decrease it and require rigorous disclosure in tax returns regardless of the transaction&#8217;s size.</p>
<p>Under Article 34(1) of the Corporate Tax Law (CTL), all transactions and arrangements between related parties must meet the arm’s length standard. When a taxable person&#8217;s financial statements do not reflect this standard, they must make a transfer pricing (TP) adjustment in their Tax Return. If this adjustment results in a decrease in the Taxable Income, it is classified as a downward adjustment.</p>
<p>The Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has outlined specific requirements and considerations for these downward adjustments to ensure strict compliance and transparency. These include:</p>
<p><strong>Self-assessment basis and audit risk </strong></p>
<p>Because the UAE Corporate Tax regime operates on a self-assessment basis, a taxable person is empowered to evaluate their own need for a TP adjustment. You do not need to obtain prior approval from the FTA to execute a downward adjustment in your Tax Return. However, this autonomy is balanced by regulatory oversight, meaning that any adjustment you make is fully subject to a potential Tax Audit by the FTA.</p>
<p><strong>Mandatory disclosure without thresholds </strong></p>
<p>The FTA imposes stringent disclosure rules specifically for downward adjustments. While upward adjustments (which increase taxable income) only require disclosure if the transactions exceed applicable prescribed thresholds, the rule for downward adjustments is absolute. All transactions and arrangements for which a downward adjustment is made must be disclosed in the Tax Return, irrespective of their value or nature. This ensures the FTA maintains total visibility over any self-directed reductions in a taxpayer&#8217;s taxable income.</p>
<p><strong>Rigorous documentation requirements </strong></p>
<p>To substantiate the downward adjustment and defend it during a potential tax audit, a taxable person must maintain sufficient and comprehensive documentation. The FTA mandates four key pillars of documentation:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>The rationale:</strong> You must clearly explain why the original pricing recorded in your Financial Statements failed to reflect the arm’s length principle, and demonstrate exactly how your revised outcome aligns with the arm&#8217;s length standard.</li>
<li><strong>Arm’s length analysis:</strong> You must provide a formal analysis, which includes a benchmarking study, to serve as evidence that your TP adjustment is consistent with applicable TP methodologies and regulations.</li>
<li><strong>Reconciliation: </strong>You must provide a clear mathematical mapping that reconciles the initial values recorded in your Financial Statements with the adjusted arm’s length values you are disclosing in the Tax Return.</li>
<li><strong>Symmetrical corresponding adjustments: </strong>You must provide evidence that the relevant related parties involved in the transactions or arrangements have made symmetrical corresponding adjustments on their end.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Scope limitation </strong></p>
<p>It is critical to note that the FTA&#8217;s clarification on this matter has a strict scope. It applies solely to initial adjustments required under Article 34(1) of the CTL to ensure transactions meet the arm&#8217;s length standard. The guidance does not extend to corresponding adjustments under Articles 34(10) and 34(11) of the CTL. To distinguish these:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Article 34(10):</strong> It applies when the FTA (or the taxable person) adjusts the taxable income of one party, and the FTA must make a corresponding adjustment to the taxable income of the related party.</li>
<li><strong>Article 34(11): </strong>It applies to international scenarios where a foreign competent authority adjusts a transaction, allowing the UAE taxable person to submit an application to the FTA for a corresponding adjustment to their own income.</li>
</ul>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has published an updated Tax Procedures Guide on Private Clarifications (TPGPC1), dated 14 July 2026, setting out the process for taxpayers seeking the authority&#8217;s official view on uncertain tax technical matters. The updated guidance explains who can apply for a Private Clarification, the types of issues that qualify, the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has published an updated <a href="https://tax.gov.ae//Datafolder/Files/Pdf/2026/Guide/Private%20Clarifications%20-%20EN%20-%2014%2007%202026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Tax Procedures Guide on Private Clarifications (TPGPC1)</a>, dated 14 July 2026, setting out the process for taxpayers seeking the authority&#8217;s official view on uncertain tax technical matters.</p>
<p>The updated guidance explains who can apply for a Private Clarification, the types of issues that qualify, the application process, applicable fees, and the circumstances under which requests may be rejected or refunded.</p>
<p><strong>Private Clarifications provide binding administrative guidance</strong></p>
<p>According to the guide, a Private Clarification is an official document issued and signed by the FTA that sets out the tax treatment of a specific transaction based on the facts presented by an applicant.</p>
<p>The FTA states that it is administratively bound by the position contained in a clarification, provided the actual facts and circumstances are consistent with those submitted in the application.</p>
<p>However, the clarification applies only to the applicant that requested it and cannot be relied upon by other taxpayers. It also becomes invalid where there has been fraud, misrepresentation, or where the transaction ultimately differs from the facts provided.</p>
<p>The guide further notes that it is not legally binding legislation and does not amend existing tax laws. In addition, a Private Clarification is not considered an official decision and therefore cannot be challenged through the FTA&#8217;s reconsideration or dispute resolution procedures.</p>
<p><strong>Eligibility rules clarified</strong></p>
<p>The updated guidance confirms that any natural or juridical person facing genuine tax uncertainty may apply for a Private Clarification.</p>
<p>For VAT and Corporate Tax groups, only the representative member or parent company may submit an application using the group&#8217;s EmaraTax account and Tax Registration Number (TRN).</p>
<p>For Pillar Two Top-up Tax matters, applications may only be submitted by the Domestic Designated Filing Entity (DDFE) on behalf of the multinational enterprise group.</p>
<p>Registered tax agents may also apply on behalf of clients, provided they are authorised and registered with the FTA for the relevant tax type.</p>
<p>Applications must relate to federal taxes, including VAT, Excise Tax, Corporate Tax or Top-up Tax, and must address genuine technical uncertainty rather than seek confirmation of provisions that are already clear in the legislation.</p>
<p><strong>Application process and fees</strong></p>
<p>All applications must be submitted through the EmaraTax portal in either Arabic or English.</p>
<p>Applicants are required to provide a cover letter explaining the background to the request, the relevant legislative provisions and a detailed technical analysis. Supporting documents, such as contracts, invoices and any third-party tax advice, must also be included.</p>
<p>The application fee is AED 1,500 for requests covering a single tax type and AED 2,250 where more than one tax is involved.</p>
<p>Once a complete application has been received, the FTA aims to issue a Private Clarification within 60 business days.</p>
<p><strong>Circumstances where requests may be rejected</strong></p>
<p>The guide identifies several situations where the FTA will reject an application, including where the applicant is ineligible, lacks appropriate authorisation, or where the request falls outside the scope of the Private Clarification process.</p>
<p>Examples include applications relating to administrative penalty waivers, information technology issues or reviews of tax assessments.</p>
<p>Requests will also be rejected if the applicant fails to provide additional information requested by the FTA within 40 business days.</p>
<p>The authority may additionally reject applications that are incomplete, lack sufficient technical analysis, concern matters already addressed in existing public guidance, involve hypothetical scenarios, or are considered to relate to tax planning, avoidance or evasion.</p>
<p><strong>Refunds available in limited circumstances</strong></p>
<p>The FTA confirms that application fees are generally non-refundable.</p>
<p>However, refunds may be issued automatically if an applicant withdraws the request within two business days of submission or where the FTA decides not to issue a clarification because the applicant was already subject to a tax audit covering the same matter at the time the application was made.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[Sri Lanka&#8217;s Inland Revenue Department (IRD), on 3 July 2026, outlined sweeping changes to the country&#8217;s Value Added Tax (VAT) regime following the certification of the Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act No. 14 of 2026 on 30 June 2026. 										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Sri Lanka&#8217;s Inland Revenue Department (IRD), on 3 July 2026, <a href="https://www.ird.gov.lk/en/Lists/Latest%20News%20%20Notices/Attachments/799/PN_VAT_2026-03_New_E.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">outlined</a> sweeping changes to the country&#8217;s Value Added Tax (VAT) regime following the certification of the Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act No. 14 of 2026 on 30 June 2026.</p>
<p>The amendments introduce VAT on digital services supplied by non-residents, increase the VAT rate on financial services, create new exemptions and zero-rating provisions, strengthen compliance obligations, and significantly increase penalties for tax offences. While most measures took effect on 1 July 2026, some provisions apply retrospectively from 1 October 2025.</p>
<p><strong>VAT extended to cross-border digital services</strong></p>
<p>From 1 July 2026, VAT applies to services supplied through electronic platforms by non-resident providers to customers in Sri Lanka.</p>
<p>Non-resident suppliers must register for VAT if the value of their supplies exceeds LKR 60 million over any consecutive 12-month period or exceeds, or is expected to exceed, LKR 15 million in any quarter beginning on or after 1 July 2026. Registration applications must be submitted electronically within three months of becoming liable to register or the publication of the prescribed registration form.</p>
<p>The new rules do not apply where the recipient is a VAT-registered person in Sri Lanka. The Commissioner-General will issue further guidance on registration, tax collection and compliance.</p>
<p>The legislation also introduces new statutory definitions for terms including &#8220;electronic platform&#8221;, &#8220;non-resident person&#8221;, &#8220;fixed place&#8221; and &#8220;marketplace in relation to educational courses&#8221;.</p>
<p><strong>New exemptions and zero-rated supplies</strong></p>
<p>The amendments expand VAT relief through new exemptions and zero-rated supplies.</p>
<p>Services provided by garment buying offices registered under the Industrial Promotion Act to overseas buyers are treated as zero-rated supplies with effect from 1 October 2025, provided the customer is located outside Sri Lanka and payment is received in foreign currency.</p>
<p>From 1 July 2026, new VAT exemptions apply to supplies made to approved Businesses of Strategic Importance under the Colombo Port City Economic Commission framework, as well as certain educational and healthcare services supplied through electronic platforms by non-resident providers. Diplomatic and qualifying international organisation supplies also receive relief where provided under applicable laws or agreements.</p>
<p><strong>Financial services rate rises and registration thresholds retained</strong></p>
<p>The VAT rate applicable to financial services increased to 20.5% for taxable periods beginning on or after 1 July 2026. Financial services subject to this rate are exempt from the Social Security Contribution Levy.</p>
<p>The Government also abandoned its proposed reduction in VAT registration thresholds. Businesses must therefore continue to register if taxable supplies exceed LKR 15 million in a quarter or LKR 60 million over a rolling 12-month period.</p>
<p><strong>New compliance requirements for VAT-registered businesses</strong></p>
<p>The amendments introduce several new compliance measures.</p>
<p>VAT-registered businesses may now submit VAT schedules from the start of the relevant taxable period using RAMIS through CSV uploads, direct portal entry or API integration with enterprise resource planning systems.</p>
<p>Registered persons will also be required to use secure point-of-sale (POS) machines for all taxable transactions within three months of the date prescribed by the Commissioner-General, who will publish the technical specifications.</p>
<p>In addition, the Commissioner-General must publish the name, address, tax registration number and registration status of every VAT-registered person to improve transparency and assist tax administration.</p>
<p><strong>Stronger enforcement and higher penalties</strong></p>
<p>The legislation substantially strengthens enforcement provisions.</p>
<p>Higher penalties now apply to tax evasion, fraudulent refund claims and other VAT offences committed on or after 1 October 2025, with maximum fines increasing from LKR 25,000 to LKR 1 million in addition to tax-based penalties. Imprisonment of up to six months remains available for serious offences.</p>
<p>From 1 July 2026, new offences include fraudulent refund claims and failing to provide valid tax invoices or authenticated customs documents.</p>
<p>The Commissioner-General has also been given explicit authority to investigate VAT offences, while criminal prosecutions will be brought by the Attorney-General or authorised officers in the name of the Commissioner-General.</p>
<p><strong>Other changes</strong></p>
<p>Additional amendments include allowing entertainment tax to be deducted when calculating the taxable value of film exhibition services, disallowing input tax deductions on certain deferred-VAT project imports that are not re-exported within the prescribed period, writing off VAT liabilities relating to qualifying tsunami relief projects, and introducing other administrative changes to the operation of the VAT system.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/sri-lanka-enacts-wide-ranging-vat-amendments/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, Sri Lanka enacted the Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act, No. 14 of 2026, introducing a series of changes to the Value Added Tax Act, No. 14 of 2002, including revised rules for digital services supplied by non-residents, higher tax rates for specified institutions, new compliance requirements and stricter enforcement measures.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Germany&#8217;s government has unveiled an ambitious 26-point package aimed at strengthening the country&#8217;s response to tax evasion, financial crime and illicit financial activity through tougher sanctions, enhanced enforcement powers and greater use of technology.</p>
<p><strong>Harsher penalties for tax offences</strong></p>
<p>Among the most significant proposals is an increase in the maximum prison sentence for organised tax crime from 10 years to 15 years. The government also plans to reclassify tax evasion as a felony rather than a misdemeanour, signalling a tougher approach to prosecuting serious tax offences.</p>
<p>The package would also abolish the current form of voluntary disclosure that allows certain tax offenders to avoid criminal prosecution by repaying evaded taxes together with a surcharge.</p>
<p><strong>Greater enforcement powers and more investigators</strong></p>
<p>To strengthen enforcement, the government intends to consolidate customs powers and recruit an additional 1,500 employees for the customs service, increasing the current workforce of around 49,000 officers.</p>
<p>Authorities would also receive stronger powers to identify and confiscate assets suspected of being linked to criminal activity. In addition, corporate fines for involvement in tax evasion would be increased.</p>
<p>The government plans to establish a joint data analysis centre with Germany&#8217;s federal states, using artificial intelligence to improve information sharing, detect fraud more effectively and coordinate investigations.</p>
<p><strong>New compliance obligations for businesses</strong></p>
<p>The proposals introduce several new obligations for businesses designed to improve tax transparency and preserve evidence.</p>
<p>Companies would be required to report value added tax more quickly through a new electronic reporting system. Accounting records would also need to be retained for 15 years instead of the current 10 years, giving prosecutors more time to secure evidence during investigations.</p>
<p>Businesses handling large volumes of cash would be subject to mandatory electronic cash-register requirements to reduce opportunities for underreporting revenue and tax liabilities.</p>
<p><strong>Broader measures against financial crime</strong></p>
<p>The package also includes stronger protections for whistleblowers, expanded systematic purchases of tax data by authorities and a review of measures to close loopholes commonly used in aggressive tax planning arrangements.</p>
<p>Collectively, the reforms represent one of Germany&#8217;s most comprehensive efforts in recent years to strengthen tax enforcement, improve detection capabilities and deter financial crime through tougher penalties, increased investigative resources and modern technology.</p>

		<title>Taiwan clarifies lower tax rates for inherited property sales through combined ownership periods</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/taiwan-clarifies-lower-tax-rates-for-inherited-property-sales-through-combined-ownership-periods/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=taiwan-clarifies-lower-tax-rates-for-inherited-property-sales-through-combined-ownership-periods</link>

					<description><![CDATA[Taiwan&#8217;s Ministry of Finance has clarified that taxpayers selling inherited or bequeathed real estate may qualify for a significantly lower property income tax rate by combining the ownership periods of successive deceased owners when calculating the applicable holding period. The clarification, issued on 16 July 2026, aims to ensure heirs are not unfairly subject to...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan&#8217;s Ministry of Finance has <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/singlehtml/384fb3077bb349ea973e7fc6f13b6974?cntId=759e824d6d4044c5ad452a30617f17d8" target="_blank" rel="noopener">clarified</a> that taxpayers selling inherited or bequeathed real estate may qualify for a significantly lower property income tax rate by combining the ownership periods of successive deceased owners when calculating the applicable holding period.</p>
<p>The clarification, issued on 16 July 2026, aims to ensure heirs are not unfairly subject to higher tax rates simply because they dispose of inherited property shortly after receiving it.</p>
<p>According to the Ministry, where inherited property is subject to Taiwan&#8217;s integrated house and land income tax regime, the ownership periods of each deceased owner or testator can be aggregated to determine the applicable tax rate. This may allow taxpayers to benefit from substantially lower rates than would apply if only their personal ownership period were considered.</p>
<p><strong>Rules introduced to protect heirs</strong></p>
<p>The Kaohsiung National Taxation Bureau explained that real estate acquired by the deceased or testator after 1 January 2016 falls within the unified real estate income tax system under Ministry of Finance Order No. 10404620870, issued on 19 August 2015.</p>
<p>However, the authorities recognised that heirs and beneficiaries often need to sell inherited property shortly after succession, for example, to support surviving family members or pay inheritance tax liabilities. Applying the highest tax rates solely because of a short post-inheritance holding period would therefore be unreasonable.</p>
<p>To address this issue, Article 14-4, Paragraph 4 of the Income Tax Act and Ministry of Finance Order No. 11204619060, issued on 2 November 2023, allow the ownership periods of each successive deceased owner or testator to be combined when determining the relevant tax rate.</p>
<p><strong>Example shows substantial tax savings</strong></p>
<p>The bureau illustrated the rules using the example of Mr. Su.</p>
<p>In the example, Mr. Su&#8217;s grandfather purchased a property on 1 May 1985. Following the grandfather&#8217;s death on 1 May 2024, ownership passed to Mr. Su&#8217;s father, before being inherited by Mr. Su after his father&#8217;s death on 15 May 2026.</p>
<p>If Mr. Su sells the property on 15 August 2026, he will have owned it for only three months. Ordinarily, a holding period of less than two years would attract the highest combined property income tax rate of 45%.</p>
<p>However, because the law allows the ownership periods of both his grandfather and father to be counted, the holding period runs continuously from 1 May 1985 until the sale on 15 August 2026. As the combined ownership exceeds ten years, the applicable tax rate falls to 15%, reducing the tax rate by 30%.</p>
<p>The bureau also reminded taxpayers that land registration records can be used to trace successive ownership and accurately calculate the combined holding period when selling inherited or bequeathed real estate.</p>

		<title>Dominican Republic consults on draft software tax rules under tax reform</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/dominican-republic-consults-on-draft-software-tax-rules-under-tax-reform/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=dominican-republic-consults-on-draft-software-tax-rules-under-tax-reform</link>

		<category><![CDATA[Assessment]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Submission of returns]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[The Dominican Republic&#8217;s General Directorate of Internal Taxes (DGII) has launched a public consultation on a draft general rule establishing the tax treatment of software transactions, introducing new rules for software acquisitions, licensing, SaaS, associated services and cross-border payments following the enactment of Tax Reform Law No. 30-26. Public consultation launched On 14 July 2026,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic&#8217;s General Directorate of Internal Taxes (DGII) has launched a <a href="https://dgii.gov.do/publicacionesOficiales/foroContribuyentes/Paginas/NG-regula-tratamiento-fiscal-operaciones-involucren-programas-informaticos.aspx" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on a <a href="https://dgii.gov.do/publicacionesOficiales/foroContribuyentes/Documents/Borrador-NG-regula-tratamiento-fiscal-operaciones-involucren-programas-informaticos.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft general rule</a> establishing the tax treatment of software transactions, introducing new rules for software acquisitions, licensing, SaaS, associated services and cross-border payments following the enactment of Tax Reform Law No. 30-26.</p>
<p><strong>Public consultation launched</strong></p>
<p>On 14 July 2026, the Dominican Republic&#8217;s General Directorate of Internal Taxes (DGII) opened a public consultation on a draft General Rule (Norma General) that establishes the tax treatment applicable to software transactions.</p>
<p>The proposal implements key changes introduced by Articles 21 and 22 of Law No. 30-26 on Tax Reform and is intended to provide a comprehensive framework governing the taxation of software acquisitions, licensing arrangements and related services.</p>
<p>The consultation is open until 15 September 2026 in accordance with Law No. 167-21 on Regulatory Improvement and Simplification of Procedures, as amended by Law No. 14-25, together with the implementing regulations under Decree No. 486-22 and the administrative procedure provisions of Law No. 107-13.</p>
<p><strong>Draft rule clarifies software transaction categories</strong></p>
<p>The proposed regulation reflects the transition from software distributed on physical media to modern digital licensing and cloud-based delivery models.</p>
<p>It applies to individuals and entities that acquire, lease or commercialise software and associated services, distinguishing between several types of transactions:</p>
<ul>
<li>Software acquisition involves the transfer of intellectual property ownership.</li>
<li>Software licensing, grants a stable or long-term right to use software without transferring ownership or source code.</li>
<li>Software lease arrangements, including recurring subscriptions and Software as a Service (SaaS).</li>
<li>Associated services, such as implementation, customisation and maintenance.</li>
</ul>
<p>The DGII states that these distinctions are intended to ensure that each type of transaction receives the appropriate tax treatment.</p>
<p><strong>New income tax rules for domestic and cross-border payments</strong></p>
<p>The draft introduces detailed income tax (ISR) rules for software-related payments.</p>
<p>Payments made to non-resident providers for software licences and lease arrangements would be subject to a 15% withholding tax, treated as a final payment. This reflects the reduction introduced by Law No. 30-26, replacing the previous 27% withholding rate.</p>
<p>However, payments made to foreign suppliers for the outright acquisition of software ownership and intellectual property rights would not be subject to the 15% withholding.</p>
<p>To claim a tax deduction for foreign software payments, taxpayers would be required to support the transaction with a Comprobante para Pagos al Exterior (Proof of Foreign Payment).</p>
<p>For domestic providers, income derived from software licensing and associated services would form part of the normal income tax base.</p>
<p>Where software is recognised as an intangible asset with a determinable useful life, it would be amortised using the straight-line method.</p>
<p><strong>ITBIS treatment distinguishes licences from standalone services</strong></p>
<p>The draft also clarifies the application of the Value Added Tax (ITBIS).</p>
<p>Software acquisitions and licensing arrangements would not be subject to ITBIS because software is treated as an intangible asset. This exemption would apply to both domestic and international transactions.</p>
<p>Services supplied together with a software licence, such as updates or support included within the licensing arrangement, would likewise remain outside the scope of ITBIS.</p>
<p>By contrast, technical services invoiced separately from a software licence or acquisition—such as independent implementation or consulting services—would be subject to ITBIS when supplied in the domestic market.</p>
<p><strong>Documentation and reporting obligations strengthened</strong></p>
<p>The proposed regulation introduces extensive documentation requirements designed to ensure that transactions reflect their economic substance.</p>
<p>Where a contract contains multiple elements, such as software licences, hardware, training and technical services, taxpayers would be required to identify each component separately in contracts or invoices so that the correct tax treatment can be applied to every element.</p>
<p>Taxpayers would also be expected to maintain a comprehensive evidentiary file containing commercial, legal and technical documentation demonstrating the true nature of each software transaction beyond the supporting invoice.</p>
<p>In addition, payments made to foreign suppliers would continue to be reportable through Formato 609 within the applicable statutory deadlines.</p>
<p><strong>Effective date</strong></p>
<p>The General Rule will enter into force upon its official publication following completion of the public consultation process and will repeal any previous provisions that are inconsistent with the new framework.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/dominican-republic-dgii-outlines-implementation-timeline-for-law-30-26-tax-reforms/">Earlier</a>, DGII issued Notice 10-26, setting out the implementation schedule for key provisions of Law 30-26 and confirming that several tax measures will take effect from 1 July 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic&#8217;s Directorate General of Internal Revenue (DGII) has opened a <a href="https://dgii.gov.do/publicacionesOficiales/foroContribuyentes/Paginas/NG-dispone-lista-de-bienes-podra-acogerse-a-depreciacion-acelerada.aspx" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on a <a href="https://dgii.gov.do/publicacionesOficiales/foroContribuyentes/Documents/Borrador-NG-dispone-lista-de-bienes-podra-acogerse-a-depreciacion-acelerada.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft general norm</a> establishing the implementation framework for the accelerated depreciation regime introduced under Law No. 30-26.</p>
<p>Stakeholders have until 15 September 2026 to submit comments on the proposed rules, which would allow eligible businesses to depreciate qualifying industrial machinery and equipment at twice the normal rate.</p>
<p><strong>Draft rules implement Law No. 30-26</strong></p>
<p>The draft General Norm provides the administrative framework for applying the accelerated depreciation incentive introduced by Law No. 30-26, enacted on 18 June 2026. The law amended the Tax Code by adding a new provision to Article 287, allowing qualifying industrial machinery and equipment to be depreciated at double the standard rate applicable to Category 3 assets.</p>
<p>The DGII states that the framework is based on constitutional principles governing public administration and taxation, including the principles of legality, efficiency, transparency, justice, equality and equity established in Articles 138 and 243 of the Constitution.</p>
<p>The Tax Code also authorises the DGII to issue general norms and administrative interpretations through Articles 34 and 35, while Article 297 identifies the corporate taxpayers eligible to claim the benefit.</p>
<p><strong>Eligibility requirements</strong></p>
<p>Under the draft norm, accelerated depreciation will apply only to assets meeting specific technical criteria.</p>
<p>Eligible assets must:</p>
<ul>
<li>Be classified as Category 3 assets;</li>
<li>Fall within tariff chapters 84 or 85 of the Customs Tariff;</li>
<li>Be new machinery or equipment intended exclusively for industrial use; and</li>
<li>Have a normal useful life of at least five years.</li>
</ul>
<p>The draft norm also includes Annex A, which establishes the official list of qualifying machinery and equipment.</p>
<p><strong>Reporting and compliance obligations</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers claiming the accelerated depreciation incentive will be required to report the qualifying depreciation expenses separately in Annex D of the IR-2 corporate income tax return.</p>
<p>In addition, businesses must submit an annual information report detailing qualifying acquisitions in accordance with Annex B of the proposed norm.</p>
<p>The DGII notes that failure to comply with the reporting requirements will be subject to the sanctions for breaches of formal tax obligations under Article 257 of the Tax Code. It also reserves the authority to reject depreciation claims that do not satisfy the requirements established by Law No. 30-26 and the implementing norm.</p>

<p>The SII also announced that Exempt Resolution No. 94 of 15 July 2026 establishes the list of unregistered platforms to which the taxpayer change mechanism will apply. The measure is intended to ensure the correct payment of taxes by betting, gambling and casino services provided remotely by digital platforms without a registered address or residence in Chile.</p>
<p>Under the taxpayer change mechanism, payment method operators will withhold 19% VAT on each transaction and remit the tax monthly to the tax authorities.</p>
<p>The SII said the oversight mechanism draws on experience gained since 2021, when VAT began to apply to Digital Services supplied by foreign platforms. Information from debit cards, credit cards, prepaid cards and other sources has enabled the authority to identify betting platforms operating in Chile.</p>
<p>The unregistered platforms listed under Exempt Resolution No. 94 are:</p>
<p>BET365, STARS, 1WIN.COM, ELECTRAWORKS, THELOTTER, POKERSTARS, GGPOKER, BETCRIS, LEOVEGAS and ROOBET.</p>
<p>As a next step, the SII will review the information submitted during the registration process. Once registrations have been confirmed, the authority will analyse whether the Digital VAT declarations and payments made by each online betting platform correspond with information received from payment providers.</p>
<p>The Deputy Director of Tax Audits, Carolina Saravia, said: “With the information we are receiving, we will be able to monitor the registration and ensure the correct payment of this tax by these platforms, through automated processes designed and built to guarantee compliance with obligations and the increased direct revenue that will be generated from the implementation of this tax.”</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The French Ministry of Economy and Finance has <a href="https://presse.economie.gouv.fr/facturation-electronique-david-amiel-ministre-de-laction-et-des-comptes-publics-annonce-une-approche-de-tolerance-et-de-bienveillance-dans-la-mise-en-oeuvre-de-la-reforme-de-la-facturation-electroniq/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced </a>the forthcoming implementation of mandatory electronic invoicing (e-invoicing) requirements in Communication No. 898 issued on 11 July 2026.</p>
<p>From 1 September 2026, all businesses must be able to receive electronic invoices, while large companies and medium-sized enterprises must also issue electronic invoices and transmit the required data to the tax administration.</p>
<p>Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), very small enterprises (VSEs), and micro-enterprises will become subject to the electronic invoicing requirement from 1 September 2027.</p>
<p>The ministry said 2 million businesses have already selected an approved invoice reception platform from the 130 approved platforms currently listed. The Directorate General of Public Finances (DGFiP) has published a practical guide on impots.gouv.fr covering the implementation of the reform and established a dedicated support line to assist businesses.</p>
<p>David Amiel, Minister for Public Action and Public Accounts, said the tax administration would adopt a tolerant and supportive approach during the initial phase, adding that businesses acting in good faith that encounter difficulties and take steps to regularise their situation will not be subject to penalties.</p>

The Special Voluntary Disclosure Program (SVDP) is effective immediately and runs from 7 July 2026 to 31 December 2027. The programme is open to taxpayers who fall...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Inland Revenue Board of Malaysia (IRBM) <a href="https://www.hasil.gov.my/wp-content/uploads/20260707_kenyataan-media-hasil-7-julai-2026-program-khas-pengakuan-sukarela-e-invois.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced </a>on 7 July 2026 that it&#8217;s rolling out an amnesty programme for businesses that haven&#8217;t fully complied with e-invoicing rules. The Special Voluntary Disclosure Program (SVDP) is effective immediately and runs from 7 July 2026 to 31 December 2027.</p>
<p>The programme is open to taxpayers who fall into any of the following categories:</p>
<ul>
<li>Taxpayers who have implemented e-Invoicing in accordance with the prescribed timeline but have not fully submitted e-Invoices for certain transactions;</li>
<li>Taxpayers who have submitted e-Invoices containing errors or information that does not comply with the prescribed specifications and requirements; and</li>
<li>Taxpayers who have failed to submit e-Invoices for any period commencing from the date on which e-Invoicing became mandatory.</li>
</ul>
<p>Participants must file corrected information that matches the General e-Invoicing Guidelines and Specific e-Invoicing Guidelines—accuracy matters, or the amnesty doesn&#8217;t apply.</p>
<p>To encourage adoption, the government attached a benefit: businesses can claim a full capital allowance within one year for ICT equipment and software development costs tied to e-invoicing implementation. This accelerates what would normally be a slower deduction schedule.</p>
<p><strong>SVDP protections and limits</strong></p>
<p>Disclosures under the programme are accepted if taxpayers act in good faith and meet all requirements. Taxpayers bear responsibility for ensuring their submissions are accurate. The amnesty shields participants from compliance reviews, enforcement actions, penalties, and prosecution related to the disclosed e-invoices. That protection doesn&#8217;t extend to invoices that fail to meet technical specifications or submissions involving fraud, willful default, or negligence. The updated e-Invoice Specific Guideline contains additional details and worked examples.</p>
<p>Besides the SVDP, the Inland Revenue Board of Malaysia (IRBM) also released the updated <a href="https://www.hasil.gov.my/wp-content/uploads/IRBM-e-Invoice-Specific-Guideline.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">e-Invoice Specific Guideline Version 4.8</a> on 7 July 2026.</p>
<p>This specific guideline assists taxpayers in implementing the e-Invoice system effectively under the Income Tax Act 1967. The guideline provides detailed technical instructions and visual workflows for various commercial activities, including e-commerce, cross-border transactions, and dividend distributions. It highlights two primary scenarios for businesses: issuing individual e-Invoices for buyers who need tax substantiation and creating consolidated e-Invoices for those who do not.</p>
<p>To ease the transition, the IRBM offers concessions for individual taxpayers, allowing them to use specific identification formats like Tax Identification Numbers (TIN) or MyKad details. Furthermore, the guide covers complex accounting situations such as self-billed e-Invoices, employee reimbursements, and currency exchange treatments.</p>
<p>Extensive tables and appendices are included to define the exact data fields required for digital validation through the MyInvois Portal or API.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina&#8217;s tax authority (ARCA) has extended the deadline for submitting financial statements and related accounting documentation until 31 July 2026 for eligible taxpayers whose fiscal year ended in December 2025, under General Resolution No. 5871/2026.</p>
<p>The extension applies to taxpayers and responsible parties covered by General Resolution No. 4,626, including corporations, sole proprietorships, trusts and other entities that maintain commercial balance sheets for income tax purposes.</p>
<p>The revised deadline covers the submission of the Annual Report (Memoria), Financial Statements, Auditor&#8217;s Report, and other documentation required by ARCA.</p>
<p>ARCA said the extension was introduced to ease the workload of accounting professionals during one of the busiest reporting periods of the year. The measure also follows requests from professional organisations representing the economic sciences sector.</p>
<p>Taxpayers and authorised professionals must file the required documentation through the Presentación Única de Balances (PUB) service using their Clave Fiscal credentials. The online system has been updated to accept submissions until the new deadline.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US is making progress in negotiations with Mexico to revise the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), while discussions with Canada have yet to produce the concessions sought by the Trump administration, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Wednesday, 15 July 2026.</p>
<p>Speaking at the Aspen Institute Security Forum in Colorado, Greer said discussions with Mexican officials had been constructive ahead of a third round of formal bilateral USMCA negotiations scheduled for next week in Mexico City.</p>
<p>&#8220;So, it&#8217;s going well with the Mexicans. They&#8217;re quite pragmatic,&#8221; Greer said. &#8220;But our trade deficit with Mexico really is a challenge. It really is a problem.&#8221;</p>
<p>Greer said the administration&#8217;s priority is to address the US trade deficit with Mexico while maintaining North American supply chains. He noted that the administration would rather see US companies source goods from Mexico than from China or Southeast Asia, but argued that the existing trade imbalance must be reduced.</p>
<p>&#8220;I have a mandate from the president to find a way in whatever deal we make with Mexico to have &#8230; tariffs or quotas or whatever it is to try to control that,&#8221; Greer said.</p>
<p>&#8220;You know, we want to do it in a way that doesn&#8217;t disrupt supply chains unnecessarily, but we do want to incentivize supply chains moving&#8221; to the US</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/us-walks-away-from-usmca-renewal-eyes-major-trade-overhaul/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, this month, Greer declined to extend the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement on 1 July, citing concerns that included the US trade deficit with Mexico. According to US Census Bureau data, the deficit increased by USD 28 billion, or 17%, to USD 197 billion in 2025. The decision began the process that could lead to the North American trade pact winding down within a decade unless the three countries agree on changes.</p>
<p>The review comes after President Donald Trump questioned the future of the USMCA in June, saying the United States would be better off without the trade pact. <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-trump-questions-usmcas-future-as-renewal-talks-intensify-ahead-of-july-deadline/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Speaking </a>in France on 17 June 2026, Trump said he would &#8220;rather not have the agreement,&#8221; while adding that he remained willing to sign a renewed deal if negotiations moved forward.</p>
<p>Although Greer did not discuss the administration&#8217;s proposal presented during bilateral USMCA talks in May to require that 50% of the value of North American-built vehicles originate in the United States, he said rules of origin for the automotive sector should require a greater share of US and Mexican content and reduce reliance on parts sourced from Asia.</p>
<p>He also said stricter rules of origin should apply to strategic sectors, including industrial goods, electronics and pharmaceuticals, adding that US and Mexican officials are identifying products that could be reshored to North America.</p>
<p>Regarding Canada, Greer said he remains in regular contact with Canadian trade officials but formal negotiations on the future of the trade agreement have not yet begun.</p>
<p>The US trade deficit with Canada, driven largely by US oil imports, declined by USD 12.9 billion, or 21%, to USD 48.3 billion last year.</p>
<p>Greer acknowledged Canada&#8217;s decision to withdraw a proposed digital services tax and an online streaming act that would have affected American companies but said he was not prepared to treat those steps as negotiating concessions.</p>
<p>He also declined to predict when an agreement could be reached, saying progress may ultimately depend on direct engagement between President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.</p>
<p>&#8220;I mean, the reality is, if the president and Prime Minister Carney, you know, have an understanding, I&#8217;m sure we can put together something that makes sense to get us over the hump.&#8221;</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The European Commission faces a pushback from ten member states over its strategy to impose a carbon price on heating and transport fuels. On 15 July 2026, Italy, Poland, Bulgaria, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Romania and Slovakia signed a joint statement urging the EU to reconsider this new scheme, known as ETS2,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The European Commission faces a pushback from ten member states over its strategy to impose a carbon price on heating and transport fuels. On 15 July 2026, Italy, Poland, Bulgaria, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Romania and Slovakia signed a joint statement urging the EU to reconsider this new scheme, known as ETS2, before it launches in 2028.</p>
<p>The countries argue that adding a climate tax on fuel now conflicts with the economic pressures and geopolitical tensions Europe is navigating. Citizens shouldn&#8217;t bear extra costs while supply chains remain fragile and energy markets unstable. The bloc has already delayed ETS2 by a year—it was originally set for 2027—signalling just how contentious this move remains.</p>
<p>The opposition cuts directly across the bloc&#8217;s climate ambitions. Germany and Sweden view the carbon price as essential for pushing consumers toward electric vehicles and heat pumps, betting that tax revenue would then fund the transition directly. The Commission backs this logic, refusing to water down ETS2 before it even starts.</p>
<p>But the ten countries want changes to how the existing carbon market operates, too. They&#8217;re demanding the EU hand out more free emissions permits to industries without requiring them to spend on decarbonization in Europe. This signals a fundamental disagreement over who pays for the green transition.</p>
<p>The European Commission will unveil its full ETS revision on 17 July 2026. When EU governments and lawmakers negotiate these changes, the ten signatory states hold enough votes to block any amendments they collectively oppose. That&#8217;s enough weight to force compromise or derail the plan entirely.</p>

		<title>Uzbekistan signs multilateral convention to tackle tax evasion and avoidance</title>

				<category><![CDATA[Exchange of Information]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[The OECD has announced that Uzbekistan signed the OECD-Council of Europe Convention on the Multilateral Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters (the Convention) as amended by the 2010 Protocol, on 15 July 2026. The Convention will enable Uzbekistan to exchange information with 152 jurisdictions, including all major financial centres, which form a network...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD has <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/about/news/announcements/2026/07/uzbekistan-joins-as-153rd-signatory-to-multilateral-convention-to-tackle-tax-evasion-and-avoidance.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> that Uzbekistan signed the OECD-Council of Europe Convention on the <a href="https://www.oecd.org/tax/exchange-of-tax-information/convention-on-mutual-administrative-assistance-in-tax-matters.htm" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Multilateral Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters</a> (the Convention) as amended by the 2010 Protocol, on 15 July 2026.</p>
<p>The Convention will enable Uzbekistan to exchange information with 152 jurisdictions, including all major financial centres, which form a network of more than 9,000 exchange relationships.</p>
<p>The Convention enables jurisdictions to engage in a wide range of mutual assistance in tax matters: exchange of information on request, spontaneous exchange, automatic exchange, tax examinations abroad, simultaneous tax examinations and assistance in tax collection. It guarantees extensive safeguards for the protection of taxpayers&#8217; rights.</p>
<p>The Convention is the primary instrument for the swift implementation of the <a href="https://www.oecd.org/tax/exchange-of-tax-information/standard-for-automatic-exchange-of-financial-account-information-for-tax-matters-9789264216525-en.htm" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Standard for Automatic Exchange of Financial Account Information in Tax Matters</a> (the Common Reporting Standard or CRS). The CRS, developed by the OECD and G20 countries, enables more than 125 jurisdictions to automatically exchange offshore financial account information.</p>
<p>Beyond the exchange of information on request and the automatic exchange pursuant to the CRS, the Convention is also a powerful tool in the fight against illicit financial flows and is a key instrument for the implementation of the transparency standards of the <a href="http://www.oecd.org/tax/beps/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) Project</a>.</p>
<p>The Convention will enter into force for Uzbekistan once it has been ratified and the instrument of ratification has been deposited.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD has <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/about/news/announcements/2026/07/oecd-publishes-new-analysis-on-the-economic-impacts-of-the-global-minimum-tax.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> a new analysis examining the economic impacts of the Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax, with the findings presented during a webinar held on 15 July 2026. Alongside the analysis, the OECD also released a working paper titled <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/mne-responses-to-the-global-minimum-tax_0bc9aac9-en.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">MNE Responses to the Global Minimum Tax</a>, which provides an early empirical, ex post assessment of how multinational enterprises have responded to the introduction of the Global Minimum Tax.</p>
<p>OECD publishes new analysis on the economic impacts of the Global Minimum Tax</p>
<p>The OECD has released the 2026 Economic Impact Assessment of the Global Minimum Tax (GMT), providing new estimates of the expected effects of the GMT and presenting preliminary evidence from its first year of implementation. The findings were presented during an <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/events/2026/07/economic-impact-assessment-of-the-global-minimum-tax-2026.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OECD webinar</a>.</p>
<p>The updated assessment incorporates more recent data, improved modelling, and information on the current state of GMT implementation and the recently agreed Side-by-Side Package. It examines the expected effects of the GMT on effective tax rates, tax rate differentials, profit shifting and tax revenues.</p>
<p>The OECD also released a separate analysis, <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/07/mne-responses-to-the-global-minimum-tax_a2b1c6a4.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">MNE Responses to the GMT</a>, based on 2024 consolidated financial statement data, providing an initial assessment of outcomes following the first year of GMT implementation. The preliminary evidence suggests increases in effective tax rates among in-scope multinational enterprises relative to out-of-scope firms, while finding no statistically significant evidence of reductions in investment or employment among in-scope firms during the first year of implementation.</p>
<p><strong>Key findings</strong></p>
<p>Relative to a hypothetical scenario where the GMT was not implemented anywhere, the analysis found the following expected effects, noting these may take time to be realised.</p>
<ul>
<li>Average jurisdiction-level effective tax rates are estimated to increase by 2.8-3.7% on average under the current GMT framework, with effective tax rates in investment hubs estimated to rise by 5.5-6.9 %.</li>
<li>Effective tax rate differentials between jurisdictions are estimated to decline by 19-25%, potentially leading to improved allocation of capital.</li>
<li>The GMT is estimated to reduce profit-shifting substantially with an estimated reduction of between 22.6-44.6%.</li>
<li>Global CIT revenues are estimated to rise by 3.2-5.4% per year.</li>
<li>Initial post-implementation 2024 data suggests positive effective tax rate impacts of the GMT and finds no evidence of negative effects on investment or employment.</li>
</ul>
<p>The webinar outlined the methodology, assumptions and results of the updated assessment and provided stakeholders with an opportunity to discuss the analysis and its implications. The webinar highlighted the role of the GMT in strengthening international tax co-operation, reducing BEPS activity, and enhancing stability in the international tax system.</p>
<p>The OECD will continue to monitor the implementation and impacts of the GMT as additional data become available. The updated assessment and accompanying analysis are intended to support the ongoing evaluation of the GMT and its effects over time.</p>
<p><strong>MNE responses to the Global Minimum Tax</strong></p>
<p>This paper provides an early empirical, ex post assessment of how MNEs have responded to the introduction of the GMT. The GMT, implemented in 2024, represents a fundamental change in international taxation. The paper analyses the realised responses of MNEs exploiting the EUR 750 million threshold to identify causal effects.</p>
<p>Specifically, the paper uses group level financial and ownership data from the Orbis database and implements a difference in differences strategy that compares MNEs just above and below the scope defining revenue threshold. The paper evaluates whether the GMT has affected MNE effective tax rates, investment, and employment, and whether firms adjusted their behaviour in anticipation of the reform.</p>
<p>The paper includes heterogeneity analysis to assess which company types and sectors drive the results. Finally, the paper uses the analysis on the impact of ETRs to estimate the potential revenues raised by the GMT in its first year of introduction.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Kenya’s government confirmed, on 14 July 2026, that it is keeping its reduced 8% value-added tax rate on petroleum products through mid-October, alongside a KES 945 million subsidy to stabilise pump prices in the July-August cycle.</p>
<p>The government first compressed VAT on fuel from 16% to 8% in April 2026, reacting to crude price shocks tied to the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran. That three-month window is now extended another quarter.</p>
<p>The subsidy matters because Kenya has no domestic oil production and sources nearly all refined products through government deals with Middle Eastern suppliers. Disruption risks along the Strait of Hormuz are real—the same regional strain that sent crude climbing in the first place. The extension is essentially a bet that holding prices flat for another 90 days won&#8217;t crater state finances, at least not faster than political heat from fuel strikes would.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Brazil&#8217;s Federal Revenue Service (RFB) opened its doors for tax debtors to settle their cases on better terms. On 13 July 2026, the agency <a href="https://www.gov.br/receitafederal/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/2026/julho/transacao-tributaria-2026-receita-federal-publica-dois-novos-editais-de-negociacao-de-debitos-em-contencioso-administrativo" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> two notices (<a href="https://www.in.gov.br/web/dou/-/edital-de-transacao-n-9-de-13-de-julho-de-2026-719190099" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Notice 9</a> and <a href="https://www.in.gov.br/web/dou/-/edital-de-transacao-n-10-de-13-de-julho-de-2026-719155502" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Notice 10</a>) offering structured payment plans with steep discounts — but the window to apply closes on 30 October 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Notice 9: Larger disputes, bigger discounts</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers tangled in administrative tax litigation over debts up to BRL 50 million have options under Notice 9. Payments can be stretched over years, with interest and penalties slashed by up to 65% (70% for individuals, micro-enterprises, or charities), and some debts can be offset using tax loss credits. The catch: Applicants need to demonstrate an ability to pay, and the minimum debt must be at least BRL 200 for individuals or BRL 300 for companies.</p>
<p>The application process runs through the Federal Revenue Service portal. Applicants log in, navigate to &#8220;My Processes,&#8221; request service through the digital system, upload the required paperwork, and await approval.</p>
<p><strong>Notice 10: Smaller debts, simpler rules</strong></p>
<p>Notice 10 targets debts under 60 minimum wages in administrative disputes. Eligibility is limited to individuals, sole proprietors, micro-entrepreneurs, and small businesses. Eligible debts may be settled under negotiated terms offering discounts of up to 50% for payment in up to 12 instalments, up to 40% for payment in up to 24 instalments, up to 35% for payment in up to 36 instalments, or up to 30% for payment in up to 55 instalments.</p>
<p>The minimum monthly payment is BRL 200.</p>
<p>Access is through &#8220;My Debt Negotiations&#8221; on the same portal, where eligible debts can be selected and a plan confirmed.</p>
<p><strong>What joining costs</strong></p>
<p>Entering either programme means dropping any appeals or objections on the relevant debts and formally accepting liability. Participants are bound by the terms set out in the notice and applicable tax law. Both programmes close on 30 October 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>United States Trade Representative (USTR) representative Jamieson Greer is taking final action, at President Trump’s direction, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 by imposing a <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-trump-administration-unveils-25-brazil-tariff-over-trade-grievances/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">25% tariff </a>on certain goods of Brazil, according to a <a href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/july/ustr-section-301-action-brazils-unreasonable-acts-policies-and-practices" target="_blank" rel="noopener">release</a> on 15 July 2026.</p>
<p>This follows a yearlong investigation by USTR that determined that certain Brazilian measures related to digital trade and electronic payment services, unfair, preferential tariffs, anti-corruption interference, intellectual property protection, ethanol market access, and illegal deforestation are unreasonable and burden or restrict the commerce of American farmers, workers, innovators, and exporters.</p>
<p>This action comes after the Office of the USTR convened two public hearings, received over 360 public comments, and negotiated intensively with the Government of Brazil to seek resolution of US concerns.</p>
<p><strong>Background</strong></p>
<p>Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting US commerce.  Section 301 may be used to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government practices that burden or restrict US commerce.  A Section 301(b) investigation examines whether the acts, policies, or practices are unreasonable or discriminatory and burden or restrict US commerce.</p>
<p>At the specific direction of the President, on 15 July 2025, the USTR initiated an investigation under Section 302(b)(1)(a) of the Trade Act regarding the acts, policies, and practices of the Government of Brazil related to digital trade and electronic payment services; unfair, preferential tariffs; anti-corruption enforcement; intellectual property protection; ethanol market access; and illegal deforestation.</p>
<p>On 15 July 2025, the Trade Representative requested consultations with the Government of Brazil pursuant to Section 303(a) of the Trade Act, which were held on 15 and 16 April 2026.</p>
<p>On 3 September 2025, USTR and the Section 301 Committee convened a public hearing regarding the investigation.</p>
<p>On 1 June 2026, the Trade Representative determined that under certain Brazil’s acts, policies, and practices related to these areas are unreasonable and burden or restrict US commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act.</p>
<p>As a result of this determination, the Trade Representative proposed responsive action and invited the public to provide written comments by 1 July 2026 on the proposed action. USTR received, reviewed, and analysed over 360 written comments.  On 6 and 7 July, USTR also held a public hearing regarding proposed responsive action in the investigation, at which 77 witnesses testified.</p>
<p>A copy of the Federal Register Notice is available <a href="https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/files/Issue_Areas/Enforcement/Section%20301/Brazil%20301%20Final%20Action%20FRN%207-15-2026%20final.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">here</a>.</p>

The Swiss government said the agreement goes beyond previous bilateral arrangements in several areas and is intended to strengthen legal certainty for businesses in both countries.</p>
<p>The government also said the agreement carries geopolitical significance, noting that amid increasing fragmentation and uncertainty in global trade policy, Switzerland and the UK are reinforcing their strategic partnership and reaffirming their commitment to open markets, reliable rules and close economic cooperation. It added that the agreement is expected to contribute to the diversification and resilience of bilateral economic relations.</p>
<p>Following completion of the remaining legal formalities, Switzerland and the UK will prepare the agreement for signature. The two countries aim to sign the agreement by the end of 2026, after which it will be subject to the required domestic approval procedures.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Nigeria <a href="https://regfollower.com/nigeria-tariff-reforms-green-tax-framework-enter-into-force/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">introduced</a> a green tax surcharge on imported vehicles under its 2026 Fiscal Policy Measures, effective 1 July 2026. The Green Tax Surcharge imposes a 2% to 4% levy on imported high-engine vehicles.</p>
<p>Collected by the Nigeria Customs Service, the surcharge aims to reduce carbon emissions, promote environmental sustainability, and encourage the importation of cleaner vehicles in line with global environmental standards.</p>
<p>The Green Tax Surcharge is based on engine capacity, with larger engines subject to higher rates. Vehicles with engines below 2,000cc are exempt; those with engines between 2,000cc and 3,999cc are subject to a 2% surcharge; and vehicles with engines of 4,000cc or more are subject to a 4% surcharge. Electric vehicles and mass transit buses are fully exempt, reflecting the government&#8217;s support for cleaner transportation.</p>
<p>At the same time, standard import duties fell sharply. New vehicles dropped from 20% to 10%. Used vehicles fell from 15% to 5%. For many smaller engines, the duty cut outweighs the absence of the green tax. For luxury or large-engine imports, the surcharge eats into the duty savings.</p>

Companies or juristic...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Thailand Revenue Department has issued a <a href="https://rd.go.th/fileadmin/user_upload/kormor/newlaw/parateA.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance</a>, on 7 July 2026, outlining the method that companies and juristic partnerships must use to convert foreign currency, foreign currency-denominated assets, and liabilities into Thai currency when calculating net profit subject to corporate income tax under Section 65 bis (5) of the Revenue Code.</p>
<p>Companies or juristic partnerships that hold foreign currency, assets, or liabilities valued in foreign currency as of the last day of their accounting period must convert those amounts into Thai currency using exchange rates calculated by the Bank of Thailand as of the last day of the accounting period.</p>
<p>For companies or juristic partnerships other than commercial banks or other financial institutions prescribed by the Minister, two calculation methods are available. They may either use the average rate between the buying and selling rates of commercial banks as calculated by the Bank of Thailand, or calculate the value or price of foreign currency or assets using the average buying rate of commercial banks as calculated by the Bank of Thailand while valuing liabilities using the average selling rate.</p>
<p>The Revenue Department said that once a company or juristic partnership selects one of the permitted methods, it must continue to apply that method consistently unless approval to change the method is granted by the Director-General.</p>
<p>For commercial banks and other financial institutions prescribed by the Minister, the announcement requires the use of the average rate between the buying and selling rates of commercial banks as calculated by the Bank of Thailand when converting the value or price of foreign currency, assets, or liabilities into Thai currency.</p>
<p>The guidance also specifies that companies or juristic partnerships using the average buying rate to value foreign currency or assets must apply either the bill buying rate or the telegraphic transfer buying rate, in accordance with generally accepted accounting practices.</p>
<p>Where the last day of an accounting period falls on a Bank of Thailand holiday, companies or juristic partnerships must instead use the exchange rate calculated by the Bank of Thailand on the last business day preceding the holiday.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Belgium’s Chamber of Deputies <a href="https://www.lachambre.be/FLWB/PDF/56/1243/56K1243001.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved </a>legislation introducing a range of personal income tax reforms on 9 July 2026.</p>
<p>This legislation outlines a comprehensive reform of the Belgian personal income tax system, scheduled for implementation through 2030. The primary objective of the proposal is to increase purchasing power for low-income workers by gradually raising the tax-exempt income threshold from EUR 10,910 to 15,600.</p>
<p>The supplements for the first and second dependent children will be increased in four stages, so that by 2029 each child will receive an equal supplement of EUR 2,650. To harmonise the system, the indexation of supplements for three or more children will be temporarily frozen between the 2026 and 2029 income years.</p>
<p>Other key reform measures include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Single parents: </strong>The tax-free allowance supplement for single parents will be restricted and granted only to &#8220;true&#8221; single parents, explicitly excluding parents who are factual cohabitants.</li>
<li><strong>Simplification of tax calculation:</strong> Starting from the 2030 assessment year, the tax on the tax-free allowance will no longer be calculated using a separate tax scale. Instead, it will be calculated at the same rate as the basic income tax.</li>
<li><strong>Integration income: </strong>Starting in 2026, the integration income will be treated as taxable replacement income.</li>
<li><strong>Working pensioners:</strong> A separate, favourable tax rate of 33% will be introduced for pensioners who choose to take on supplementary work after completing a 45-year career or reaching the statutory retirement age.</li>
<li><strong>Overtime and work bonus:</strong> To reward extra work, the limit for voluntary overtime hours will be increased to 360 hours per year, with 240 of those hours being exempt from income tax. Additionally, the fiscal &#8220;work bonus&#8221; for low-wage earners will be significantly reinforced.</li>
<li><strong>Independent entrepreneurs:</strong> An &#8220;entrepreneur deduction&#8221; will be introduced for self-employed individuals without a company, allowing them to exempt 10% of a first tranche of their profits/benefits. The reform also abolishes the tax surcharge applied to independent individuals for the absence or insufficiency of advance tax payments.</li>
<li><strong>Benefits in kind and company directors: </strong>The reform discourages the excessive use of flat-rate benefits in kind; advantages exceeding 20% of a worker&#8217;s or director&#8217;s gross salary will be subject to a separate tax (7.5% or 10% depending on the specific application). The minimum remuneration required for company directors to benefit from reduced corporate tax rates will also be raised to EUR 50,000.</li>
<li><strong>Private wealth operations:</strong> To provide legal certainty, operations managing private wealth (real estate, portfolio values, etc., excluding financial assets) will irrefragably be presumed as &#8220;normal management&#8221; if the resulting gross income does not exceed EUR 2,000.</li>
</ul>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Lithuania&#8217;s parliament has <a href="https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalActPrint/lt?jfwid=-1ch27kf8ja&amp;documentId=04b7a8c06aeb11f1aa9cfebedf36d56d&amp;category=TAP" target="_blank" rel="noopener">proposed </a>amendments to the Law on Personal Income Tax (PIT) that would introduce a new Personal Income Tax (PIT) exemption for individuals investing in startups. If enacted, the measure will take effect on 1 January 2027 and apply when calculating and declaring income for the 2027 and subsequent tax periods.</p>
<p><strong>Proposed exemption for startup investments</strong></p>
<p>Under the draft amendments to Article 17 of the Law on Personal Income Tax, income derived from the sale or other transfer of ownership of shares, interests or member units will be exempt from Personal Income Tax (PIT) where the entity met the definition of a start-up under the Law on the Development of Small and Medium-sized Business at the time the investment was made.</p>
<p>To qualify, the startup must also have been registered in a European Economic Area state no earlier than five years before the date the shares, interests or member units were acquired.</p>
<p><strong>Holding period and ownership conditions</strong></p>
<p>The proposed relief will apply only if the shares, interests or member units are sold or otherwise transferred at least three years after acquisition.</p>
<p>The draft law also sets a 25% ownership cap, requiring that, during the three-year holding period, the individual, acting alone or together with related persons, did not directly or indirectly hold more than 25% of the shares, interests or member units of the entity.</p>
<p><strong>Transactions excluded from the exemption</strong></p>
<p>The exemption will not apply where shares, interests or member units are sold back to the issuing entity, where securities are deemed to have been sold under Article 11 of the Law on Personal Income Tax, or where the shares were received following an increase in nominal value as specified in Article 2(14)(1) of the law. In the latter case, the exemption will not apply to the portion of income equal to the amount of the increase in nominal value.</p>
<p>The proposal also extends the existing restriction that denies specified exemptions where the relevant income is received from foreign entities registered or otherwise organised in target territories, or from individuals whose permanent place of residence is in a target territory.</p>
<p><strong>Effective date</strong></p>
<p>The draft amendments, dated 7 July 2026, provide that the new Personal Income Tax (PIT) relief would enter into force on 1 January 2027 and would apply when calculating and declaring income for the 2027 tax period and later years, if approved by the Seimas and promulgated by the President of the Republic.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina’s tax authority (ARCA) announced the <a href="https://servicioscf.afip.gob.ar/publico/sitio/contenido/novedad/ver.aspx?id=5817" target="_blank" rel="noopener">publication</a> of <a href="https://biblioteca.arca.gob.ar/search/query/norma.aspx?p=t:RAG%7Cn:5875%7Co:9%7Ca:2026%7Cf:13/07/2026" target="_blank" rel="noopener">General Resolution 5875/2026</a> on 14 July 2026, which allows for the regularisation of tax, customs, and social security debts that were due up to 30 June 2026, in up to 18 instalments with a financing rate of 2.75% per month.</p>
<p>The programme does not waive interest or penalties, but it facilitates debt cancellation and prevents the initiation of collection proceedings as long as the plan is fulfilled. Enrollment is done digitally through the ARCA website and will be available until 30 October 2026.</p>
<p>The goal is to facilitate voluntary compliance with tax obligations, especially for key players such as SMEs, small taxpayers and non-profit entities, which tend to have less liquidity.</p>
<p><strong>Who can join?</strong></p>
<p>The relief measures apply to Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) classified under sections 1 and 2 that hold a valid MSME Certificate and are correctly registered in the relevant registry system. Eligibility also extends to small taxpayers, including individuals and undivided estates registered under characterisation code &#8220;547 – Small Taxpayer,&#8221; as well as non-profit organisations registered with ARCA, such as associations, foundations, cooperatives, mutuals, churches, and institutes of consecrated life.</p>
<p><strong>What debts can be included?</strong></p>
<p>Eligible debts include outstanding tax and social security obligations, together with related interest and other accessories, tax withholdings and collections, debts from expired payment plans, customs liabilities related to import and export taxes and associated interest, and fines imposed up to 30 June 2026.</p>

<p><strong>Deadlines and how to join</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers may apply for the payment plan until 30 October 2026 through the &#8220;My Facilities&#8221; web service by selecting the &#8220;Special Payment Facility Regime – Obligations due as of 06/30/2026&#8221; option. The debt is consolidated on the date the down payment is made, which automatically submits the payment plan. ARCA subsequently confirms the filing through the taxpayer&#8217;s Electronic Tax Address.</p>
<p><strong>Which debts are excluded?</strong></p>
<p>Certain liabilities are excluded from the regime, including most social security withholdings and collections (except employee personal contributions), tax advances and payments on account, VAT on digital and certain cross-border services, contributions to social works (with limited exceptions), SCVO, ART, RENATRE/RENATEA, internal taxes on cigarettes, and instalments relating to existing payment plans.</p>
<p><strong>Plan expiration: What happens if it&#8217;s not paid?</strong></p>
<p>The payment plan is subject to automatic cancellation if the taxpayer fails to meet the repayment terms. Expiration occurs if two instalments, whether consecutive or non-consecutive, remain unpaid for more than 60 days after the due date of the second missed instalment, or if the final instalment remains unpaid for more than 60 days after its due date.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Germany’s Federal Council (Bundesrat) approved the amendment of the <a href="https://www.bundesrat.de/SharedDocs/drucksachen/2026/0201-0300/291-26.pdf?__blob=publicationFile&amp;v=1" target="_blank" rel="noopener">regulation</a> on the application of the minimum taxation law (Mindeststeuer-Bericht-Verordnung – MinStBV) on 10 July 2026.</p>
<p>The measure expands the framework under the Minimum Tax Act (MinStG) by identifying jurisdictions that have implemented qualified minimum tax rules, while retaining provisions governing the automatic exchange of minimum tax reporting information with other EU member states.</p>
<p><strong>Renaming and expanded scope</strong></p>
<p>The ordinance renames the Minimum Tax Reporting Ordinance (Mindeststeuer-Bericht-Verordnung – MinStBV) as the Minimum Tax implementation Ordinance.</p>
<p>A key change is the formal designation of tax jurisdictions that have implemented qualified domestic top-up tax rules, primary tax rules, or secondary tax rules as defined under the Minimum Tax Act (MinStG). The amendment also introduces editorial revisions and restructures the regulation to reflect its expanded scope.</p>
<p><strong>Four-part structure</strong></p>
<p>The MinStDV is organised into four sections:</p>
<ul>
<li>Section 1: Scope and definitions.</li>
<li>Section 2: Scope, design and information exchange of minimum tax reports.</li>
<li>Section 3: Designation of specific tax jurisdictions through a detailed Annex (Anlage).</li>
<li>Section 4: Application rules.</li>
</ul>
<p>The ordinance continues to regulate the automatic exchange of information relating to minimum tax reporting obligations with other EU member states.</p>
<p><strong>Compliance impact</strong></p>
<p>The Federal Ministry of Finance said the ordinance does not impose additional compliance costs on citizens, businesses, including small and medium-sized enterprises, or the public administration.</p>
<p>According to the ministry, all fulfilment costs had already been taken into account under the legislation implementing the EU Global Minimum Taxation Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2523). The measure also supports the German Sustainable Development Strategy by helping to secure state tax revenue.</p>
<p><strong>Effective date</strong></p>
<p>The provisions of the Minimum Tax Implementation Ordinance (MinStDV) apply to fiscal years beginning after 30 December 2023. It will enter into force after its publication in the Official Gazette.</p>
