<li>to taxes levied other than on the basis of a taxable year for taxes levied on or after 1 January 2027.</li>
</ul>
<p>In the Kyrgyz Republic, the treaty will apply:</p>
<ul>
<li>to taxes withheld at source on amounts paid on or after 1 January 2026; and</li>
<li>to other taxes for taxable years beginning on or after 1 January 2027.</li>
</ul>
<p>The treaty&#8217;s exchange of information provisions will take effect from 26 July 2026, regardless of when the relevant taxes are levied or the taxable year to which they relate.</p>
<p>The agreement also confirms that it will not affect the existing Convention between the Government of Japan and the Government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics for the Avoidance of Double Taxation with respect to Taxes on Income, which will continue to apply between Japan and the countries other than the Kyrgyz Republic.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/japan-kyrgyzstan-sign-new-income-tax-treaty/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, Japan and Kyrgyzstan signed a new tax treaty on 19 December 2025 to eliminate double taxation on income and strengthen measures against tax evasion and avoidance.</p>

For taxes with a tax period, the amendments apply to tax periods beginning on or after 28 June 2026.</p>
<p>The inclusion of the Russian international holding company regime will take effect six months after publication, on 28 December 2026. The same application rules will apply from that date, covering taxes without a tax period and taxes accrued from the date of entry into force, as well as tax periods beginning on or after 28 December 2026.</p>
<p>The order also includes a transitional provision under which the previous list established by Order HFP/115/2023 will continue to apply to taxes whose tax period was already in progress when the new order entered into force until the end of that tax period.</p>
<p>The Ministry of Finance stated that the revision is intended to keep Spain&#8217;s framework for identifying non-cooperative jurisdictions aligned with international developments on tax transparency and fair taxation.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) updated its guidance on the taxation of permanent establishments (PEs) on 24 June 2026, outlining when enterprises may be subject to tax in Australia or overseas under Australia&#8217;s double tax agreements (DTAs). Taxation under DTAs The guidance explains that an enterprise can be taxed in Australia even if it is...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) updated its <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/about-ato/international-tax-agreements/income-tax-treaties/permanent-establishments" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance</a> on the taxation of permanent establishments (PEs) on 24 June 2026, outlining when enterprises may be subject to tax in Australia or overseas under Australia&#8217;s double tax agreements (DTAs).</p>
<p><strong>Taxation under DTAs</strong></p>
<p>The guidance explains that an enterprise can be taxed in Australia even if it is not resident in the country. Similarly, an Australian enterprise may be taxed overseas despite not being resident in the foreign jurisdiction. In both cases, taxation arises where the enterprise carries on business through a permanent establishment, with tax applying only to the profits attributable to that permanent establishment under the relevant DTA.</p>
<p><strong>Definition of a permanent establishment</strong></p>
<p>The ATO said a permanent establishment is generally defined in Australia&#8217;s DTAs as a fixed place of business through which an enterprise carries on all or part of its business. The definition typically includes a branch, office or workshop and may also extend to the furnishing of services for specified periods.</p>
<p>The guidance also states that each place of business meeting the relevant DTA definition constitutes a separate permanent establishment.</p>
<p><strong>Attribution of profits</strong></p>
<p>Where a permanent establishment exists, the profits attributable to that PE must be calculated using certain arm&#8217;s length principles. The ATO referred taxpayers to <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?DocID=TXR/TR200111/NAT/ATO/00001&amp;PiT=99991231235958" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Taxation Ruling TR 2001/11</a> Income tax: international transfer pricing for further information on Australia&#8217;s attribution rules.</p>
<p><strong>GloBE permanent establishments</strong></p>
<p>The ATO also noted that Pillar Two top-up tax may apply to a permanent establishment where the arrangement meets the definition of a Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) permanent establishment.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The South African Revenue Service (SARS) has published a statement welcoming the unanimous Constitutional Court judgment in Lueven Metals (Pty) Ltd v Commissioner for the South African Revenue Service, delivered on 23 June 2026, which confirms SARS&#8217; interpretation of section 11(1)(f) of the Value-Added Tax Act, 1991. SARS Commissioner Dr Johnstone Makhubu welcomed the ruling,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The South African Revenue Service (SARS) has published a <a href="https://www.sars.gov.za/latest-news/media-release-sars-commissioner-welcomes-constitutional-court-judgement-on-zero-rating-of-gold/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">statement </a>welcoming the unanimous Constitutional <a href="https://www.sars.gov.za/wp-content/uploads/Legal/Judgments/CC/Legal-DRJ-CC-2026-02-%E2%80%93-Lueven-Metals-Ltd-v-CSARS-CCT-320-23-2026-ZACC-24-23-June-2026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Court judgment</a> in Lueven Metals (Pty) Ltd v Commissioner for the South African Revenue Service, delivered on 23 June 2026, which confirms SARS&#8217; interpretation of section 11(1)(f) of the Value-Added Tax Act, 1991.</p>
<p>SARS Commissioner Dr Johnstone Makhubu welcomed the ruling, which concerns the VAT zero-rating of gold.</p>
<p>The judgment clarifies that the zero-rating of gold supplied to the South African Reserve Bank, the South African Mint Company (Proprietary) Limited, or a registered bank applies only where the gold is supplied in one of the prescribed forms and has not undergone any manufacturing process other than refining or the manufacture or production of those prescribed forms.</p>
<p>The court confirmed that the zero-rating of gold under section 11(1)(f) does not apply to second-hand or recycled gold that has already undergone prior manufacturing. This ruling provides clear legal guidance, puts an end to aggressive VAT interpretations, and reinforces SARS’ commitment to enforcing tax law in a principled manner. This judgement aims to protect the tax base and safeguard revenue for the benefit of all South Africans.</p>
<p>SARS Commissioner Dr Johnstone Makhubu said: “This judgment reaffirms a foundational principle of our constitutional democracy: that legislation must be applied as written, consistently, and fairly. The Constitutional Court has provided unequivocal clarity, and that certainty benefits vendors, financial institutions, the precious metal industry regarding the VAT treatment of gold supplied under section 11(1)(f).”</p>
<p>The matter arose from a dispute concerning the VAT treatment of refined gold supplied to prescribed purchasers such as registered banks. Lueven Metals, a buyer and refiner of second-hand gold, treated its sales of refined gold bars to a commercial bank as zero-rated, despite the gold originating from previously manufactured sources, such as scrap jewellery. Following an audit, SARS determined that these supplies did not qualify for zero-rating under the VAT Act. The High Court upheld SARS’ interpretation, and the Constitutional Court has now conclusively confirmed that position, dismissing the appeal with costs.</p>
<p>In its unanimous judgment, the Constitutional Court held that section 11(1)(f) sets out three cumulative requirements for zero rating: the supply must be to a prescribed purchaser; the gold must be supplied in one of the prescribed forms; and critically, the gold must not have undergone any manufacturing process other than refining or manufacturing into those prescribed forms. Gold that has previously been manufactured into non prescribed forms, such as jewellery or other fabricated items, falls outside the scope of the zero rating.</p>
<p>The Court found that SARS’ interpretation gives proper meaning to the statutory text and avoids rendering key provisions redundant.</p>
<p>The Court was clear in its reasoning, stating: “While refining does eradicate the recycled gold’s previous form, it does not alter the fact that such gold previously underwent a disqualifying manufacturing process. Thus, on a purely textual reading, Lueven’s supply of recycled gold cannot benefit from zero-rating.”</p>
<p>Commissioner Makhubu states that this judgment provides long-awaited clarity for gold, refining, and banking sectors by confirming that recycled or second-hand gold remains subject to VAT at the standard rate, supporting compliant businesses and fair competition.</p>
<p>“Voluntary compliance is built on trust, and trust depends on certainty. This ruling removes ambiguity as it reinforces that when taxpayers know precisely where the law stands, they can comply with confidence,” said Commissioner Makhubu, adding that the judgment also aligns directly with SARS’ strategic intent of promoting voluntary compliance. This also helps to protect the tax base while ensuring that all revenue due to the State is collected.</p>
<p>“Fair tax administration means that no taxpayer gains an unintended advantage at the expense of others. This outcome ensures that compliant businesses are not undercut by aggressive practices that erode fairness and distort competition. As SARS, we have a constitutional and statutory responsibility to protect the revenue base for the benefit of all South Africans. Every rand improperly lost through misinterpretation or non-compliance is a rand unavailable for schools, healthcare, infrastructure and social protection.&#8221;</p>
<p>Commissioner Makhubu reiterated that SARS will continue to use all lawful tools available to it to promote compliance. “SARS respect the right of taxpayers to exercise their constitutionally enshrined right to litigate where they feel aggrieved. It is also equally important that the litigation route be followed by allowing the parties to a dispute to find clarity and certainty from the Court in areas where there are interpretive challenges, and this judgment represents such an opportunity.”</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Luxembourg Administration of Direct Tax (ACD) issued a <a href="https://impotsdirects.public.lu/fr/archive/newsletter/2026/nl26062026.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">statement</a> on 26 June 2026 concerning the <a href="https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/news/pillar-2-global-minimum-tax-directive-new-faq-available-2026-05-29_en" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)</a> published by the European Commission on 29 May 2026. The FAQ clarifies that, under the EU Pillar Two Directive, all EU Member States must treat Cyprus as having a qualified Income Inclusion Rule (IIR), even though it does not yet appear on the OECD Central Record of legislation granted transitional qualified status or the OECD document Global Minimum Tax: Support for Central GloBE Information Return Filing and Exchange (2024 Reporting Fiscal Year).</p>

<p>The Income Inclusion Rules implemented by Cyprus do not currently appear on the OECD Central Record of legislation granted transitional qualified status or on the OECD document Global Minimum Tax: Support for Central GloBE Information Return Filing and Exchange (2024 Reporting Fiscal Year). In light of this, how should those rules be treated within the EU for fiscal years for which filing is due before Cyprus appears on the OECD Central Record of legislation?</p>
<p><strong>Answer:</strong></p>
<p>For the purposes of and in accordance with the Pillar Two Directive, the qualified status of the Cypriot IIR is directly derived from Article 3(18) of the Directive for fiscal years commencing on or after 31 December 2023. Accordingly, all EU Member States should treat Cyprus as having a qualified IIR in effect. Cyprus has been able to receive top-up tax information returns since 31 May 2026 and is committed and required under EU law to exchange the information with other Member States under DAC9 in time for the first exchange deadline. If an MNE opts to file its top-up tax information return centrally in Cyprus, other Member States should not require a separate domestic filing in line with DAC9.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/business-bulletins-newsroom/private-capital-program-new-guidance" target="_blank" rel="noopener">issued </a>new guidance under its Private Capital Program on 26 June 2026, outlining security arrangements and evidentiary requirements for fiscally transparent entities to support compliance by large multinational enterprises and private equity groups, including in relation to treaty benefit claims.</p>
<p><strong>Private capital program</strong></p>
<p>The ATO&#8217;s <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/private-capital-program/about-the-private-capital-program" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Private Capital Program</a> continues to focus on ensuring large multinational and private equity groups pay the right amount of tax in Australia.</p>
<p>The ATO is seeing increasing complexity in private capital structures, from acquisition through to disposal. The most effective way for taxpayers to avoid disputes and ensure smooth transaction execution is to engage with the ATO early to address risks before they crystallise, particularly in high-value or cross-border transactions.</p>
<p>The ATO has now published web content outlining its approach to <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/private-capital-program/pre-disposal-security-arrangements" target="_blank" rel="noopener">security arrangements</a> and evidentiary expectations for <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/private-capital-program/fiscally-transparent-entities-and-tax-treaty-residency-claims" target="_blank" rel="noopener">fiscally transparent entities</a> to ensure Australian tax liabilities are appropriately safeguarded.</p>
<p><strong>Expectations for fiscally transparent entities</strong></p>
<p>Where treaty benefits are claimed through fiscally transparent entities, the ATO expects robust, primary evidence supporting the residency of ultimate investors.</p>
<p>Strong documentation upfront reduces uncertainty and supports timely outcomes.</p>
<p>The ATO encourages taxpayers to engage with it well ahead of transactions or exits to resolve issues and provide certainty. The ATO&#8217;s aim is not to impede commercial activity, but to provide clarity, manage risks and support compliant investment into Australia.</p>
<p>When taxpayers come to the ATO early with quality information, the ATO can help facilitate smoother transactions and more predictable outcomes.</p>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=84122</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has issued a Basic Tax Information Bulletin – Corporate Tax Losses  on 25 June 2026, providing guidance on the treatment of Corporate Tax Losses under the Corporate Tax Law. The bulletin explains the definition of a Tax Loss, the available relief mechanisms, and the conditions and restrictions governing the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has issued a <a href="https://tax.gov.ae//Datafolder/Files/Pdf/2026/CT-Tax-Bulletin-Corporate-Tax-Losses-EN.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Basic Tax Information Bulletin – Corporate Tax Losses  on 25 June 2026</a>, providing guidance on the treatment of Corporate Tax Losses under the Corporate Tax Law. The bulletin explains the definition of a Tax Loss, the available relief mechanisms, and the conditions and restrictions governing the use and transfer of losses.</p>
<p>The guidance is presented in a question-and-answer format covering the following key topics:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong> Who should read this information bulletin?</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>Anyone who is responsible for the tax affairs of a Taxable Person who wants to understand:</p>
<ul>
<li>What is a Tax Loss?</li>
<li>What is not a Tax Loss?</li>
<li>What relief is available for Tax Losses?</li>
<li>How does relief for carried forward Tax Losses work?</li>
<li>What are the limitations on the carry forward of Tax Losses?</li>
<li>Under what circumstances are Tax Losses forfeited?</li>
<li>What are the conditions for the transfer of Tax Losses and what is available for transfer?</li>
<li>What is the impact of electing for Small Business Relief (SBR)?</li>
</ul>
<ol start="2">
<li><strong> What is a Tax Loss?</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>For Corporate Tax purposes, a Tax Loss arises when deductible expenses exceed income that is subject to Corporate Tax in a given Tax Period. It is effectively negative Taxable Income, calculated by adjusting Accounting Income according to the Corporate Tax Law.</p>
<ol start="3">
<li><strong> What is not a tax loss?</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>The following are not considered Tax Losses and cannot be used to offset Taxable Income:</p>
<ul>
<li>Losses incurred before Corporate Tax came into effect on 1 June 2023.</li>
<li>Losses incurred before a person became a Taxable Person under the Corporate Tax Law.</li>
<li>Losses from activities that do not result in Taxable Income (e.g., those related to Exempt Income).</li>
</ul>
<ol start="4">
<li><strong> What relief is available for tax losses?</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>A Taxable Person has two primary relief options:</p>
<ol>
<li>Carry forward Tax Losses to offset against their own future Taxable Income.</li>
<li>Transfer Tax Losses to another Taxable Person to offset against that person&#8217;s Taxable Income.</li>
</ol>
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<ol start="5">
<li><strong> How does relief for carried forward Tax Losses work?</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>A Taxable Person can carry forward their own Tax Losses indefinitely into future periods. Key utilization rules include:</p>
<ul>
<li>75% Limit: The total Tax Losses offset in a subsequent period is limited to 75% of the Taxable Income for that period (before any loss relief).</li>
<li>FIFO Basis: The oldest Tax Losses must be offset before more recent ones.</li>
<li>Fullest Extent Rule: A Taxable Person must utilise carried forward losses to the maximum extent allowed (the 75% limit) before carrying any remainder forward; they cannot choose to offset a lower amount to save losses for later.</li>
<li>Priority: A Taxable Person must use their own carried forward losses before using losses transferred from another person. Similarly, they must fully utilise their own losses before they are permitted to transfer any remaining losses to another person.</li>
</ul>
<ol start="6">
<li><strong> What are the limitations on the carry forward of Tax Losses?</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>Carry forward is restricted if there is a change in ownership of more than 50%. This occurs if the ownership interests (direct or indirect) at the end of the utilisation period differ by more than 50% from those at the start of the period when the loss arose.</p>
<ul>
<li>Continuity of Business: If ownership changes by more than 50%, losses can only be carried forward if the Taxable Person continues the same or a similar Business or Business Activity.</li>
<li>Factors for Continuity: Evaluation factors include using the same assets, maintaining core identity/operations, and ensuring changes result from developing existing assets or products.</li>
<li>Listed Exception: These limitations do not apply if the Taxable Person’s shares are listed on a Recognised Stock Exchange.</li>
</ul>
<ol start="7">
<li><strong> Under what circumstances are Tax Losses forfeited?</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>Tax Losses are forfeited in various circumstances, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>When a Taxable Person changes its Business or Business Activity following a change in ownership of more than 50%.</li>
<li>When a Taxable Person deregisters for Corporate Tax.</li>
</ul>
<ol start="8">
<li><strong> What are the conditions for the transfer of Tax Losses?</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>The following conditions must be met to transfer losses between Taxable Persons:</p>
<table>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>No.</td>
<td>Condition</td>
<td>Explanation</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>1</td>
<td>Juridical person</td>
<td>Both must be juridical persons (e.g., LLCs); losses cannot be transferred to or from a natural person.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2</td>
<td>Resident Person</td>
<td>Both must be Resident Persons; transfer to/from a Non-Resident (including UAE branches of foreign companies) is not possible.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3</td>
<td>75% ownership</td>
<td>One must own at least 75% of the other, or a third person must own at least 75% of each. This must be maintained from the start of the loss period to the end of the offset period.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>4</td>
<td>Not Exempt</td>
<td>Neither person can be an Exempt Person.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>5</td>
<td>Not a QFZP</td>
<td>Neither person can be a Qualifying Free Zone Person.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>6</td>
<td>Financial Year</td>
<td>Both must have Financial Years ending on the same date.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>7</td>
<td>Accounting Standard</td>
<td>Both must use the same accounting standards (e.g., both IFRS).</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>What is available for transfer? Taxable Persons can transfer unused Tax Losses from the current period or those carried forward from previous periods. The parties choose the amount to transfer, but the total offset (own losses + transferred losses) cannot exceed 75% of the recipient&#8217;s Taxable Income.</p>
<ol start="9">
<li><strong> What is the impact of electing for Small Business Relief (SBR)?</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>When a Resident Person elects for SBR:</p>
<ul>
<li>No new Tax Losses can arise in that period.</li>
<li>Existing losses carried forward from non-SBR periods cannot be utilized or transferred during the SBR period.</li>
<li>These losses can still be carried forward and used or transferred in future periods when SBR no longer applies.</li>
</ul>
<ol start="10">
<li><strong> Further information</strong></li>
</ol>
<p>For more details, refer to the Corporate Tax guides and public clarifications on the Federal Tax Authority (FTA) website. Relevant provisions are also found in Articles 37, 38, and 39 of the Corporate Tax Law.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<pubDate>Mon, 29 Jun 2026 10:21:15 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Pillar Two-Global Minimum Tax (GMT)]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[The Slovak Republic’s Ministry of Finance has launched a consultation on the Draft Law No. LP/2026/369 amending Act No. 507/2023 Coll., on 25 June 2026, which implemented the EU Minimum Taxation Directive. The proposed amendments aim to incorporate adjustments arising from the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework’s Side-by-Side Package on global minimum tax rules, confirmed by the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Slovak Republic’s Ministry of Finance has launched a consultation on the <a href="https://www.slov-lex.sk/elegislativa/legislativne-procesy/SK/LP/2026/369" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Draft Law No. LP/2026/369</a> amending <a href="https://static.slov-lex.sk/pdf/SK/ZZ/2023/507/ZZ_2023_507_20251231.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Act No. 507/2023 Coll.</a>, on 25 June 2026, which implemented the EU Minimum Taxation Directive. The proposed amendments aim to incorporate adjustments arising from the <a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-sub-issues/global-minimum-tax/side-by-side-package.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework’s Side-by-Side Package</a> on global minimum tax rules, confirmed by the European Commission on 12 January 2026.</p>
<p>The OECD <a href="https://regfollower.com/oecd-presents-side-by-side-pillar-2-deal-as-a-stabilising-compromise-for-the-global-minimum-tax-critics-argue-it-does-the-opposite/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced </a>on 5 January 2026 that the 147 members of the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS agreed on key elements of a side-by-side arrangement, including two safe harbours for multinational enterprise groups headquartered in jurisdictions with eligible tax regimes.</p>
<p>Act No. 507/2023 regarding a top-up tax designed to ensure a minimum level of taxation for large multinational and domestic groups. This legislation establishes a 15% minimum tax rate to align with global standards, targeting corporate entities with annual revenues exceeding EUR 750 million.</p>
<p>The Act also specifies methods for determining adjusted covered taxes and the proper allocation of income between parent companies and their subsidiaries. This legal framework serves as the basis for implementing qualified domestic minimum top-up tax rules within Slovakia.</p>
<p>The key details of the amending Act No. 507/2023 Coll. are as follows:</p>
<p><strong>Additional time for simplified reporting (&#8220;Safe Harbour&#8221; extension)</strong></p>
<p>The current law gives companies a temporary &#8220;grace period&#8221; (a safe harbour) where they can use simplified country-by-country reports to avoid doing highly complex top-up tax calculations. Currently, this break is set to expire for accounting periods starting after 31 December 2026.   The draft law extends this grace period by one year. It also confirms that a special transitional tax rate of 17%, which is already written into the law for the year 2026, will continue to apply during this extended period.</p>
<p><strong>Protecting real local investments (Economic substance)</strong></p>
<p>The existing law already lowers a company&#8217;s minimum tax burden if they have a real physical presence in Slovakia—specifically, by looking at how much they spend on local employee payroll and physical assets like buildings, machines, and equipment. The proposed update introduces a new, specific exemption to protect local tax incentives that are tied to this genuine business activity. It ensures that when Slovakia gives a company a tax break for creating real jobs and building infrastructure, the global minimum tax doesn&#8217;t accidentally cancel that benefit out.</p>
<p><strong>Closing a loophole for shut-down companies</strong></p>
<p>The current law defines exactly who is considered a taxpayer and how the tax is administered. However, it lacks a specific rule for what happens to a company&#8217;s tax bill if the business simply ceases to exist without leaving a legal successor behind. The new update creates a clear rule to seamlessly transfer the closed company&#8217;s tax obligations to another entity. This ensures that the responsibility to pay any owed minimum tax doesn&#8217;t just disappear when a company closes its doors.</p>
<p>The proposed amendments are expected to take effect on 31 December 2026, with the exception of the extension of the CbCR safe harbour, which is scheduled to apply from 30 December 2026.</p>
<p>The consultation on Draft Law No. LP/2026/369 runs until 15 July 2026, after which the law must pass parliamentary approval and presidential signature before entering into force.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[Austria&#8217;s Federal Council (Bundesrat) approved the Budget Measure Act 2026 on 25 June 2026, adopting a package of amendments to various tax laws aimed at promoting tax fairness, combating tax fraud, reducing the tax burden on workers and simplifying administrative procedures. Income tax changes The Act introduces a tax-free Mitarbeiterprämie 2026 (Employee Bonus) of up...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Austria&#8217;s Federal Council (Bundesrat) approved the <a href="https://www.parlament.gv.at/dokument/XXVIII/I/504/fname_1758248.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Budget Measure Act 2026 on 25 June 2026</a>, adopting a package of amendments to various tax laws aimed at promoting tax fairness, combating tax fraud, reducing the tax burden on workers and simplifying administrative procedures.</p>
<p><strong>Income tax changes</strong></p>
<p>The Act introduces a tax-free Mitarbeiterprämie 2026 (Employee Bonus) of up toEUR 500 per employee for payments made between July and December 2026. The bonus must be granted under specified wage-forming regulations, such as collective agreements, and must represent an additional payment not previously provided.</p>
<p>Where an employee also receives a profit-sharing bonus under § 3 Abs. 1 Z 35, the combined tax-exempt amount for both payments cannot exceed EUR 3,000 per year.</p>
<p>The legislation also sets the monthly tax-free limit for dirt, hardship and danger allowances, together with Sunday, holiday and night work supplements, at EUR 400 for wage payment periods ending after 31 December 2025.</p>
<p>New reporting obligations are introduced for deferred exit taxation. Taxpayers with deferred tax liabilities arising from the relocation of assets or derivatives must submit annual written confirmation through FinanzOnline that no taxable event has occurred where the related income exceeds EUR 100,000 in a calendar year. A transitional rule requires taxpayers with deferred tax debts exceeding EUR 100,000 established after 2005 and not yet fully assessed to submit the required confirmation by 31 December 2026.</p>
<p><strong>VAT and administrative measures</strong></p>
<p>From 1 July 2026, buyers will no longer be required to submit a separate VAT registration where a professional representative calculates and pays the tax under the NoVAG (Standard Consumption Tax Act).</p>
<p>The Act also introduces new administrative fees for residence cards issued under the Asylum Act 2005. In addition, reimbursement for employee travel costs will be linked to the actual cost of a nationwide annual public transport pass (Klimaticket), replacing the previous fixed monetary limit.</p>
<p><strong>Anti-fraud and enforcement</strong></p>
<p>To strengthen tax enforcement, the Office for Combating Fraud will gain access to the account register to identify suspected shell companies, subject to approval by the Federal Tax Court. Authorities investigating intentional financial offences will also receive broader powers to obtain information from telecommunications and digital service providers.</p>
<p><strong>Price marking rules</strong></p>
<p>The legislation amends the Price Marking Act by allowing tourism levies to be displayed separately or included in the gross price. It also increases penalties for breaches of price marking requirements, with repeat offences carrying fines of up to EUR 15,000.</p>
<p>The Budget Measure Act 2026 will enter into force after its publication in the Official Gazette.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Vietnam&#8217;s Tax Department issued <a href="https://www.gdt.gov.vn/wps/wcm/connect/0d406ab0-43c7-4b19-9fe9-070fb76b4c30/3896_CT-CS.pdf?MOD=AJPERES&amp;CACHEID=ROOTWORKSPACE0d406ab0-43c7-4b19-9fe9-070fb76b4c30" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Official Letter 3896/CT-CS</a>, confirming that eligible foreign-invested small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) can benefit from a three-year corporate income tax (CIT) exemption under the country&#8217;s new private sector incentive regime.</p>
<p>The clarification confirms that foreign ownership does not prevent access to the incentive, provided the enterprise satisfies the statutory eligibility criteria set out in Resolution 198/2025/QH15 and Decree 20/2026/ND-CP.</p>
<p><strong>Eligibility for CIT exemption</strong></p>
<p>Under the guidance, qualifying foreign-invested SMEs are entitled to a corporate income tax exemption for three years starting from the date of first issuance of the Enterprise Registration Certificate (ERC). The exemption period is applied continuously from the first year the ERC is issued.</p>
<p>The Tax Department confirmed that foreign ownership alone does not disqualify an enterprise from the incentive, provided all statutory conditions are satisfied.</p>
<p>Enterprises that were issued an ERC before Resolution 198/2025/QH15 took effect may continue to enjoy any remaining incentive period in accordance with the applicable rules.</p>
<p><strong>Exclusions from the incentive</strong></p>
<p>The three-year CIT exemption does not apply to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Newly established enterprises formed through merger, consolidation, division, separation, change of ownership, or conversion of enterprise type</li>
<li>Enterprises where the legal representative, general partner, or largest capital contributor has previously held similar roles in an operating enterprise or in an enterprise dissolved for less than 12 months prior to establishment</li>
<li>Income specified in Clause 3, Article 18 of the Law on Corporate Income Tax No. 67/2025/QH15</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>SME classification criteria</strong></p>
<p>Under Article 4 of the Law on Support for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises No. 04/2017/QH14, SMEs include micro, small and medium-sized enterprises with:</p>
<ul>
<li>An average annual number of employees participating in social insurance not exceeding 200 persons; and</li>
<li>Either total capital not exceeding VND 100 billion, or total revenue of the preceding year not exceeding VND 300 billion.</li>
</ul>
<p>Enterprises are classified by sector, covering agriculture, forestry and fisheries; industry and construction; and trade and services.</p>
<p><strong>Conditions for eligibility</strong></p>
<p>To qualify for the incentive, an enterprise must:</p>
<ul>
<li>Be established and registered under Vietnamese law;</li>
<li>Have received its first Enterprise Registration Certificate;</li>
<li>Meet SME criteria under Law 04/2017/QH14 and Decree 80/2021/ND-CP; and</li>
<li>Not fall within the exclusion cases specified under Article 7(3)(b) of Decree 20/2026/ND-CP.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Implementation guidance</strong></p>
<p>Official Letter 3896/CT-CS is intended to guide tax authorities in implementing the CIT exemption framework introduced under Vietnam’s private sector development policies. It aims to ensure consistent application of incentives for eligible foreign-invested SMEs across the tax administration system.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Swedish government has submitted a <a href="https://www.regeringen.se/rattsliga-dokument/lagradsremiss/2026/06/utvidgad-avdragsratt-for-sponsring-och-liknande-atgarder/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">bill</a> to the Council on Legislation proposing to expand the corporate income tax deduction for sponsorship and similar expenses, with the aim of making the tax treatment of such costs clearer and more favourable.</p>
<p>The proposal would allow companies to deduct certain commercially motivated expenses incurred to improve or maintain the reputation of their business activities, even where no direct benefit is received in return.</p>
<p>Under the proposed new provision in the Income Tax Act, the extended deduction would apply in addition to the existing general deduction rules. <p>To qualify, the activity must be communicated externally to a relevant target group, and companies must demonstrate that the expense forms part of their brand-building or long-term business strategy rather than proving an immediate increase in sales.</p>
<p>The government said the proposal reflects the growing importance of strong brands and business reputation for long-term profitability and competitiveness. It also expects the changes to encourage greater support for civil society by improving the tax treatment of sponsorship involving sports, culture, social sustainability projects and other socially beneficial activities.</p>
<p>The proposal also clarifies that expenses meeting the new reputation-based criteria should not be treated as non-deductible gifts under existing tax rules.</p>
<p>The expanded deduction would not apply to expenses relating to representation or similar purposes, political activities or religious activities, which remain outside the scope of the proposal.</p>
<p>The new rules are scheduled to enter into force on 1 January 2027 and will apply to tax years beginning after 31 December 2026. The government estimates the measure will reduce annual tax revenue by approximately SEK 530 million from 2027.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Danish government has reintroduced a series of tax measures that were originally included in the 2026 Finance Act but lapsed when the election was called. The proposals, which fall under the Ministry of Taxation and Growth, are intended to increase disposable income, encourage labour market participation and simplify parts of the tax system.</p>
<p>If approved, several of the measures will apply from the 2026 income year, while others are scheduled to take effect from 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Senior tax relief</strong></p>
<p>One of the main proposals is the expansion of the additional employment tax credit for seniors. Under the plan, eligible workers in the final five years before reaching the state pension age would receive annual tax relief of up to DKK 9,500.</p>
<p>The government said the measure is designed to encourage older workers to remain in employment for longer before retirement. The expanded employment tax credit is expected to apply from the 2026 income year.</p>
<p><strong>VAT and indirect tax changes</strong></p>
<p>The government has also reintroduced legislation to abolish VAT on books and eliminate the coffee tax. Both measures are expected to come into force from 2027, subject to parliamentary approval.</p>
<p>At the same time, the government has withdrawn its previous proposal to abolish the tax on chocolate and sugar confectionery. Instead, revenue from the tax will be retained to support future plans, including proposals to reduce VAT on food and remove VAT entirely on fruit and vegetables.</p>
<p><strong>New tax deductions and family measures</strong></p>
<p>The legislative package also revives the proposed exercise tax deduction, which is intended to compensate individuals participating in sports and exercise activities following EU court judgments requiring VAT to be applied to services such as group fitness classes.</p>
<p>In addition, the government plans to increase the standard deduction for childminders from the 2026 income year.</p>
<p>Other measures being reintroduced include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Equal treatment of siblings&#8217; children with immediate family for inheritance tax purposes.</li>
<li>An increase in compensation for volunteers.</li>
<li>A tax deduction for exercise and music lessons.</li>
<li>A tax deduction for salary expenses relating to software development from 2025.</li>
<li>More flexible rules for the payment of registration duty in connection with the registration of the electricity grid and related infrastructure.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Legislative programme</strong></p>
<p>The government said the reintroduced measures will be included in its updated legislative programme. Their implementation will depend on the adoption of the relevant bills by Parliament, with most income tax measures targeted for the 2026 income year and indirect tax changes, including the abolition of VAT on books and the coffee tax, expected to take effect from 2027.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The OECD has published a revised version of the common understanding on Pillar Two GloBE Information Return (GIR) filing on 25 June 2026. The first version of the common understanding on Pillar Two GIR filing was released on 18 May 2026, titled, Global Minimum Tax: Support for Central GloBE Information Return Filing and Exchange (2024...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD has published a revised version of the common understanding on Pillar Two GloBE Information Return (GIR) filing on 25 June 2026.</p>
<p>The first version of the common understanding on Pillar Two GIR filing was <a href="https://regfollower.com/oecd-issues-new-guidance-on-pillar-two-global-minimum-tax-compliance/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">released</a> on 18 May 2026, titled, <a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-sub-issues/global-minimum-tax/support-for-central-gir-filing-and-exchange-2024-reporting-fiscal-year.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Global Minimum Tax: Support for Central GloBE Information Return Filing and Exchange (2024 Reporting Fiscal Year)</a>.</p>
<p>The common understanding stipulates that jurisdictions implementing the Global Minimum Tax from 2024 have agreed to waive penalties or defer enforcement of local GIR filing obligations, provided that the GIR has been centrally filed in a jurisdiction included in the published list by the relevant filing deadline and that a GIR notification has been submitted in the local jurisdiction within the applicable timeframe.</p>
<p>A “common understanding” has been agreed among jurisdictions implementing Pillar Two and published by the OECD to facilitate the central filing of 2024 year-end GIRs.</p>
<p>The agreement includes an annex identifying 33 jurisdictions expected to have fully operational GIR portals available for central filing by 31 May 2026, including Australia, Austria, Barbados, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Gibraltar, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Korea, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, and the UK.</p>
<p>The common understanding provides that implementing jurisdictions will waive penalties and refrain from enforcing local GloBE Information Return (GIR) filing requirements, provided that the GIR is submitted by the applicable deadline in a jurisdiction included in the annex, notification of the filing is submitted, and the GIR is exchanged by the required deadline (31 December 2026 for the first year).</p>
<p>In some cases, such as Poland, this relief applies only to GIR filings made in other EU Member States. The updated version also confirms the inclusion of the Bahamas and Greece, while the Slovak Republic has joined the arrangement for all jurisdictions listed in the annex, except those without an active exchange relationship with the Slovak Republic.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

It will focus on key outcomes such as effective tax rates, profit shifting and tax revenues, and will also highlight preliminary analysis based on post-implementation data, offering early insights into how the GMT is impacting MNEs’ effective tax rates and investment and employment decisions.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies <a href="https://www.diputados.gov.ar/prensa/noticia/DIPUTADOS-LE-DIO-MEDIA-SANCION-AL-SUPER-RIGI-QUE-INCENTIVA-GRANDES-INVERSIONES-EN-NUEVAS-INDUSTRIAS/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved</a> a new incentive framework for large-scale investments in emerging industries, known as the Super RIGI, on 24 June 2026.</p>
<p>The newly proposed &#8220;Super RIGI&#8221; scheme was established to offer incentives and regulatory certainty for investment projects focused exclusively on developing new economic activities.</p>
<p>The Super RIGI scheme is an expanded version of President Milei&#8217;s original 2024 incentive program, aimed at attracting large-scale investment in sectors like critical mineral processing, biotechnology, battery manufacturing, renewable energy (including green hydrogen, EVs, wind, and solar), small modular nuclear reactors, semiconductors, and AI.</p>
<p>Unlike the original framework, which had a USD 200 million investment threshold, the new version requires a minimum of USD 1 billion and excludes natural resource extraction, infrastructure projects, and expansions of existing ventures—making it a more narrowly targeted regime.</p>
<p>Qualifying projects will still receive 30 years of fiscal, customs, and foreign exchange stability, and the scheme itself will stay open for five years (with potential extension), compared to the original&#8217;s two-plus-one-year run.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Portugal&#8217;s Council of Ministers has approved an amendment to the General Tax Law to replace the country&#8217;s existing <a href="https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/legislacao-consolidada/portaria/2004-105808897" target="_blank" rel="noopener">list </a>of countries, territories and regions with privileged tax regimes with the EU list of non-cooperative jurisdictions, aligning its blacklist with the European Union&#8217;s framework.</p>
<p>The amendment will reduce the number of jurisdictions subject to Portugal&#8217;s anti-abuse tax measures, from 77 under the current national list to 10 under the<a href="https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/eu-list-of-non-cooperative-jurisdictions/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> EU list</a>. Under the existing rules, jurisdictions on Portugal&#8217;s blacklist are subject to a range of tax consequences, including a 35% withholding tax on dividends, interest and royalties, as well as ineligibility for Portugal&#8217;s participation exemption.</p>
<p>Portugal&#8217;s blacklist was established under Ministerial Order (Portaria) No. 150/2004 as a measure to combat international tax evasion and fraud. The list applies across several tax regimes, including IRS (Personal Income Tax), IRC (Corporate Income Tax), Stamp Duty, IMI and IMT, and has been updated periodically through subsequent amendments.</p>
<p>The government has not yet announced when the revised framework will take effect or how the transition will be implemented. Further details are expected to be published once the implementing measures are finalised.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The OECD has announced that Kuwait signed the Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement on the Exchange of Country-by-Country Reports (CbC MCAA) on 22 June 2026, further expanding the international framework for the automatic exchange of Country-by-Country (CbC) reports. With Kuwait&#8217;s accession, the number of signatories to the agreement has reached 116 countries and jurisdictions, reflecting continued...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD has <a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-issues/tax-transparency-and-international-co-operation/cbc-mcaa-signatories.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> that Kuwait signed the Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement on the Exchange of Country-by-Country Reports (CbC MCAA) on 22 June 2026, further expanding the international framework for the automatic exchange of Country-by-Country (CbC) reports.</p>
<p>With Kuwait&#8217;s accession, the number of signatories to the agreement has reached 116 countries and jurisdictions, reflecting continued global participation in the OECD&#8217;s tax transparency initiative.</p>
<p>The CbC MCAA provides the legal framework for tax authorities to automatically exchange CbC reports filed by multinational enterprise groups. The exchange of these reports is intended to support tax administrations in assessing transfer pricing and other base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS) risks.</p>
<p>According to the OECD&#8217;s updated list of participants, the agreement has steadily expanded since its launch in January 2016. Initial signatories included major economies such as Australia, France, Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States&#8217; treaty partners, with additional countries and jurisdictions joining over the following decade.</p>
<p>Recent additions before Kuwait included Benin (6 January 2026), Fiji (22 April 2026), Serbia (4 March 2025), Mongolia (6 March 2025), Viet Nam (3 January 2025), Botswana (9 April 2025) and Cabo Verde (9 April 2025).</p>
<p>The current list of 116 signatories spans all regions and includes major economies as well as smaller jurisdictions such as the Cayman Islands, Bermuda, Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man. The OECD maintains the official register of signatories together with their respective signing dates.</p>

		<title>UK announces reforms to simplify tax system, strengthen customs enforcement</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/uk-announces-reforms-to-simplify-tax-system-strengthen-customs-enforcement/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=uk-announces-reforms-to-simplify-tax-system-strengthen-customs-enforcement</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Abdur Rouf]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Fri, 26 Jun 2026 11:56:40 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Policy announcements by government]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Europe]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[UK]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=84079</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The UK government has unveiled a broad package of tax and customs reforms aimed at simplifying compliance, expanding digital services and strengthening tax enforcement. Announced in a statement by Exchequer Secretary to the Treasury Dan Tomlinson on 23 June 2026, the measures build on commitments made in the HMRC Transformation Roadmap published in July 2025...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UK government has unveiled a broad package of tax and customs reforms aimed at simplifying compliance, expanding digital services and strengthening tax enforcement. Announced in a <a href="https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-statements/detail/2026-06-23/hcws141" target="_blank" rel="noopener">statement </a>by Exchequer Secretary to the Treasury Dan Tomlinson on 23 June 2026, the measures build on commitments made in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hmrc-transformation-roadmap/hmrcs-transformation-roadmap" target="_blank" rel="noopener">HMRC Transformation Roadmap</a> published in July 2025 and reaffirmed at Budget 2025.</p>
<p>The package includes a series of consultations on tax policy, customs modernisation and compliance initiatives intended to reduce administrative burdens for taxpayers and businesses while improving fairness and protecting government revenue.</p>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Tax simplification measures</strong></span></p>
<p><strong>VAT relief for social housing land</strong></p>
<p>The government has launched a consultation on introducing a new zero rate of VAT for the sale of land intended for the construction of social housing. The consultation will examine how the current rules operate and seek views on whether the proposed relief would help reduce barriers to housing development while remaining fair and fiscally sustainable.</p>
<p><strong>Review of employer travel expense rates</strong></p>
<p>HMRC will review its Benchmark Scale Rates (BSR) and Overseas Scale Rates (OSR), which employers may use to reimburse employee travel expenses without checking individual receipts.</p>
<p>The review will consider whether BSR better reflects current travel costs and whether OSR can be simplified by aligning it more closely with domestic reimbursement rules.</p>
<p><strong>More timely income tax self assessment payments</strong></p>
<p>The government has opened a consultation on implementing more timely payment arrangements for Income Tax Self Assessment (ITSA).</p>
<p>Under proposals announced at Budget 2025, taxpayers with Pay As You Earn (PAYE) income who also submit Self Assessment returns would begin paying more of their estimated annual liabilities through PAYE from April 2029. The consultation also considers reforms to Payments on Account for other Self Assessment taxpayers, with the aim of spreading tax payments more evenly throughout the year.</p>
<p><strong>Review of PAYE settlement agreements</strong></p>
<p>HMRC has issued a call for evidence on PAYE Settlement Agreements (PSAs) to examine how employers apply the current rules and identify areas of complexity or uncertainty.</p>
<p>The review will help determine whether legislative or administrative changes are needed to reduce compliance burdens and improve consistency.</p>
<p><strong>Consultation on company distributions rules</strong></p>
<p>The government is consulting on modernising the rules governing whether payments made by companies to non-corporate shareholders fall within the distributions regime.</p>
<p>The review reflects the complexity of legislation that, in many cases, has remained largely unchanged since 1965 and aims to ensure the rules operate as intended without disrupting commercial practice.</p>
<p><strong>Digital option to tax process</strong></p>
<p>HMRC will replace paper-based procedures for the option to tax with a digital system covering notifications, revocations and VAT registration cancellations.</p>
<p>The new process is expected to include features such as bulk uploads, following discussions with business groups and industry representatives.</p>
<p><strong>Double taxation proposals for overseas entities</strong></p>
<p>The government is consulting on proposals affecting members of US Limited Liability Companies and other reverse hybrids.</p>
<p>The reforms seek to remove unintended cases of double taxation arising from differences in how certain overseas entities are treated for tax purposes.</p>
<p><strong>First Time Buyer ISA</strong></p>
<p>A consultation has also been launched on implementing a new First Time Buyer ISA, which is intended to replace the Lifetime ISA with a simpler savings product designed to support home purchases.</p>
<p><strong>Help to save reform</strong></p>
<p>The government confirmed that the reformed Help to Save scheme will operate through a multi-provider model, allowing financial institutions to offer accounts directly to eligible customers in an effort to improve accessibility.</p>
<p><strong>HMRC digital transformation</strong></p>
<p>HMRC said it continues to improve customer guidance and digital services as part of its wider transformation programme.</p>
<p>During the past year, the department updated more than 4,000 guidance pages and has now developed 118 interactive guidance tools. Customer feedback indicates that nearly 80% of users were able to complete their task using the interactive guidance, while HMRC data shows more than 96% did not subsequently visit HMRC&#8217;s contact pages.</p>
<p>The department is also continuing work under its Better Letters Together initiative to improve the clarity of correspondence sent to taxpayers.</p>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Customs modernisation</strong></span></p>
<p><strong>Consultation on customs reform</strong></p>
<p>The government has launched a call for evidence seeking industry views on the future of the UK&#8217;s customs regime, including opportunities arising from trade digitalisation and technological change.</p>
<p><strong>Digital trade and artificial intelligence</strong></p>
<p>HMRC plans to expand digital customs services by testing Electronic Trade Documents and participating in the next phase of the Department for Business and Trade&#8217;s Digital Trade Corridors programme.</p>
<p>The department will also trial the use of artificial intelligence to assist customs caseworkers with real-time documentary checks at the border.</p>
<p><strong>Customs intermediary standards</strong></p>
<p>Following publication of a new standard for customs intermediaries earlier this month, the government will develop a voluntary certification scheme and consult on mandatory registration requirements for customs intermediaries.</p>
<p><strong>Digital ATA Carnets</strong></p>
<p>The UK adopted digital ATA Carnets from 1 June 2026, becoming one of the first countries to digitise the international &#8220;passport for goods&#8221; used for the temporary movement of goods across borders.</p>
<p><strong>Northern Ireland duty reimbursement scheme</strong></p>
<p>Legislative changes that took effect on 26 May 2026 simplify access to the Duty Reimbursement Scheme for goods brought into Northern Ireland that are later shown not to be &#8220;at risk&#8221; of entering the EU market.</p>
<p>The reforms are intended to ease cash-flow pressures by making duty repayments more accessible.</p>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Compliance and enforcement measures</strong></span></p>
<p><strong>Low value imports</strong></p>
<p>The government will accelerate reforms to the customs treatment of low value imports by six months, bringing implementation forward to no later than October 2028.</p>
<p>Legislation is expected to be introduced through this year&#8217;s Finance Bill following publication of the consultation response.</p>
<p><strong>Online marketplace VAT liability</strong></p>
<p>A consultation has been launched on extending Online Marketplace VAT Liability to cover both UK and overseas businesses selling goods through online marketplaces.</p>
<p>The proposals are intended to reduce VAT non-compliance and prevent overseas sellers from falsely presenting themselves as UK-based businesses.</p>
<p><strong>Electronic sales suppression</strong></p>
<p>The government is consulting on new software standards for Electronic Point of Sale and Mobile Point of Sale systems to combat electronic sales suppression, which allows traders to under-report sales and evade tax.</p>
<p>The proposed standards aim to improve record-keeping while minimising additional compliance burdens for legitimate businesses.</p>
<p><strong>Recovery of lower-value tax debts</strong></p>
<p>HMRC has also opened a consultation on extending its powers to recover lower-value tax debts from customers who have failed to respond after repeated contact attempts despite being able to pay.</p>
<p>Under the proposals, eligible debts could be recovered through regular instalments directly from customer accounts, subject to safeguards intended to ensure the powers are exercised fairly and proportionately.</p>
<p>The reforms mark the next phase of the government&#8217;s programme to modernise the UK&#8217;s tax and customs framework through greater digitalisation, simplified administration and targeted enforcement. Many of the measures are now subject to consultation, with stakeholder feedback expected to shape future legislation and implementation as HMRC continues its wider transformation agenda.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

<p>The GIC applies if a tax amount or other liability remains unpaid beyond its due date. The GIC rates are updated quarterly, with new rates announced about two weeks before each quarter begins.</p>

<p>The guidance, set out in <a href="https://www.gdt.gov.vn/wps/wcm/connect/c193fc71-47f3-46af-830a-ab1cc3e27847/3870_CT-CS.pdf?MOD=AJPERES&amp;CACHEID=ROOTWORKSPACEc193fc71-47f3-46af-830a-ab1cc3e27847" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Official Letter No. 3870/CT-CS dated 10 June 2025</a>, clarifies when the Vietnamese tax authority will receive CbC reports through the automatic exchange of information instead of requiring local filing by taxpayers.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Dominican Republic has enacted Law 30-26, following its signature by the president on 18 June 2026, introducing a broad package of tax and fiscal measures that amend the Tax Code and related legislation. The reforms include a temporary increase in the corporate income tax rate for large taxpayers, revisions to Income Tax (ISR), Value...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic has enacted<a href="https://presidencia.gob.do/leyes/ley-30-26" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Law 30-26</a>, following its signature by the president on 18 June 2026, introducing a broad package of tax and fiscal measures that amend the Tax Code and related legislation. The reforms include a temporary increase in the corporate income tax rate for large taxpayers, revisions to Income Tax (ISR), Value Added Tax (ITBIS) and Select Consumption Tax (ISC), as well as changes to tax administration, compliance procedures and sector-specific taxes.</p>
<p><strong>Corporate income tax</strong></p>
<p>A temporary 3% surcharge on corporate income tax has been introduced for large taxpayers with annual revenue exceeding DOP 1 billion. As a result, the effective corporate income tax rate for affected companies will increase from 27% to 30% for the 2026, 2027 and 2028 fiscal years.</p>
<p>The standard corporate income tax rate for other legal entities remains 27%.</p>
<p><strong>Value Added Tax (ITBIS) and select consumption Tax (ISC)</strong></p>
<p>The legislation establishes a perception regime for informal importers, applying a 30% surcharge on the ITBIS tax base.</p>
<p>Additional ITBIS exemptions apply to selected goods, including asphalt, fire trucks, ambulances, milk, natural water and pasta.</p>
<p>Under the Select Consumption Tax (ISC), electronic cigarettes become subject to a 55% ad valorem tax. A tax of 0.002 (2.0 per thousand) also applies to checks and electronic transfers.</p>
<p>The tax on life insurance will be reduced in stages, falling to 11% in 2027 and 6% in 2028 before being fully exempt from 2029.</p>
<p><strong>Sector-specific measures</strong></p>
<p>The law introduces revised taxation for gambling operations, with casinos taxed according to the number of gaming tables, while lottery and betting shops will pay fixed annual or monthly fees.</p>
<p>New fuel-related charges include a contribution of USD 174.50 per metric ton on Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) imports and an additional DOP 2.00 per gallon on gasoline and gasoil.</p>
<p>The passenger exit contribution has been increased to USD 30.00, or its equivalent in Dominican pesos.</p>
<p>The legislation also establishes new exemptions for direct-line inheritances of up to DOP 2,000,000 and for donations made to public institutions or social welfare purposes.</p>
<p><strong>Individual income tax </strong></p>
<p>The law introduces a new progressive Individual Tax Scale, effective from 2027, with tax brackets ranging from exempt income of up to DOP 480,000 to a maximum tax liability of DOP 274,800.</p>
<p>Capital gains derived by individuals from the sale of real estate will be subject to a fixed 10% tax rate.</p>
<p>The Simplified Taxation Regime (RST) has been expanded to cover small businesses with annual sales of up to DOP 30 million and independent professionals with annual income of up to DOP 15 million.</p>
<p>New rules also revise the calculation of advance payments (Anticipos), with micro-businesses exempt from making advance payments.</p>
<p><strong>Tax administration and compliance</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers may select the tax regime that best suits their circumstances but cannot claim benefits under more than one incentive regime for the same economic activity.</p>
<p>The law also allows debtors to request payment agreements with the General Directorate of Internal Taxes (DGII), subject to an initial payment of at least 15% of the outstanding liability. Repayment may be made over up to 12 monthly instalments, or up to 24 months in exceptional cases.</p>
<p>Late payment surcharges are set at 3% per month or part of a month, with the total surcharge capped at 100% of the unpaid tax.</p>
<p>A temporary fiscal amnesty will remain available until 31 December 2026, allowing taxpayers to settle outstanding liabilities by paying the principal amount together with only one year of accumulated interest and surcharges.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has updated its guidance on 19 June 2026 regarding requests for mutual agreement procedures (MAPs) to resolve cross-border tax disputes arising from alleged violations of double taxation agreements (DTAs). This process allows the Australian competent authority to negotiate with foreign jurisdictions to eliminate double taxation and clarify the application of...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/in-detail/doing-business-in-australia-or-overseas/mutual-agreement-procedure" target="_blank" rel="noopener">updated</a> its guidance on 19 June 2026 regarding requests for mutual agreement procedures (MAPs) to resolve cross-border tax disputes arising from alleged violations of double taxation agreements (DTAs). This process allows the Australian competent authority to negotiate with foreign jurisdictions to eliminate double taxation and clarify the application of tax treaties.</p>
<p>The update details the eligibility criteria, specific time limits for filing, and the three-stage process involving submission, negotiation, and implementation. Furthermore, the guidance explains arbitration options available when agreements cannot be reached and provides guidance on dual residency determinations. Ultimately, these guidelines serve as a comprehensive manual for taxpayers seeking to ensure their cross-border activities are taxed in accordance with global treaty obligations.</p>
<p>Below are additional details regarding the Mutual Agreement Procedure (MAP) process and requirements:</p>
<p><strong>Detailed procedural stages</strong></p>
<p><strong>The MAP process follows a structured three-stage path:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Stage 1 (Submission &amp; validation): The MAP Program Management Unit (PMU) first confirms if a request is valid (e.g., submitted on time to the correct authority). The Competent Authority (CA) then determines if the case is &#8220;justified&#8221; based on whether treaty-inconsistent taxation is at least probable.</li>
<li>Stage 2 (Negotiation): If unilateral relief isn&#8217;t possible, the Australian CA negotiates with the foreign CA. The taxpayer is kept informed of progress but cannot attend these negotiations, though the taxpayer may be allowed to present arguments to both CAs jointly if they agree.</li>
<li>Stage 3 (Implementation): Once an agreement is reached, the taxpayer has two months to accept or reject it. If accepted, the ATO will process adjustments, which may include withdrawing original tax adjustments or providing foreign tax offsets.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Required information for a request</strong></p>
<p>To ensure a MAP request is accepted, taxpayers must provide comprehensive documentation, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Identity details: Names, addresses, and taxpayer identification numbers for all parties involved.</li>
<li>Legal basis: Specific articles of the treaty that the taxpayer believes are being misapplied.</li>
<li>Factual analysis: A detailed history of the case, amounts to be adjusted, and supporting documents like transfer pricing records or audit position papers.</li>
<li>Prior rulings: Information on whether the issue was previously addressed in a settlement, court decision, or Advance Pricing Arrangement (APA).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Interactions with domestic law and anti-avoidance</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Protective MAP requests: If a taxpayer is pursuing domestic remedies (like an objection) but is worried about the three-year treaty time limit expiring, the taxpayer can lodge a &#8220;protective&#8221; request to preserve their rights while the domestic process proceeds.</li>
<li>General anti-avoidance rules (Part IVA): While a taxpayer can request a MAP for tax resulting from Australia&#8217;s anti-avoidance rules, the ATO cannot resolve a case through MAP to the extent it involves Part IVA, as these domestic rules prevail over treaty provisions.</li>
<li>Settlements: A taxpayer can request a MAP for matters already settled with the ATO, but should check the settlement deed for clauses that might restrict continuing the dispute through the MAP process.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Arbitration and timeframes</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Mandatory binding arbitration: If CAs cannot resolve a case within two to three years, the taxpayer may request arbitration under specific treaties (e.g., Germany, Japan, United Kingdom) or the Multilateral Instrument (MLI). However, cases already decided by a court or tribunal are generally ineligible for arbitration.</li>
<li>Performance goals: The ATO strives to resolve MAP cases within an average of 24 months, though actual times vary; for example, in the 2024–25 financial year, transfer pricing cases averaged roughly 41 months to resolve.</li>
</ul>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Malaysia has gazetted the<a href="https://lom.agc.gov.my/ilims/upload/portal/akta/outputp/3571177/PUA%20229_2026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Income Tax (Deduction for Employment of Approved Individual) Rules 2026</a> on 23 June 2026, providing qualifying employers with an additional deduction equal to 50% of remuneration paid to approved individuals for a period not exceeding 12 months.</p>
<p>As previously <a href="https://regfollower.com/malaysia-exempts-returning-women-workers-from-income-tax-for-up-to-12-months/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reported</a>, the Rules define &#8220;approved individual&#8221; by reference to the<a href="https://lom.agc.gov.my/ilims/upload/portal/akta/outputp/3519995/PUA%20215_2026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Income Tax (Income of Approved Individual) (Women Returning to Work After Ceasing from Employment Temporarily) (Exemption) Order 2026</a>, which grants eligible women returning to work after temporary employment cessation an income tax exemption on gross employment income for up to 12 months.</p>
<p>The combined effect provides tax relief to both employers and returning women workers for the same 12-month period.</p>
<p>The Income Tax (Deduction for Employment of Approved Individual) Rules 2026 include the following details:</p>
<p><strong>Tax deduction benefit</strong></p>
<p>Qualifying employers are granted an additional deduction equal to 50% of remuneration paid to approved individuals, available in addition to the standard deduction for remuneration permitted under section 33 of the Income Tax Act 1967. The deduction applies for a period not exceeding twelve consecutive months and is effective for the years of assessment 2025 through 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Definition of a qualifying employer</strong></p>
<p>While a &#8220;qualifying employer&#8221; generally includes any person who employs an approved individual, the Rules specifically exclude the following from eligibility:</p>
<ul>
<li>Any company controlled either directly or indirectly by the approved individual.</li>
<li>All sole proprietorships are excluded.</li>
<li>Any employer who is a relative of the approved individual. &#8220;Relative&#8221; is broadly defined to include parents (and parents-in-law), children (including stepchildren and legally adopted children), siblings, grandparents, grandchildren, and spouses.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Approved individuals and verification</strong></p>
<p>An &#8220;approved individual&#8221; is defined according to the Income Tax (Income of Approved Individual) (Women Returning to Work After Ceasing from Employment Temporarily) (Exemption) Order 2026 [P.U. (A) 215/2026]. To claim the deduction, a qualifying employer shall comply with the conditions imposed by the Minister, and the compliance of the conditions shall be verified by Talent Corporation Malaysia Berhad.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Green Party of New Zealand has released its 2026 tax policy, “A tax system for all of us,” proposing a broad restructuring of the country&#8217;s tax framework aimed at reducing wealth inequality, increasing contributions from large corporations and high-net-worth individuals, and lowering income tax for most workers. According to the party, the package would...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Green Party of New Zealand has released its 2026 tax policy, “<a href="https://assets.nationbuilder.com/beachheroes/pages/71965/attachments/original/1782084525/GreensTaxPolicy2026.pdf?1782084525" target="_blank" rel="noopener">A tax system for all of us</a>,” proposing a broad restructuring of the country&#8217;s tax framework aimed at reducing wealth inequality, increasing contributions from large corporations and high-net-worth individuals, and lowering income tax for most workers.</p>
<p>According to the party, the package would provide tax relief to 96% of salaried and waged earners while generating an estimated net fiscal gain of NZD 5.14 billion in its first year of implementation.</p>
<p><strong>Wealth taxes to address inequality</strong></p>
<p>A central feature of the proposal is the introduction of new taxes on accumulated wealth and large asset transfers.</p>
<p>The plan would impose a 2.5% annual Super-Rich Tax on the net assets of individuals with wealth exceeding NZD 10 million, or NZD 20 million for couples. The tax would apply to assets such as property, shares and bonds, while exempting family homes, Māori land and charitable assets.</p>
<p>The Green Party also proposes a Capital Acquisitions Tax of 33% on inheritances and gifts worth more than NZD 1 million. Family homes and family farms would be excluded from the measure. The party says the tax is intended to reduce the concentration of wealth across generations.</p>
<p>The Super-Rich Tax is projected to raise NZD 3.76 billion in the 2027/28 fiscal year, while the Capital Acquisitions Tax is expected to generate NZD 953 million.</p>
<p><strong>Higher taxes for large corporations and banks</strong></p>
<p>The policy includes measures aimed at increasing tax contributions from large businesses, multinational corporations and major financial institutions.</p>
<p>Under the proposal, the corporate tax rate would rise from 28% to 33% for companies with annual turnover exceeding NZD 30 million. The higher rate would apply to approximately 0.7% of companies, while small and medium-sized enterprises would continue to pay the existing 28% rate.</p>
<p>The Green Party also proposes a 0.06% annual levy on the liabilities of banks holding more than NZD 100 billion in liabilities. The measure would primarily affect the country&#8217;s four largest Australian-owned banks: ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac.</p>
<p>In addition, the party would introduce a 5% withholding tax on profits that large technology companies transfer offshore through service or licence fee arrangements. The proposal specifically targets multinational firms such as Google, Microsoft and Amazon.</p>
<p>The corporate tax increase is forecast to generate NZD 1.37 billion in additional revenue during 2027/28.</p>
<p><strong>Property tax changes</strong></p>
<p>The policy seeks to reverse several tax settings introduced for residential property investors.</p>
<p>The Green Party would reinstate restrictions on interest deductibility, reversing recent changes that allow landlords to deduct mortgage interest from taxable profits.</p>
<p>The party also proposes restoring the bright-line test period to 10 years from the current two years. Under the proposal, income tax would apply to gains from residential investment properties sold within 10 years of acquisition.</p>
<p>According to the party, these measures would remove tax advantages enjoyed by property investors and speculators.</p>
<p><strong>Personal income tax reset</strong></p>
<p>The package includes significant changes to personal income tax settings. The first NZD 10,000 of annual income would become tax-free for all taxpayers.</p>
<p>A new 45% top income tax rate would apply to earnings above NZD 160,000 annually.</p>
<p>The Green Party says everyone earning less than NZD 160,000 per year would receive a tax reduction, with lower-income households benefiting the most in proportional terms.</p>
<p>However, the income tax changes are expected to reduce government revenue by NZD 2.33 billion in 2027/28.</p>
<p><strong>Fiscal impact</strong></p>
<p>Based on the Green Party&#8217;s modelling, the package would generate substantial additional revenue despite the cost of income tax reductions.</p>
<p>The largest revenue sources would be the Super-Rich Tax (NZD 3.76 billion), higher taxes on large corporations (NZD 1.37 billion) and the Capital Acquisitions Tax (NZD 953 million).</p>
<p>After accounting for the NZD 2.33 billion cost of revised income tax settings, the party estimates the overall package would deliver a net fiscal gain of NZD 5.14 billion in its first year, providing additional funding for public services and social programmes.</p>
