		<category><![CDATA[UAE]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=83915</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The UAE Ministry of Finance has issued the UAE Electronic Invoicing Guidelines Version 1.1, dated 1 June 2026. The key updates introduced in Version 1.1 include the addition of: Appendix 4 &#8211; Further guidance in respect of storage obligations under Article 11 of Ministerial Decision No. 243 of 2025; and Appendix 5 – Advance Payments...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UAE Ministry of Finance has issued the <a href="https://mof.gov.ae/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/UAE-Electronic-Invoicing-Guidelines_V-1.1-01June2026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">UAE Electronic Invoicing Guidelines Version 1.1</a>, dated 1 June 2026. The key updates introduced in Version 1.1 include the addition of:</p>
<ul>
<li>Appendix 4 &#8211; Further guidance in respect of storage obligations under Article 11 of Ministerial Decision No. 243 of 2025; and</li>
<li>Appendix 5 – Advance Payments and Retention Clarification.</li>
</ul>
<p>The updates are as follows:</p>
<p><strong>Appendix 4 &#8211; Further guidance in respect of storage obligations under Article 11 of Ministerial Decision No. 243 of 2025</strong></p>
<p>This appendix clarifies storage and retention obligations under the Electronic Invoicing System, as set out under Article 11 of Ministerial Decision No. 243 of 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Obligation of the Person (as defined in the Ministerial Decision No. 243 of 2025)</strong></p>
<p>Any Person subject to the Electronic Invoicing System must retain all Electronic Invoices, Electronic Credit Notes, and related data for the retention period set under the Tax Procedures Law, and must be able to produce these records to the Authority on request.</p>
<p><strong>Role and Obligations of Accredited Service Providers (ASPs)</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Transactional Logs and Technical Traceability:</strong> ASPs must keep transactional logs separate from invoice content itself. These logs need unique transaction identifiers covering the full invoice exchange and reporting cycle, including transmission status and routing data. This technical data is treated as part of the ASP&#8217;s own operational/compliance duties, not as business document data the Person is required to retain under Article 11. Logging must follow both the Service Provider Agreement with OpenPeppol and the UAE Peppol Authority Specific Requirements (PASR).</li>
<li><strong>Delegation of Storage:</strong> A Person may contractually delegate storage to an ASP, but this doesn&#8217;t shift the underlying legal retention obligation under Article 11 — the Person remains ultimately responsible. ASPs may store invoices, credit notes, and associated data on the Person&#8217;s behalf, subject to their commercial agreement.</li>
<li><strong>Storage Location and Architecture:</strong> There&#8217;s no requirement that storage sit at any particular system layer (e.g., C1/C4). Any storage setup is acceptable as long as data is kept for the required period, integrity and security are maintained, and records can be produced to the Authority on request.</li>
<li><strong>Transmission Confirmation:</strong> ASPs must notify Persons, on an event-driven basis and without undue delay, once Electronic Invoices or Tax Data Documents have been successfully transmitted to the Authority — so the Person stays aware of compliance status.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Appendix 5 – Advance Payments and Retention Clarification</strong></p>
<p>This Appendix clarifies how advance payments and retention should be treated for PINT AE e-invoicing purposes.</p>
<p><strong>Advance Payments</strong></p>
<p>In cases where the businesses receive an advance payment, a tax invoice must be issued at the time of receipt.</p>
<p>Therefore, when issuing the final invoice, it should cover only the remaining balance, not the full amount, as a tax invoice has already been issued for the advance.</p>
<p>A reference to the original invoice may be included under IBT-25 and IBT-26, or a note can be provided in IBT-022. The cbc: PrepaidAmount field may be left blank, since the subsequent invoice reflects only the outstanding amount and does not require any further adjustment of the advance.</p>
<p>For example, the total contract is for AED 10,000 plus VAT of 5 %. An advance payment is received for AED 1,000 + 5% VAT.</p>
<p><strong>Retention</strong></p>
<p>In contracts where retention arrangements apply, Businesses may continue following their existing commercial and accounting practices, provided such practices remain compliant with the applicable VAT and Electronic Invoicing requirements.</p>
<p>One such acceptable practice is outlined below:</p>
<ul>
<li>An Electronic Invoice may be issued for the amount payable by the Supplier after adjusting for the retention amount.</li>
<li>A separate Electronic Invoice may subsequently be issued for the retained amount at the point in time when the Buyer becomes liable to release and settle the retained amount.</li>
</ul>
<p>Businesses should ensure that the relevant contractual arrangements and payment obligations are appropriately reflected in the corresponding Electronic Invoices issued.</p>

<p>The package includes a significant expansion of small business capital gains tax (CGT) concessions, a proposed new CGT incentive for innovative startups, amendments to existing legislation, and targeted trust tax reforms.</p>
<p>The government said the measures are intended to support investment, entrepreneurship, and economic growth, with additional business and startup tax relief expected to exceed AUD 3.8 billion.</p>
<p><strong>Tax reform implementation for small business and startups</strong></p>
<p>The reforms aim to help first-home buyers, cut taxes for workers, and align tax treatment of labour and asset income.</p>
<p>New CGT concessions for small businesses and startups mean all 2.7 million active small businesses (98% of all active businesses) will now qualify.</p>
<p>Key announcements:</p>
<ul>
<li>Raising the turnover threshold for the small business 50% active asset CGT reduction from AUD 2 million to AUD 10 million</li>
<li>Releasing a consultation paper on a new Innovative Business CGT Concession (50% discount for early-stage investors, founders, and employee share scheme participants)</li>
<li>Confirming all testamentary trust income will be exempt from the minimum tax</li>
<li>Committing to implement changes via legislation rather than legislative instruments</li>
</ul>
<p>Combined, these measures bring new business and startup tax relief to over AUD 3.8 billion, on top of existing tax cuts and housing measures.</p>
<p><strong>Small businesses concessions</strong></p>
<p>The Government will keep all four existing small business CGT concessions, which let small businesses reduce, defer, or eliminate CGT on active business asset sales.</p>
<ul>
<li>The 50% active asset reduction turnover threshold rises from AUD 2 million to AUD 10 million</li>
<li>This aligns it with the instant asset write-off threshold</li>
<li>Extends eligibility to 2.7 million small businesses (98% of active businesses)</li>
<li>Sits alongside the existing inflation discount where eligible</li>
<li>Amendments will be introduced to the legislation already before the Senate</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Consultation on arrangements for innovative start-ups</strong></p>
<p>A consultation paper has been released on a proposed 50% CGT discount for early-stage investors, founders, and employee share scheme participants in innovative start-ups.</p>
<p>The Innovative Business CGT Concession would let individuals, partnerships, and trusts choose between a 50% discount or indexation and the minimum tax, for gains accrued from 1 July 2027.</p>
<p>Proposed eligibility criteria:</p>
<ul>
<li>Shares must be new equity in a company under 10 years old (up to 15 years in certain circumstances)</li>
<li>Company turnover under AUD 50 million</li>
<li>Must meet principles-based innovation criteria</li>
<li>Shares held for five years before sale</li>
<li>Subject to a lifetime cap</li>
</ul>
<p>The government may extend the age threshold to 15 years for slower-to-commercialise sectors like biotech and medtech.</p>
<ul>
<li>Consultation closes 10 July</li>
<li>Will shape final design for a later legislative tranche</li>
<li>Small business measure costed at AUD 300 million over the forward estimates (bringing total business/startup support to over AUD 3.8 billion)</li>
<li>Startup measure costed at AUD 125 million</li>
<li>Both to be finalised at the next Budget update</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Amendments to the legislation</strong></p>
<p>The government will move targeted amendments to the current Bill, removing ministerial powers to lock in implementation detail.</p>
<p>Planned for the next sitting fortnight:</p>
<ul>
<li>Raising the active asset reduction turnover threshold to AUD 10 million</li>
<li>Ensuring deductible donations reduce capital gains subject to the minimum tax</li>
<li>Specifying income support payments exempt from the minimum tax on capital gains</li>
<li>Embedding the Working Australians Tax Offset calculation method in legislation</li>
<li>Removing now-unnecessary ministerial powers</li>
</ul>
<p>Later this year, following further consultation, the Government will also move into primary legislation:</p>
<ul>
<li>The definition of eligible &#8220;new builds&#8221; (for the 50% discount on gains from 1 July 2027, and negative gearing access for purchases after 12 May 2026)</li>
<li>Definitions of exempt housing investment types, including affordable housing</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Trusts reform and other elements of the tax reform package</strong></p>
<p>Further legislative tranches will follow the Budget package, with a consultation paper on implementing the minimum tax on discretionary trusts due in the coming weeks.</p>
<p>Following targeted consultation, the government will exempt income from all discretionary testamentary trusts from the minimum tax, provided they:</p>
<ul>
<li>Serve genuine testamentary purposes</li>
<li>Are limited to deceased estate assets</li>
</ul>
<p>For trusts established on or after 1 July 2028, the exemption will only apply where the trust benefits individuals and tax-exempt entities.</p>
<ul>
<li>The government reiterated there is no tax on inheritances or deceased estates</li>
<li>This measure is costed at AUD 50 million over the forward estimates, to be finalised at the next Budget update</li>
<li>Separately, legislation making loss carry-back and the small business instant asset write-off permanent will be introduced next week</li>
<li>The government thanked stakeholders and the Senate Economics Legislation Committee for their input during consultation</li>
</ul>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic’s General Directorate of Internal Taxes (DGII) has launched a <a href="https://dgii.gov.do/publicacionesOficiales/foroContribuyentes/Paginas/NG-dispone-no-aplicacion-retenciones-ITBIS-NG-02-05-e-CF.aspx" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on a <a href="https://dgii.gov.do/publicacionesOficiales/foroContribuyentes/Documents/Borrador-NG-dispone-no-aplicacion-retenciones-ITBIS-NG-02-05-e-CF.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft</a> General Norm that would exempt authorised electronic invoicing taxpayers from the withholding regime for the Tax on the Transfer of Industrialised Goods and Services (ITBIS) when transactions are documented through Electronic Tax Receipts (e-CF).</p>

The exemption would apply only when the transfer of goods or provision of services is invoiced using an Electronic Tax Receipt (e-CF).</p>
<p>The DGII said the measure is intended to simplify tax compliance and reduce administrative costs for businesses that have adopted electronic invoicing. To qualify, taxpayers must satisfy two conditions: they must be authorised as electronic issuers by the DGII, and the relevant transaction must be supported by an e-CF.</p>
<p>According to the draft, the proposal reflects changes in the tax administration environment since the introduction of General Rule No. 02-05. The withholding mechanism was originally designed as a control measure when the tax authority did not have immediate access to transaction data. However, the implementation of Electronic Tax Receipts under Law No. 32-23 now provides the DGII with real-time information on taxpayer transactions.</p>
<p>The tax authority noted that access to real-time transaction data strengthens fiscal oversight and enables faster detection of inconsistencies, reducing the need for traditional withholding controls for taxpayers operating through the electronic invoicing system.</p>
<p>The consultation process is being conducted under the framework established by Law No. 167-21 on Regulatory Improvement and Administrative Simplification, as amended by Law No. 14-25, as well as Decree No. 486-22 and Law No. 107-13 on the Rights of Individuals in Their Relations with the Administration and Administrative Procedure.</p>
<p>If adopted, the exemption will take effect from the date the General Norm is officially issued.</p>
<p>The public consultation will remain open until 20 August 2026.</p>

		<title>Luxembourg clarifies Pillar Two compliance, registration, transitional requirements</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/luxembourg-clarifies-pillar-two-compliance-registration-transitional-requirements/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=luxembourg-clarifies-pillar-two-compliance-registration-transitional-requirements</link>

				<category><![CDATA[Filing obligations of GMT]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Scope of GMT]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Europe]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Luxembourg]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=83890</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Luxembourg’s Administration of Direct Contributions (ACD), on 17 June 2026, published a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) document providing further guidance on the implementation of the Pillar Two Law of 22 December 2023 on minimum effective taxation. The guidance clarifies tax assessment procedures, registration and reporting obligations, and transitional provisions applicable to multinational enterprise (MNE) groups...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Luxembourg’s Administration of Direct Contributions (ACD), on 17 June 2026, published a <a href="https://impotsdirects.public.lu/dam-assets/fr/echanges-electroniques/pilier-2/faq-pilier-2-de-ladministration-des-contributions-directes-acd-17062026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) </a>document providing further guidance on the implementation of the Pillar Two Law of 22 December 2023 on minimum effective taxation.</p>
<p>The guidance clarifies tax assessment procedures, registration and reporting obligations, and transitional provisions applicable to multinational enterprise (MNE) groups and other entities within the scope of the regime.</p>
<p><strong>Tax assessments and payment</strong></p>
<p>The ACD said it intends to issue tax assessment notices within three years after the end of the relevant fiscal year, provided tax returns have been submitted on time. Taxes paid under these assessments generally should not be taken into account for tax reductions under Article 21, paragraph 3, letter e) of the Law.</p>
<p><strong>Registration obligations</strong></p>
<p>Under Article 49, all Constituent Entities, Joint Ventures (JVs) and JV Affiliates located in Luxembourg must register for Pillar Two purposes, regardless of whether they qualify for a safe harbour or are subject to other reporting requirements.</p>
<p>The obligation also extends to Investment Entities that meet the criteria set out in the Law.</p>
<p>For multi-compartment legal entities, each compartment must register separately using a dedicated Luxembourg tax identification number (NIF) reserved exclusively for Pillar Two compliance. Stateless Entities are excluded from the registration requirement because they are not considered to be located in Luxembourg.</p>
<p>The FAQ also clarifies that entities created and liquidated within the same fiscal year remain subject to registration and de-registration requirements. Administrative tolerances are available for de-registration during the Transition Year. When an entity transfers from one MNE group to another, it must first de-register from its original group before registering with the new one.</p>
<p><strong>GIR notification requirements</strong></p>
<p>The guidance explains the notification requirements linked to the GloBE Information Return (GIR) under Article 50. When a Luxembourg entity is exempt from filing a GIR locally because the return is filed in another jurisdiction, it must inform the ACD of the identity and jurisdiction of the filing entity during registration.</p>
<p>The ACD also introduced a temporary administrative tolerance for GIRs filed in Barbados, Switzerland and Turkey. Because information exchange arrangements may not be effective by 30 June 2026, Luxembourg entities relying on filings in those jurisdictions will not be required to submit a local GIR before 31 December 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Filing obligations for Pillar Two taxes</strong></p>
<p>The FAQ includes practical examples covering reporting obligations under the Income Inclusion Rule (RIR/IIR), the Undertaxed Profits Rule (RBII/UTPR) and the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (Impôt National Complémentaire).</p>
<p>For the RIR/IIR, filing obligations generally apply to Parent Entities. Returns must still be submitted even where the resulting top-up tax is reduced to zero through substance-based income exclusions. However, entities benefiting from a safe harbour are not required to file.</p>
<p>For the RBII/UTPR, filing is required for entities to which UTPR amounts are allocated. Where a Designated Filing Constituent Entity has been appointed in Luxembourg, a single filing may be made on behalf of all Luxembourg group entities.</p>
<p>A similar approach applies to the Impôt National Complémentaire. Low-taxed Luxembourg entities are generally required to report, although a designated filing entity may submit returns on behalf of multiple entities. The FAQ also outlines specific rules for Joint Venture groups.</p>
<p><strong>Transitional provisions</strong></p>
<p>The guidance further explains the application of transitional rules under Article 53.</p>
<p>To benefit from the transitional measures, entities may rely either on their own annual financial statements or on the consolidated financial statements of the Ultimate Parent Entity, provided the relevant information can be reliably traced.</p>
<p>The ACD confirmed that transitional deferred tax provisions apply from the Transition Year onwards. It also clarified the distinction between the terms “reflected” (constatés) and “disclosed” in financial reporting. According to the guidance, items reflected in financial statements refer to amounts recorded on the balance sheet, while disclosed items refer to information included in the notes to the accounts.</p>
<p>Importantly, the ACD confirmed that deferred taxes disclosed solely in the notes to the financial statements are sufficient to meet the transitional requirements under the Pillar Two framework.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, the Philippines House of Representatives has issued a <a href="https://cpbrd.congress.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/DP2026-19-THE-FUTURE-OF-PHILIPPINE-FISCAL-INCENTIVES-UNDER-OECD-PILLAR-TWO.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">discussion paper</a> titled “The Future of Philippine Fiscal Incentives under OECD Pillar Two”, which examines the impact of Pillar Two global minimum tax rules on existing tax incentives in the Philippines, including possible policy considerations.</p>
<p>This paper examines the evolution of the Philippine fiscal incentive regime from the CREATE Act (Republic Act No. 11534) in 2021 to CREATE MORE (Republic Act No. 12066) in 2024, both of which sought to streamline investment processes and harmonise local taxation through mechanisms such as the Registered Business Enterprise Local Tax (RBELT).</p>
<p>In the context of the OECD Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax (GMT), the paper discusses the emerging “incentive paradox,” wherein traditional income-based incentives such as the Income Tax Holiday (ITH) and the Special Corporate Income Tax (SCIT) may reduce effective tax rates below the 15% global threshold, thereby triggering top-up taxes in foreign jurisdictions and diminishing the intended benefits of such incentives.</p>
<p>The paper further explores how the OECD Pillar Two framework may reshape the future relevance and design of Philippine fiscal incentives, arguing that while GMT is likely to constrain the effectiveness of traditional income-based incentives, fiscal incentives themselves remain relevant as instruments for investment promotion and economic development.</p>
<p>However, the changing global tax environment may drive a structural shift in incentive design and policy orientation — from income-based tax reductions toward cost-based, performance-driven, and strategically targeted instruments. The paper underscores the need for a recalibrated Philippine incentive framework that sustains competitiveness, enhances fiscal efficiency, and preserves domestic taxing rights within an increasingly coordinated global tax regime.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The President of Finland ratified a law that brings amendments to the Income Tax Act concerning the tax residency rules for certain foreign investment funds on 16 June 2026. Under Finland’s general rules, a foreign entity can be treated as a Finnish tax resident if its place of effective management is located in Finland. However,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The President of Finland ratified a <a href="https://vm.fi/paatos?decisionId=6599" target="_blank" rel="noopener">law</a> that brings amendments to the Income Tax Act concerning the tax residency rules for certain foreign investment funds on 16 June 2026.</p>
<p>Under Finland’s general rules, a foreign entity can be treated as a Finnish tax resident if its place of effective management is located in Finland. However, a temporary exemption—applicable for tax years 2021 to 2026—has applied to specific foreign undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities (UCITS) and alternative investment funds (AIF).</p>
<p>To qualify for this exemption, the management company must operate independently, handle at least three distinct funds, and receive market-based compensation for its professional services. Additionally, the law provides strict definitions for fund independence, requiring that ownership and income distribution remain largely separate from the managing entity.</p>
<p>This law, which comes into effect on 1 January 2027, provides a permanent framework following the temporary exception that applied through the 2026 tax year.</p>
<p>Under the new legislation, a foreign fund will not be considered to have a place of effective management in Finland solely based on the activities of its Finnish management company, provided the following conditions are met:</p>
<p><strong>Conditions for the fund management company</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>The three-fund standard: A fund management company must qualify as an independent operator by administering at least three separate, independent funds or sub-funds. This threshold is fundamental to establishing the company&#8217;s professional standing in the sector.</li>
<li>Permitted activities and compensation: The company&#8217;s work on behalf of any fund must remain within its ordinary business scope, either as prescribed by law or under a contractual arrangement with the fund. Equally important, the management company must receive compensation that reflects market rates—essentially, an arm&#8217;s length price for the services rendered.</li>
<li>Implications for tax residence: When a fund management company satisfies these conditions—managing multiple independent funds, operating within defined activity parameters, and receiving fair-market compensation—it does not automatically establish a place of effective management in Finland. However, if the company fails to meet even one of these criteria, it cannot claim automatic exemption from having its effective place of management considered to arise in the country.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Defining an &#8220;Independent Fund&#8221;</strong></p>
<p>A foreign fund qualifies as &#8220;independent&#8221; from its management company if it meets two criteria. First, the total fees and compensation the management company receives from the fund cannot exceed 50% of the company&#8217;s total revenue during the relevant tax year. Second, at least 50% of the fund&#8217;s units must be held by investors unrelated to the management company.</p>
<p><strong>Flexibility and transition rules</strong></p>
<p>The law provides a ramp-up period allowing newly managed funds to be deemed independent starting from the year the management company begins managing them in Finland, provided the independence criteria are satisfied within three tax years.  Additionally, if the 50% revenue threshold is not met in a subsequent year due to changes in the manager&#8217;s other funds rather than changes to the fund itself, the fund retains its independent status.</p>
<p><strong>Scope of the law</strong></p>
<p>The amendment applies to collective investment undertakings established or registered outside Finland that are equivalent to UCITS, as well as Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) established in an EEA state with managers operating in Finland. Sub-funds are treated as individual funds under these rules.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<link>https://regfollower.com/cjeu-advocate-general-supports-luxembourgs-atad-transposition-on-securitisation-entities-from-interest-limitation-rules/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=cjeu-advocate-general-supports-luxembourgs-atad-transposition-on-securitisation-entities-from-interest-limitation-rules</link>

				<category><![CDATA[Interest received]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[The  Advocate General (AG) Juliane Kokott of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has issued her opinion in Case C-138/24, involving an infringement claim by the European Commission against the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg on 18 June 2026. The case centres on whether Luxembourg incorrectly transposed the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD) by...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The  Advocate General (AG) Juliane Kokott of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has issued her <a href="https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:62024CC0138" target="_blank" rel="noopener">opinion</a> in Case C-138/24, involving an infringement claim by the European Commission against the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg on 18 June 2026.</p>
<p>The case centres on whether Luxembourg incorrectly transposed the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD) by including securitisation special purpose entities (SSPEs) within the definition of &#8220;financial undertakings,&#8221; thereby exempting them from interest limitation rules.</p>
<p><strong>Core legal dispute</strong></p>
<p>The ATAD includes a &#8220;rule of limitation of interests&#8221; to prevent multinational groups from artificially reducing their tax base through excessive interest payments. However, Article 4(7) of the ATAD allows Member States to exempt &#8220;financial undertakings&#8221; from these rules because their specific business models—where interest is often a core component of their activity—require a more tailored approach.</p>
<p>The Commission argued that the definition of &#8220;financial undertaking&#8221; in Article 2(5) of the ATAD provides an exhaustive list of entities. Since SSPEs (as defined by the Securitisation Regulation (EU) 2017/2402) are not on that list, the Commission contended that Luxembourg breached EU law by adding them to its national list of exempted entities.</p>
<p>Under ATAD, interest deductions are generally capped at 30% of EBITDA, with limited exceptions such as a EUR 3 million safe harbour and optional exclusions for certain financial undertakings.</p>
<p>The Commission argued that securitisation special purpose entities are not covered, because Article 2(5) sets out an exhaustive list of financial undertakings that does not include them.</p>
<p><strong>AG Kokott’s assessment</strong></p>
<p>AG Kokott acknowledged that, while SSPEs are not literally mentioned in the ATAD&#8217;s list, a purely formalistic interpretation would be insufficient. Her analysis focused on several key areas:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Comparability of SSPEs:</strong> The AG found that SSPEs are comparable to the financial undertakings explicitly listed in the ATAD. Like banks or investment funds, SSPEs primarily deal with borrowed capital and interest as their core business activity rather than as a means of financing industrial production.</li>
<li><strong>Regulatory framework:</strong> SSPEs became specifically regulated at the EU level through the Securitisation Regulation in late 2017—after the ATAD was adopted but before the deadline for its transposition. This regulation imposes transparency and oversight requirements similar to those of the financial entities already listed in the ATAD, making SSPEs less susceptible to the specific tax abuses the interest limitation rules target.</li>
<li><strong>Principle of equal treatment:</strong> A central pillar of the AG&#8217;s opinion is the principle of equal treatment (Article 20 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights). The AG argued that failing to treat SSPEs as financial undertakings would constitute unjustified unequal treatment of comparable situations.</li>
<li><strong>Primacy of primary law:</strong> The AG noted that when Member States transpose EU directives, they are bound by the Charter. Therefore, Luxembourg was not only permitted but obliged to interpret and apply the ATAD in conformity with primary law, which included ensuring equal treatment for comparable financial entities like SSPEs.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Conclusion and recommendation</strong></p>
<p>AG Kokott concluded that Luxembourg did not fail its obligations under the ATAD or the TFEU. She argued that by including SSPEs in the exemption, Luxembourg correctly applied the principle of equal treatment while exercising its margin of appreciation in transposing the directive. Consequently, she proposed that the Court of Justice should dismiss the Commission&#8217;s action and order the Commission to pay the costs.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[Turkey&#8217;s Revenue Administration, on 19 June 2026, published an updated Accommodation Tax Guide, providing revised explanations and examples on the application of the Accommodation Tax (Konaklama Vergisi) following a temporary reduction in the tax rate from 2% to 1% through 31 December 2026 under Presidential Decision No. 11263. The Accommodation Tax is regulated under Article...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Turkey&#8217;s Revenue Administration, on 19 June 2026, <a href="https://www.gib.gov.tr/duyuru-arsivi/guncel/18242_konaklama_vergisi_rehberi_yayimlandi" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> an updated <a href="https://cdn.gib.gov.tr/api/gibportal-file/file/getFile?objectKey=DUYURU/UNIVERSAL/2026/2026_Konaklama_Vergisi_Rehberi.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Accommodation Tax Guide</a>, providing revised explanations and examples on the application of the Accommodation Tax (Konaklama Vergisi) following a temporary reduction in the tax rate from 2% to 1% through 31 December 2026 under Presidential Decision No. 11263.</p>
<p>The Accommodation Tax is regulated under Article 34 of the Expense Taxes Law No. 6802 and has been in force since 1 January 2023. The updated guide aims to assist taxpayers by clarifying key aspects of the tax, including the taxable event, liable taxpayers, taxable and exempt services, the tax base, invoicing requirements, and declaration and payment procedures.</p>
<p>The tax applies to overnight accommodation services provided by facilities such as hotels, motels, holiday villages, pensions, apart-hotels, guesthouses and campsites. It also covers services supplied within the accommodation facility and sold together with the stay, including food and beverage services, entertainment activities, and the use of swimming pools, sports facilities and thermal spas.</p>
<p>Accommodation packages offered under concepts such as &#8220;all-inclusive&#8221; and &#8220;half-board&#8221; remain fully subject to the tax.</p>
<p>According to the guide, the operator of the accommodation facility is responsible for the tax. The taxable event occurs when the accommodation service is provided, regardless of whether payment is made in advance, after the service is rendered, or not collected. Complimentary stays provided for promotional purposes or to employees and relatives may also trigger a tax liability.</p>
<p>The tax base is the total value of the accommodation service excluding VAT (KDV). Where charges are denominated in foreign currency, amounts must be converted into Turkish lira using the Central Bank buying exchange rate applicable on the date the service is provided. The Accommodation Tax must be shown separately on invoices and similar documents.</p>
<p>The guide also outlines exemptions for services provided to students in student-only dormitories, pensions and camps, as well as services supplied to diplomatic missions, consulates and eligible diplomatic personnel where reciprocity conditions are met.</p>
<p>For compliance purposes, taxpayers must file Accommodation Tax returns electronically and pay the tax by the evening of the 26th day of the month following the relevant service period. Returns are submitted to the tax office where the taxpayer is registered for VAT or, where no VAT registration exists, to the competent local tax office.</p>
<p>The publication of the updated guide provides taxpayers with revised administrative guidance ahead of the expiry of the temporary 1% Accommodation Tax rate at the end of 2026, helping accommodation providers apply the tax and meet their reporting obligations correctly.</p>

		<title>Sweden expands tonnage tax regime, eases rules for shipping companies</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/sweden-expands-tonnage-tax-regime-eases-rules-for-shipping-companies/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=sweden-expands-tonnage-tax-regime-eases-rules-for-shipping-companies</link>

					<description><![CDATA[Sweden&#8217;s Parliament has approved a package of reforms to the country&#8217;s tonnage taxation system, broadening access to the regime and introducing more flexible rules for shipping companies. The legislation was adopted on 11 June 2026 and is intended to strengthen the competitiveness of the Swedish maritime sector while aligning national rules with European Union State...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Sweden&#8217;s Parliament has <a href="https://data.riksdagen.se/fil/CB6B351D-4C79-4B51-8B17-09713AA85B60" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved</a> a package of reforms to the country&#8217;s tonnage taxation system, broadening access to the regime and introducing more flexible rules for shipping companies.</p>
<p>The legislation was adopted on 11 June 2026 and is intended to strengthen the competitiveness of the Swedish maritime sector while aligning national rules with European Union State aid requirements.</p>
<p>The amendments, which are scheduled to enter into force on 20 July 2026 and apply to fiscal years beginning after 31 December 2026, expand the scope of the tonnage tax regime to cover a range of specialised maritime activities previously outside the system.</p>
<p><strong>Expanded scope for specialised maritime activities</strong></p>
<p>Under the new rules, tonnage taxation will be available for certain special shipping operations, including offshore construction, repair and maintenance services for wind farms and oil platforms. The expanded regime also covers cable and pipe laying, icebreaking, marine environment exploration linked to offshore construction projects, as well as towing activities where at least 50% of operations relate to transport. Salvage operations, bunkering services, environmental rescue activities, and support services such as providing workshop capacity or crew accommodation for qualifying activities will also be eligible.</p>
<p><strong>More flexible bareboat rental rules</strong></p>
<p>The reforms introduce greater flexibility for bareboat rentals. The maximum proportion of a shipping company&#8217;s total gross tonnage that may be rented out without a crew is increased from 20% to 50%, a change aimed at helping operators manage fluctuations in demand and vessel utilisation.</p>
<p><strong>Updated vessel eligibility requirements</strong></p>
<p>Changes have also been made to the criteria for qualifying vessels. The previous requirement that ships must mainly operate in international traffic will be replaced with a test based on whether the vessel is engaged in traffic exposed to international competition. In addition, the minimum size requirement for vessels engaged in special shipping activities will be reduced from 100 gross tons to 20 gross tons. Vessels operating exclusively on rivers, canals or lakes will remain outside the regime.</p>
<p><strong>Relaxed rules for depreciation funds and fleet renewal</strong></p>
<p>The legislation further relaxes rules governing depreciation funds (Överavskrivningsfond). Shipping companies will no longer need to demonstrate an increase in net tonnage to defer taxation; instead, they must show only that net tonnage has not decreased. Vessels covered by delivery contracts and scheduled for delivery within three years may also be counted as owned vessels, reducing the risk of unintended tax consequences during fleet renewal programmes.</p>
<p><strong>State aid safeguards and blocking period changes</strong></p>
<p>To ensure compliance with EU State aid rules, companies considered to be in financial difficulty will be excluded from the tonnage tax system. The reforms also revise rules governing blocking periods (Spärrtid), making re-entry conditions more consistent regardless of whether a company voluntarily leaves the regime or is removed by the Swedish Tax Agency.</p>
<p><strong>European Commission approval and rejected proposal</strong></p>
<p>The legislative package follows approval by the European Commission, which determined that the revised tonnage tax scheme is compatible with EU State aid rules for the period from 1 January 2027 to 31 December 2036.</p>
<p>One proposal that did not gain support would have allowed unlimited intra-group bareboat rentals. Lawmakers concluded that introducing such a measure would require a more extensive legal definition of corporate groups and therefore fell outside the scope of the current reform package.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

The Income Tax (Deduction for the Costs of Implementation of Flexible Work Arrangements) Rules 2026 provide a tax incentive for employers to adopt flexible work practices, including versatile scheduling and remote locations. Business...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Malaysia has gazetted the <a href="https://lom.agc.gov.my/ilims/upload/portal/akta/outputp/3558499/PUA%20225%20(2026).pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Income Tax (Deduction for the Costs of Implementation of Flexible Work Arrangements) Rules 2026</a>  on 16 June 2026.</p>
<p>The Income Tax (Deduction for the Costs of Implementation of Flexible Work Arrangements) Rules 2026 provide a tax incentive for employers to adopt flexible work practices, including versatile scheduling and remote locations. Business owners can claim a 50% tax deduction on qualifying expenses such as software procurement and capacity development for staff.</p>
<p>To qualify, these initiatives must be formally verified by Talent Corporation Malaysia Berhad and submitted within a specific timeframe between 2025 and 2027.</p>
<p>These rules are deemed effective starting from the year of assessment 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Scope of the deduction</strong></p>
<p>Employers can claim a deduction equivalent to 50% of the expenditure incurred for implementing flexible work arrangements (FWA). This deduction is granted in addition to any other deductions allowed under section 33 of the Income Tax Act 1967. The eligible expenditures fall into two main categories:</p>
<ul>
<li>Capacity development costs, which include training costs for employees.</li>
<li>Software acquisition costs.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Detailed capacity development costs: </strong>The rules define qualifying capacity development costs across five categories: training fees for courses and programmes, materials and space rental for training delivery, examination fees, and travelling expenses for employees and trainers. Travel costs are subject to defined limits—international transportation is capped at economy class airfare, while domestic travel uses economy class airfare or actual transport costs; accommodation is limited to MYR 300 per day and meals to MYR 150 per day.</p>
<p><strong>Definition of flexible work arrangements (FWA): </strong>Flexible work arrangements encompass three core dimensions: the location where work is performed, the timing and scheduling of working hours, and the total number of hours worked. These arrangements allow organisations and employees to establish tailored working conditions beyond traditional fixed office schedules.</p>
<p><strong>Mandatory conditions and limitations</strong></p>
<p>Employers seeking to claim FWA-related deductions must satisfy the following conditions:</p>
<ul>
<li>Talent Corporation Malaysia Berhad must verify both the FWA implementation and associated expenses.</li>
<li>Applications must be submitted between 1 January 2025 and 31 December 2027.</li>
<li>The total deductible expenditure is capped at MYR 500,000 and may be claimed only once</li>
<li>The Director General of Inland Revenue retains discretion to disallow any amounts considered excessive or unreasonable relative to ordinary business practice.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Exclusions</strong></p>
<p>These rules do not apply to employers who have already claimed deductions for FWA implementation under previous versions of these rules, specifically:</p>
<ul>
<li>The Income Tax (Deduction for Consultation and Training Costs for the Implementation of Flexible Work Arrangements) Rules 2015.</li>
<li>The Income Tax (Deduction for the Costs of Implementation of Flexible Work Arrangements) Rules 2021.</li>
</ul>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Nigeria’s Federal Ministry of Finance <a href="https://finance.gov.ng/federal-government-issues-transition-guidelines-for-tax-acts-2025/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a>, on 18 June 2026, that the federal government has issued the <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/179uCoDBBuS-H9H_O1MdKXlPBL8eNiYRl/view?usp=drive_link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">General Guidelines for the implementation of the Tax Acts 2025</a>, setting out the process for the transition from the repealed tax laws to the new tax framework effective from 1 January 2026.</p>
<p>Issued by the Federal Ministry of Finance, the guidelines provide direction to taxpayers, tax practitioners, revenue authorities and other stakeholders on how to address various issues arising from the old regime to the new framework.</p>
<p>Under the guidelines, the Tax Acts 2025 comprising the Nigeria Revenue Service (Establishment) Act, the Nigeria Tax Act, the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, and the Joint Revenue Board (Establishment) Act apply from the respective commencement dates as enacted in each law. In particular, 1 January 2026 for the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025.</p>
<p>Tax liabilities, assessments, audits, investigations, disputes and enforcement actions relating to periods before that date will be treated under the repealed tax laws.</p>
<p>Tax returns relating to accounting periods ending before 1 January 2026 will be filed under the previous tax laws, while returns relating to accounting periods ending from 1 January 2026 onward will be administered under the new tax framework.</p>
<p>The document also covers the treatment of income taxes, transaction taxes, development levies, tax incentives, exemptions, record-keeping obligations and transactions that span both the old and new tax regimes.</p>
<p>Existing tax incentives and exemptions granted under the repealed laws will remain in place until their expiration dates. New applications and pending requests, however, will be considered under the provisions of the Tax Acts 2025.</p>
<p>Speaking on the release of the Guidelines, the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, said the document provides a framework for managing transitional issues while ensuring that the new laws are not applied retrospectively. He described the Tax Acts 2025 as a significant milestone in Nigeria’s tax reform programme, noting that the guidelines set out how existing obligations, ongoing matters and future transactions will be treated under the new regime.</p>
<p>According to the Minister, the guidelines are anchored on three key principles – clarity, fairness and administrative certainty.</p>
<p>The guidelines are intended to promote uniform implementation and support effective administration across the Nigeria Revenue Service, State Internal Revenue Services, the FCT Internal Revenue Service, Local Government Revenue Committees, tax practitioners and taxpayers nationwide.</p>

It delivers targeted measures to support Canadians, build a strong economy and ensure that Canada is well positioned to navigate current...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Canada’s Department of Finance <a href="https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/news/2026/06/legislation-passes-to-implement-measures-from-the-spring-economic-update-2026.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> that Bill C‑30, An Act to implement certain provisions of the Spring Economic Update tabled in Parliament on 28 April 2026, has received Royal Assent on 19 June 2026.</p>
<p>It delivers targeted measures to support Canadians, build a strong economy and ensure that Canada is well positioned to navigate current global challenges and achieve long-term prosperity.</p>
<p>Bill C-30 introduces key measures to help reduce everyday costs, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Suspending the federal fuel excise tax on gasoline and diesel from 20 April to 7 September 2026, cutting costs by 10 cents per litre on gasoline and 4 cents on diesel fuel. The federal fuel excise tax on aviation fuels is also temporarily suspended.</li>
<li>Extending excise duty relief for the alcohol sector, including a 2% cap on annual inflationary duty increases and reduced rates for the first 15,000 hectolitres of beer brewed in Canada—providing over CAD 30 million in relief through 2028 and supporting thousands of jobs.</li>
<li>Easing homeownership costs by extending the Home Buyers’ Plan repayment grace period from two to five years for withdrawals made from RRSPs between 2026 and 2028, helping new homeowners manage costs in the early years of ownership.</li>
</ul>
<p>To support workers and families, measures adopted include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Enhancing the Labour Mobility Deduction by reducing the minimum distance threshold from 150 km to 120 km and increasing the maximum deduction from CAD 4,000 to CAD 10,000 annually – helping tradespeople who travel for work save more on taxes.</li>
<li>Supporting seasonal workers by extending the temporary Employment Insurance measure providing seasonal workers in targeted regions with up to five extra weeks of benefits to help cover income gaps between seasons.</li>
<li>Lowering Canada Pension Plan contributions by reducing the base CPP contribution rate from 9.9% to 9.5% starting in 2027, saving about CAD 133 annually for an employee earning CAD 70,000, with matching savings for employers.</li>
</ul>
<p>Bill C-30 also takes steps to support Canadian businesses and create a positive investment climate:</p>
<ul>
<li>Encouraging employee ownership by making permanent the CAD 10 million capital gains exemption for qualifying business transfers to employee ownership trusts and worker co‑operatives, supporting succession planning and preserving local jobs.</li>
<li>Expanding agricultural production by allowing immediate expensing for greenhouses, helping expand domestic food production and strengthening food security.</li>
</ul>
<p>To strengthen Canada’s financial frameworks and economic security, measures adopted include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Streamlining national security reviews by amending the Bank Act to ensure that investments by foreign banks and their affiliates can be reviewed for national security risks under one framework only, reducing duplication and ensuring clear, efficient oversight.</li>
<li>Consolidating cost recovery by amending the Bank of Canada Act to consolidate the Bank of Canada’s cost recovery responsibilities for its supervisory mandates, ensuring transparent and consistent rules.</li>
</ul>

		<title>Germany updates guidance on permanent establishments under domestic, international tax law</title>

					<description><![CDATA[Germany’s Ministry of Finance has published updated administrative principles on the concept and establishment of permanent establishments (PEs) under domestic and international tax law, providing detailed guidance for both resident and non-resident taxpayers engaged in cross-border activities. The updated circular, issued by the Federal Ministry of Finance (BMF) on 18 June 2026, sets out the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Germany’s Ministry of Finance has published updated administrative principles on the concept and establishment of permanent establishments (PEs) under domestic and international tax law, providing detailed guidance for both resident and non-resident taxpayers engaged in cross-border activities.</p>
<p>The updated <a href="https://www.bundesfinanzministerium.de/Content/DE/Downloads/BMF_Schreiben/Internationales_Steuerrecht/Allgemeine_Informationen/2026-06-18-grunds-verwal-betriebsstaettenbegriff.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">circular</a>, issued by the Federal Ministry of Finance (BMF) on 18 June 2026, sets out the administrative framework for determining when a taxpayer has a taxable presence in Germany through a permanent establishment or permanent representative.</p>
<p><strong>Two-step assessment for taxing rights</strong></p>
<p>According to the guidance, the assessment generally follows a two-step process. Authorities must first determine whether a PE exists under German domestic law, particularly Sections 12 and 13 of the Fiscal Code (Abgabenordnung – AO). Where a Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) applies, a second assessment is required to establish whether treaty provisions limit Germany’s taxing rights.</p>
<p>The principles apply to taxpayers with both unlimited and limited tax liability and are intended primarily for cross-border tax situations.</p>
<p>Under Section 12 AO, a PE is generally defined as a fixed place of business or facility serving the activities of an enterprise. The BMF states that four conditions must be satisfied: the existence of a business facility, a fixed geographical connection, a sufficient duration of use and the enterprise’s power of disposal over the facility.</p>
<p>The guidance explains that a business facility may include offices, workshops, individual workspaces and, in certain circumstances, equipment such as laptops. A facility must generally be intended to remain in place for at least six months and be available to the enterprise on a non-temporary basis through ownership, lease or another right of use.</p>
<p>The circular also confirms that a place of management constitutes a PE where key day-to-day management decisions are made. Construction and assembly projects may create a PE if an individual project, or connected projects, exceeds six months under domestic law.</p>
<p><strong>Domestic law and treaty differences highlighted</strong></p>
<p>The BMF provides further clarification on the concept of a permanent representative under Section 13 AO. A permanent representative may exist where a natural or legal person conducts an enterprise’s business on a sustained basis while acting under its instructions, even if no fixed place of business is present.</p>
<p>The guidance highlights several differences between domestic legislation and treaty provisions based on the OECD Model Tax Convention. While German domestic law generally recognises a construction or assembly PE after six months, many tax treaties apply a 12-month threshold. Tax treaties also commonly include a “negative list” excluding facilities used solely for preparatory or auxiliary activities from PE status, an exception not contained in domestic law.</p>
<p>The circular further addresses anti-fragmentation rules found in many modern tax treaties. These provisions are designed to prevent businesses from splitting a unified operation into multiple activities that appear preparatory or auxiliary in order to avoid creating a PE.</p>
<p><strong>Guidance covers modern business arrangements</strong></p>
<p>The updated principles also provide guidance on contemporary business models and working arrangements. In relation to home offices, the BMF states that an employee’s private residence will generally not constitute a PE for an employer because the employer lacks the necessary power of disposal over the premises. However, a management PE may arise where management functions are carried out from the home office. The guidance also indicates that an employer PE will generally not be created where an employee works from home for less than 50% of their working time.</p>
<p>For social media content creators, the BMF notes that influencers will typically establish a management PE at the location where content is planned, produced and uploaded.</p>
<p>Additional examples cover ships, third-party premises and shared workspaces. Mobile ships are generally not regarded as PEs, while permanently moored vessels used for commercial activities, such as hotel or restaurant ships, may qualify. Work performed at a client’s premises will create a PE only where the contractor maintains a sufficiently fixed business presence and carries out its core activities at that location. Desk-sharing arrangements may also constitute a PE where a workspace is reliably available for at least six months.</p>
<p>The updated administrative principles replace previous guidance and provide a consolidated interpretation of Germany’s PE rules under domestic legislation and applicable tax treaties.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Sri Lanka unveils major tax law changes covering income, WHT, registration</title>

					<description><![CDATA[Sri Lanka has enacted a wide-ranging set of tax reforms under the Inland Revenue (Amendment) Act, No. 11 of 2026, introducing changes to income tax, withholding tax (WHT), capital gains tax, taxpayer registration and compliance requirements. The legislation was certified on 3 June 2026, while the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) outlined the key measures in...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Sri Lanka has enacted a wide-ranging set of tax reforms under the Inland Revenue (Amendment) Act, No. 11 of 2026, introducing changes to income tax, withholding tax (WHT), capital gains tax, taxpayer registration and compliance requirements.</p>
<p>The legislation was certified on 3 June 2026, while the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) outlined the key measures in <a href="https://www.ird.gov.lk/en/Lists/Latest%20News%20%20Notices/Attachments/793/SEC_PN_IT_2026-02_E.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Notice SEC/PN/IT/2026/02 issued on 8 June</a>.</p>
<p>The amendments affect individuals, businesses, financial institutions and withholding agents, with several provisions taking effect retrospectively and others applying from the 2025/2026 and 2026/2027 years of assessment.</p>
<p><strong>Withholding tax regime expanded</strong></p>
<p>The Act introduces a series of withholding tax amendments.</p>
<p>From 1 April 2026, the National Gem and Jewellery Authority must submit monthly tax returns containing information specified by the Commissioner-General.</p>
<p>Resident individuals earning interest income from bank and financial institution deposits may submit self-declarations from 1 April 2025 if they do not derive taxable income during the relevant year. False declarations may attract penalties of up to LKR 200,000.</p>
<p>The scope of the 5% withholding tax on service fee payments to resident individuals has also been significantly broadened. Effective from 3 June 2026, the tax applies to a wide range of professions and service providers, including auditors, personal trainers, coaches, artists, actors, photographers, counsellors, dentists, veterinarians, information technology specialists, translators, writers and others where monthly payments exceed LKR 100,000.</p>
<p>Withholding agents that fail to comply with annual reporting requirements may face penalties of up to LKR 200,000 per year of assessment.</p>
<p><strong>Selected professions added to the 5% WHT regime</strong></p>
<table>

<td style="text-align: center">Auditors, valuers, advisors, translators</td>

<td style="text-align: center">Photographers, videographers, social media specialists, brand ambassadors</td>
</tr>

<td style="text-align: center">Technical services</td>
<td style="text-align: center">Information technology specialists, electricians</td>

</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Pass-through tax treatment introduced for unit trusts and mutual funds</strong></p>
<p>A new pass-through taxation framework has been established for unit trusts and mutual funds. These entities must provide unit holders with annual certificates detailing income, exempt amounts and withholding tax information within five months of the end of the year of assessment.</p>
<p>Entities that fail to issue the required certificates will instead be treated as companies and become liable for tax. The new regime applies from 1 April 2025, with further guidance expected from the IRD.</p>
<p><strong>Motor vehicle gains excluded from taxable income</strong></p>
<p>Under the revised rules, gains from the realisation of motor vehicles will no longer be treated as other income under Section 8 of the Inland Revenue Act where the vehicles are neither trading stock nor depreciable assets eligible for capital allowances. Corresponding losses will also not be deductible. The measure applies retrospectively from 1 April 2024.</p>
<p><strong>Cash transaction restrictions revised</strong></p>
<p>The Act amends provisions designed to discourage large cash transactions. Payments of LKR 500,000 or more made in cash or by non-approved methods in connection with a single transaction or related transactions may not be claimed as deductible expenses or included in the tax cost of an asset.</p>
<p>However, the amendments now allow cash deposits made directly into the recipient&#8217;s bank account to qualify as an approved payment method. This change is effective from 8 May 2023.</p>
<p><strong>New relief for gifts, donations and life insurance proceeds</strong></p>
<p>Transfers of assets by gift or donation to the Government of Sri Lanka or qualifying universities will not trigger tax because consideration for the transfer will be deemed equal to the asset&#8217;s net cost. This provision applies from 3 June 2026.</p>
<p>Donations to the Government or government-established funds that qualify as deductible payments may now be carried forward to future years of assessment after deduction from total assessable income. The change takes effect from 1 April 2025.</p>
<p>The legislation also introduces Section 52A, which clarifies the treatment of amounts received under life insurance policies. Payments received by policyholders or beneficiaries upon death, maturity or surrender of a policy will generally be excluded from assessable income, subject to specified exceptions. The measure applies from 1 April 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Residence rules updated for foreign workers and investors</strong></p>
<p>Several changes have been made to Sri Lanka&#8217;s tax residence rules.</p>
<p>Individuals working on Sri Lankan ships who are citizens or subjects of another country will only be taxed as residents on employment income earned from that ship.</p>
<p>In addition, holders of an Investor Category Residence Visa will not be treated as Sri Lankan tax residents from 1 April 2025. The amendments also clarify that individuals working abroad for at least one year under contracts with unrelated foreign employers will not be regarded as Sri Lankan tax residents during the</p>
<p><strong>Statement of Estimated Tax requirement abolished</strong></p>
<p>The requirement to file a Statement of Estimated Tax (SET) has been removed. Quarterly income tax instalments will instead be based on the income tax payable in the immediately preceding year of assessment.</p>
<p>Taxpayers with no taxable income in the prior year or expecting lower taxable income will be able to determine instalments under procedures to be specified by the Commissioner-General.</p>
<p><strong>Return filing relief for employees and senior citizens</strong></p>
<p>From 1 April 2025, individuals whose only income is employment income fully subject to Advance Personal Income Tax (APIT) will generally not be required to maintain an income tax file or submit tax returns.</p>
<p>The exemption also applies where interest income does not exceed LKR 5,000 and no quarterly instalments or final tax payments are due.</p>
<p>Senior citizens will be permitted to file returns either electronically or in writing from the 2025/2026 year of assessment.</p>
<p><strong>TIN registration requirements strengthened</strong></p>
<p>The amendments significantly expand Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) requirements.</p>
<p>All companies incorporated or registered in Sri Lanka must register with the Commissioner-General within 30 days. TINs will no longer be treated as confidential information and will become mandatory for a range of activities, including opening bank accounts, registering land, registering businesses, obtaining building plan approvals, registering motor vehicles and transferring shares in Sri Lankan companies.</p>
<p>The requirements will take effect once verification procedures are published by the Commissioner-General.</p>
<p>Capital gains tax rates revised and investment incentives introduced</p>
<p>Capital gains tax rates have been revised from 3 June 2026.</p>

</table>
<p>The legislation also introduces a 100% Enhanced Capital Allowance (ECA) from 1 April 2026 for investments exceeding USD 250,000 in depreciable assets used in a new business undertaking in Sri Lanka, excluding intangible assets.</p>
<p>Tax compliance, enforcement and penalty provisions updated</p>
<p>The Act expands information-sharing powers, allowing taxpayer information to be disclosed to the Financial Intelligence Unit of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, the Inspector-General of Police and the Sri Lanka Accounting and Auditing Standards Monitoring Board for specified purposes.</p>
<p>Default tax recovery procedures have also been strengthened. Beginning with the year of assessment commencing on 1 April 2026, unpaid taxes may be recovered through court proceedings based on certificates issued by the Commissioner-General, subject to appeal safeguards.</p>
<p>Failure to register, file returns, submit annual statements or comply with requests from the Commissioner-General may result in prosecution. Upon conviction, offenders may face fines of up to LKR 400,000, imprisonment for up to six months, or both.</p>
<p>Interest waiver available for outstanding tax liabilities</p>
<p>As part of a relief measure, interest on late payments and underpayments of tax, including surcharge tax and debt repayment levy, will be waived up to the 2024/2025 year of assessment provided the principal tax liability is settled in full by 2 December 2026 or has already been paid.</p>
<p>The amendments represent one of the most extensive overhauls of Sri Lanka&#8217;s Inland Revenue framework in recent years, affecting tax administration, compliance obligations, withholding tax procedures and investment-related tax incentives.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Brazil’s Federal Revenue Service (RFB) has <a href="https://www.gov.br/receitafederal/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/2026/junho/receita-federal-atualiza-regras-do-adicional-da-csll-no-contexto-das-regras-globe" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> the <a href="https://normasinternet2.receita.fazenda.gov.br/#/consulta/externa/151902" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Normative Instruction RFB No. 2,329</a> on 19 June 2026, amending the rules governing the Additional Social Contribution on Net Profit (CSLL) surcharge as per <a href="https://normasinternet2.receita.fazenda.gov.br/#/consulta/externa/140884" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Normative Instruction RFB No. 2,228</a> of 3 October 2024 on 19 June 2026.</p>
<p>The update strengthens Brazil&#8217;s implementation of the OECD&#8217;s Global Rules against Base Erosion (GloBE Rules) and provides multinational groups with clearer operational guidance for compliance.</p>
<p>The CSLL Surcharge represents Brazil&#8217;s implementation of the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (QDMTT), designed to ensure multinational enterprises pay a minimum level of tax on their Brazilian operations. Developed under the OECD&#8217;s Inclusive Framework initiative, the GloBE Rules aim to establish a global framework preventing tax base erosion through aggressive planning strategies.</p>
<p><strong>Centralised payment option clarified</strong></p>
<p>The revised rules refine how multinational groups may elect to concentrate CSLL Surcharge payments through a single constituent entity, rather than distributing liabilities across multiple Brazilian entities. Under the amendment to Normative Instruction RFB No. 2,228 (3 October 2024), groups can now designate one entity as the sole taxpayer and responsible party for the entire group&#8217;s surcharge obligation.</p>
<p>The Federal Revenue Service (RFB) will distinguish between individual entity payments and centralised payments using separate identification codes on the Federal Revenue Collection Document (DARF). If a group elects centralised payment, the designated entity must apply its specific centralisation code when remitting funds. All payment amounts and calculated tax liabilities will be reported through DCTFWeb, Brazil&#8217;s digital tax filing system.</p>
<p>Importantly, multinational groups retain annual flexibility to switch between centralised and other payment allocation methods, allowing them to adapt their structure based on changing circumstances.</p>
<p><strong>Simplifying fiscal year alignment for GloBE compliance</strong></p>
<p>The update addresses practical complications arising from misalignment between jurisdictional fiscal years and Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) periods under the GloBE Transition Simplifying Rule (RSGT). Previously, groups faced complexity when their Declared Policy Position (DPP) fiscal year did not align with Brazil&#8217;s calendar year.</p>
<p>Groups can now choose either:</p>
<ul>
<li>A DPP that closes during Brazil&#8217;s fiscal year, or</li>
<li>A DPP that begins during Brazil&#8217;s fiscal year</li>
</ul>
<p>Consider a multinational with a July-to-June fiscal year operating in Brazil (January-to-December jurisdiction). For the 2025 fiscal year, the group may elect to use either the DPP ending 30 June 2025 or the one beginning 1 July 2025. This flexibility eliminates the need to consolidate data from multiple declarations, streamlining compliance and reducing administrative burden.</p>
<p><strong>Advancing tax transparency</strong></p>
<p>This refinement reflects Brazil&#8217;s continued commitment to aligning domestic regulations with international tax transparency standards while reducing administrative complexity for multinationals operating in the country. The amendments increase legal certainty and support Brazil&#8217;s role as a participant in the OECD&#8217;s efforts to create a more equitable global tax environment.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer <a href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/june/ustr-announces-initiation-section-301-investigation-germanys-persistent-underpayment-innovative" target="_blank" rel="noopener">initiated</a> an investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 against Germany on 18 June 2026.  This investigation will seek to determine whether persistent underpayment for innovative pharmaceutical products by Germany is unreasonable or discriminatory and burdens or restricts US commerce. This investigation follows months of meaningful discussions with German partners in an effort to resolve this issue.</p>
<p><em>“President Trump has made clear that American patients should not be shouldering a disproportionate share of global pharmaceutical research and development,” said Ambassador Greer. “I am particularly concerned with news that Germany is fast-tracking legislation that would further reduce its spending on innovative pharmaceuticals. This is a serious step backwards at a time when our trading partners need to step up and start paying their fair share to fund innovative pharmaceutical research and development. We believe that the United States and Germany can find a path forward that expands access to the most innovative drugs for the German people while ensuring fair reimbursement for the pharmaceuticals made by American workers.&#8221;</em></p>
<p><em>“On 2 April 2026, the US and the UK announced a ground-breaking arrangement on pharmaceutical pricing that will help drive investment and innovation in both countries. Germany should follow suit with constructive negotiations to address this imbalance. Fighting the war against disease is a shared burden across wealthy nations,” said US Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “The United States is calling on Germany to pay its fair share for the innovative treatments its people use. I commend Ambassador Greer for his leadership in confronting this imbalance. Fair reimbursement strengthens medical innovation and helps ensure the development of the next generation of lifesaving cures.”</em></p>
<p><strong>Background</strong></p>
<p>On 12 May 2025, the President directed the US Trade Representative to “take all necessary and appropriate action” to address foreign countries’ unfair actions that have the “effect of forcing American patients to pay for a disproportionate amount of global pharmaceutical research and development, including by suppressing the price of pharmaceutical products below fair market value in foreign countries.”</p>
<p>Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting US  commerce. Section 301 may be used to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government practices that burden or restrict US  commerce. Under Section 302(b) of the Trade Act, the US  Trade Representative may self-initiate an investigation under Section 301.</p>
<p>A Section 301(b) investigation examines whether the acts, policies, or practices are unreasonable or discriminatory and burden or restrict US  commerce. After considering the advice of the inter-agency Section 301 Committee, the US  Trade Representative initiates investigations. The US  Trade Representative must seek consultations with the foreign government whose acts, policies, or practices are at issue in each investigation. The Office of the US  Trade Representative (USTR) has requested consultations with Germany in connection with this investigation.</p>
<p>To be assured of consideration, interested persons should submit written comments, requests to appear at the hearing, and a summary of the testimony, by 10 August 2026. USTR will hold a hearing in connection with these investigations on 22 September 2026.</p>
<p>As set out in the Federal Register notice, the investigation relates to allegations of Germany’s unfair pricing policies and practices with regard to innovative pharmaceutical products, which result in the United States paying a disproportionate share of global research and development (R&amp;D) costs for innovative pharmaceuticals.</p>
<p>Although the means and tools for payment disparities for innovative pharmaceuticals vary, they may include the imposition of:</p>
<ul>
<li>supplemental discounts in exchange for confidentiality of negotiated prices; and</li>
<li>mandatory variable rate rebates.</li>
</ul>
<p>A copy of the Federal Register Notice is available <a href="https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/files/Press/Releases/2026/Germany%20Pharma%20Section%20301%20Initiation%20FRN%206-18-26.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">here</a>.</p>
<p>A docket for comments regarding the investigation will be available <a href="https://comments.ustr.gov/s/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">here</a>.</p>

		<title>Australia: ATO issues guidance on GIR XML file requirements for globe information return</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/australia-ato-issues-guidance-on-gir-xml-file-requirements-for-globe-information-return/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=australia-ato-issues-guidance-on-gir-xml-file-requirements-for-globe-information-return</link>

					<description><![CDATA[The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has recently issued guidance on the XML file requirements for the GloBE Information Return (GIR), offering clarification to assist filers in completing specific GIR data elements. When preparing the GloBE Information Return (GIR) XML file, ensure that you complete each part of the schema correctly to avoid processing delays or...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has recently issued guidance on <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/in-detail/multinationals/global-and-domestic-minimum-tax/lodging-paying-and-other-obligations-for-pillar-two/globe-information-return-gir-xml-file-requirements" target="_blank" rel="noopener">the XML file requirements for the GloBE Information Return (GIR)</a>, offering clarification to assist filers in completing specific GIR data elements.</p>
<p>When preparing the GloBE Information Return (GIR) XML file, ensure that you complete each part of the schema correctly to avoid processing delays or errors. The following information will assist you to prepare the file correctly.</p>
<p><strong>Bulk Business Document Message wrapper</strong></p>
<p>All XML files lodged with the ATO require a Bulk Business Document Message (BBDM) wrapper. See the following table for key BBDM wrapper element values required for the GIR XML schema file.</p>
<table style="border-collapse: collapse">

Allowed values are &#8216;ABN&#8217;, &#8216;TFN&#8217; or &#8216;ARN&#8217;<br />
We expect, in most cases, the entity lodging the GIR with the ATO will be the Australian UPE or DFE</td>
</tr>

<td>TFN or ABN or ARN of the entity lodging the GIR. The value of the identifier provided in the IdentifierName</td>
