The temporary windfall tax, set to take effect on 1 August 2026, aims to recoup some of the billions in subsidies the state has poured into keeping...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Poland&#8217;s government has <a href="https://www.gov.pl/web/finanse/rzad-przyjal-przepisy-chroniace-polakow-przed-skutkami-wysokich-cen-paliw" target="_blank" rel="noopener">introduced</a> emergency legislation targeting fuel companies that have reaped unusually large profits from Middle East-driven energy turmoil, according to a release on 16 June 2026.</p>
<p>The temporary windfall tax, set to take effect on 1 August 2026, aims to recoup some of the billions in subsidies the state has poured into keeping fuel prices affordable for consumers and businesses.</p>
<p>The trigger for this measure is the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz following conflict in the Middle East, which sent global oil prices surging. While ordinary citizens and businesses struggled with rising costs, some fuel-sector firms—particularly those engaged in production and international trading of liquid fuels—saw their margins balloon far beyond normal levels, not through better management or investment, but simply through supply shock windfall.</p>
<p><strong>How the tax captures extraordinary profits</strong></p>
<p>To identify excessive gains, the government will compare each company&#8217;s actual 2026 revenues against a calculated benchmark. That benchmark is based on their average profit margins from 2025, with an added 20% cushion. This buffer protects businesses from being taxed on profits resulting from legitimate market growth or normal annual fluctuations. Only profits exceeding this reference point face taxation at a 60% rate.</p>
<p>The tax applies throughout the period from 1 March to 31 December 2026 for enterprises holding licenses to trade fuels internationally.</p>
<p><strong>Payment schedule and implementation</strong></p>
<p>Companies will submit monthly advance payments calculated cumulatively. The first batch, covering March through July 2026, will be divided into four equal instalments payable between September and December 2026. The final annual settlement is due by 30 April 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Why this matters</strong></p>
<p>Poland has already spent several billion zloty (PLN) protecting households and firms through emergency fuel measures—slashing VAT on petrol and diesel to just 8% and cutting excise duties to EU-permitted minimums.</p>
<p>By implementing a windfall tax similar to those adopted across Europe during the post-Ukraine energy crisis, the government seeks to share the burden more equitably, ensuring that taxpayers don&#8217;t shoulder the entire cost while energy firms pocket record gains from the same market disruption.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bolivia&#8217;s National Tax Service (SIN) <a href="https://www.impuestos.gob.bo/index.php/nota_prensa/baja-al-5-el-pago-inicial-y-las-garantias-para-facilidades-de-pago-de-deudas-tributarias/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced </a>on 12 June 2026 that it has slashed the financial barriers for taxpayers seeking to defer their tax obligations.</p>
<p>Under Board Resolution (RND) 102600000020, effective 12 June 2026, the agency has unified down payment and guarantee requirements at a flat 5% across all debt levels.</p>
<p>The measure represents a significant departure from traditional tax collection rigidity, designed to support struggling businesses while maintaining revenue generation.</p>
<p><strong>Dramatic simplification of entry costs</strong></p>
<p>The change eliminates a tiered system that previously imposed sliding-scale requirements based on debt size. Companies or individuals registering a tax debt once faced down payments ranging from 10% to 15% and guarantees (in cash or government securities) reaching up to 20%. Combined, these upfront costs frequently exceeded 35% of the total obligation and had to be satisfied within five days.</p>
<p>The new unified 5% rate for both the initial payment and guarantee requirement applies uniformly, whether a taxpayer owes BOB 10,000 or more than BOB 1 million. This simplification removes bureaucratic layers while dramatically reducing the cash reserves needed to access financing arrangements.</p>
<p><strong>Strategic response to economic strain</strong></p>
<p>SIN leadership positioned the resolution as a deliberate policy response to mounting liquidity pressures across Bolivia&#8217;s commercial and productive sectors. Rather than viewing tax collection as a punitive function, the authority has reframed itself as a facilitator of business continuity. By lowering entry thresholds into payment plans, SIN aims to encourage voluntary compliance among debtors who might otherwise default or abandon formalisation due to prohibitive entry costs.</p>
<p><strong>Measuring state efficiency differently</strong></p>
<p>The measure signals a broader shift in how Bolivia&#8217;s tax administration evaluates its own performance—prioritising the viability and fairness of tax solutions over the severity of enforcement mechanisms.</p>

Flexible payment plans extend up to 36 months for those unable to pay immediately.</p>
<p><strong>Structural reforms</strong></p>

<p>The Income Tax Act, 1962, provides specifically that certain amounts expressed in a foreign currency must be translated into rand by the application of an applicable average exchange rate.</p>
<p>The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) determines weighted average exchange rates, based on the foreign exchange transactions of commercial banks. SARS publishes these rates on a quarterly basis, which may be used by stakeholders (taxpayers) in the determination of the average exchange rate when required in the Act.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Swedish Government <a href="https://www.regeringen.se/pressmeddelanden/2026/06/skattelattnader-for-att-oka-foretagens-investeringar-i-forskning-och-utveckling/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">proposed</a>, on 11 June 2026, additional tax relief for companies with employees engaged in research and development (R&amp;D) activities to boost business investment in R&amp;D, strengthen Sweden’s competitiveness and support economic growth.</p>

<li>Allowing the Swedish Tax Agency, when necessary, to obtain opinions from other authorities to better assess whether particular work qualifies as research and development.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>More generous expert tax relief</strong></p>
<p>The Government is also proposing more generous rules for expert tax relief. The expert tax regime provides a tax concession for foreign experts working in Sweden. Under the current rules, 25% of salary is exempt from taxation for a specified period. The proposal would increase the tax-exempt portion of salary from 25% to 30%.</p>
<p>The legislative amendments are proposed to enter into force on 1 January 2027.</p>

				<category><![CDATA[Policy announcements]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[UK]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=83650</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The UK’s HMRC outlined changes to Section 137 of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 (TCGA) that took effect on 26 November 2025, published in the Capital Gains Manual on the Anti-avoidance rule for share exchanges and company reconstructions from November 2025. The UK anti-avoidance rules for share exchanges and company reconstructions took effect...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UK’s HMRC outlined changes to Section 137 of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 (TCGA) that took effect on 26 November 2025, published in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/capital-gains-manual" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Capital Gains Manual</a> on the<a href="https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/capital-gains-manual/cg-app20" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Anti-avoidance rule for share exchanges and company reconstructions from November 2025</a>.</p>
<p>The UK anti-avoidance rules for share exchanges and company reconstructions took effect on 26 November 2025, following legislation in the Finance Act 2026.</p>
<p>The revised rule, primarily centered on Section 137 of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992, shifts from focusing on the &#8220;bona fide commercial reasons&#8221; of an exchange to a more targeted &#8220;purpose&#8221; test. It now applies when:</p>
<ul>
<li>There are arrangements relating to an exchange of securities.</li>
<li>A main purpose of those arrangements is to reduce or avoid a capital gains liability.</li>
</ul>
<p>This change was driven by court rulings suggesting the previous wording was too narrow, often failing to capture tax avoidance arrangements embedded within otherwise commercial transactions.</p>
<p><strong>Key principles and application</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Deferral vs. avoidance:</strong> HMRC maintains that the mere deferral of tax is not avoidance. The rule targets arrangements designed to eliminate or reduce a tax charge altogether, rather than just delaying it in accordance with the intended purpose of the legislation.</li>
<li><strong>Proportionate counteraction:</strong> Unlike the previous rule, which could disapply &#8220;no disposal&#8221; treatment for all participants, the revised rule allows HMRC to make &#8220;just and reasonable&#8221; adjustments. This ensures counteraction is proportionate and only affects the specific shareholders obtaining a tax advantage.</li>
<li><strong>Removal of the 5% threshold:</strong> The previous exemption for shareholders holding 5% or less of a company has been removed. Small shareholdings can still yield significant tax advantages, so they are now within scope if they benefit from avoidance arrangements.</li>
<li><strong>Self-Assessment and HMRC powers: </strong>While HMRC uses its enquiry powers to apply the rule, taxpayers are expected to self-assess and include adjustments in their returns if they believe the rule applies.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Exclusions and safe harbours</strong></p>
<p>HMRC has clarified that the rule is not intended to disrupt standard commercial restructuring that aligns with the intent of tax reliefs, including:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Preparatory reorganisations:</strong> Restructuring to prepare a business for entry into beneficial regimes, such as Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) or the Substantial Shareholding Exemption (SSE), is generally acceptable if it does not subvert the regime&#8217;s requirements.</li>
<li><strong>Private equity structures: </strong>Arrangements allowing management to choose between tax-deferred reinvestment or post-tax cash proceeds, or the use of &#8220;blocker&#8221; companies for overseas structures, are typically not viewed as avoidance.</li>
<li><strong>Earn-outs:</strong> Structuring an earn-out as securities (under Section 138A) rather than cash is generally considered consistent with the purpose of the legislation.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/uk-finance-act-2026-receives-royal-assent/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, The UK’s Finance (No. 2) Bill 2025-26 was granted Royal Assent on 18 March 2026, introducing measures across income, corporate, and inheritance taxes, environmental levies, and tax administration.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore has published <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/docs/default-source/uploadedfiles/pdf/advance-ruling-summary-no-8-2026.pdf?sfvrsn=dff2d94f_4" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advance Ruling Summary No. 8/2026 </a>on 2 Jun 2026, clarifying the application of Section 10L of the Income Tax Act 1947 in determining whether a company qualifies as an excluded incentive entity or an excluded entity that meets the prescribed economic substance requirements.</p>
<p>The ruling determines whether gains derived by Company A (a Singapore-incorporated entity) from transferring shares in Company B (a foreign-incorporated entity) are subject to tax under Section 10L.</p>
<p><strong>Relevant background and facts</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>The parties</strong>: Company A is a Singapore company involved in sales, marketing, and packaging. Company B is a foreign-incorporated related company.</li>
<li><strong>The transaction:</strong> Company A transferred its shares in Company B to a new Singapore company (&#8220;New Company&#8221;) in exchange for shares in that New Company.</li>
<li><strong>Tax incentives:</strong> Company A was enjoying a tax incentive under the Economic Expansion Incentives (Relief from Income Tax) Act 1967. However, the qualifying activities for this incentive did not include the holding or disposal of shares in related companies.</li>
<li><strong>Economic substance:</strong> Company A is not a pure equity-holding entity (non-PEHE). It maintains adequate human resources with necessary qualifications in Singapore, its key business decisions are made in Singapore, and it expects to incur more than a specified amount (SGD) in local business expenditure.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>The rulings</strong></p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Not an excluded incentive entity:</strong> Company A did not qualify as an &#8220;Excluded Incentive Entity&#8221; under section 10L(8)(c) because the sale of shares was not part of or incidental to its specific incentivised qualifying activities.</li>
<li><strong>Status as an excluded entity:</strong> Because Company A is a non-PEHE and satisfied the prescribed economic substance requirements, it is regarded as an &#8220;excluded entity&#8221; under section 10L(8)(d).</li>
<li><strong>Tax impact:</strong> The foreign-sourced disposal gains from the sale will not be chargeable to tax under section 10(1)(g) of the ITA when remitted or deemed remitted to Singapore.</li>
<li><strong>Duration:</strong> This ruling applies to foreign-sourced disposal gains from any sale of foreign assets by Company A from the Year of Assessment T through T+4.</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>Reasons for the decision</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Incentive scope:</strong> Section 10L generally does not apply to gains from disposals that are incidental to activities covered by specific tax incentives. Since Company A&#8217;s incentive did not cover share disposals, this specific exemption did not apply.</li>
<li><strong>Substance test:</strong> Company A successfully met the economic substance requirements for a non-PEHE by having sufficient qualified staff and local decision-making processes in Singapore.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>General guidance for taxpayers</strong></p>
<p>The ruling notes that taxpayers should refer to the IRAS e-Tax Guide &#8220;Income Tax: Tax Treatment of Gains or Losses from the Sale of Foreign Assets (Third Edition)&#8221; for further details. Specifically:</p>
<ul>
<li>Paragraph 7.2 provides examples of exclusions for entities with tax incentives.</li>
<li>Paragraphs 8.7 to 8.9 explain the economic substance test for non-PEHEs.</li>
</ul>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan&#8217;s Ministry of Finance (MoF) has released a <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/eng/singlehtml/f48d641f159a4866b1d31c0916fbcc71?cntId=32f3aa3977f8464b899e3c9209cd3d1b" target="_blank" rel="noopener">notice</a> on 1 June 2026, reminding taxpayers of the requirements governing reasonable interest on inter-company lending arrangements.</p>
<p>To protect the rights and interests of company shareholders and creditors, the Company Act stipulates that companies may lend to shareholders or any other person only under the circumstances that an inter-company transaction calls for such lending arrangement or an inter-company short-term financing facility is necessary provided. Furthermore, interest income must be calculated in accordance with Paragraph 2, Article 24-3 of the Income Tax Act.</p>
<p>The National Taxation Bureau of the Southern Area, Ministry of Finance stated that, in accordance with Paragraph 2, Article 24-3 of the Income Tax Act, “a company that lends money to a shareholder or any person without charging interest or charging the stipulated interest at an obviously lower rate, except for paying in advance the salary of an employee, shall calculate interest income based on the lending base rate of the Bank of Taiwan on 1 January of each respective year and an interest income tax shall be levied on the profit-seeking enterprise.”</p>
<p>The National Taxation Bureau calls on profit-seeking enterprises to pay attention to these regulations to avoid tax adjustments and being asked to pay any additional tax levied.</p>
<p>For example, the National Taxation Bureau found during an audit that the asset-liability statement of Company A’s income tax return for the year 2023 reported other receivables of TWD 30 million.</p>
<p>Upon investigation, it was determined that this amount was a short-term financing loan to a peer company, for which Company A charged an interest rate of 1% per annum. Since the agreed interest rate was deemed excessively low, the interest income should be adjusted upward based on the lending base rate of the Bank of Taiwan on 1 January 2023 (2.867% per annum), in accordance with Paragraph 2, Article 24-3 of the Income Tax Act.</p>
<p>The Bureau would like to remind profit-seeking enterprises that when lending money to shareholders or any person, they should ensure the reasonableness of the interest charged to avoid tax adjustments and  additional tax levied from obviously too low rates.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Sweden has enacted an amendment to the Value Added Tax Act (2023:200) that lowers the VAT rate on admission to dance events from 25% to 6%.</p>
<p>The change was approved by the Riksdag and formalised through<a href="https://svenskforfattningssamling.se/sites/default/files/sfs/2026-05/SFS2026-841.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Act SFS 2026:841</a>, which was issued on 28 May 2026 and published on 3 June 2026. The legislation amends Chapter 9, Section 14 of the Value Added Tax Act (2023:200).</p>
<p>Under the revised provision, tax will be levied at 6% of the tax base for admission to concerts, circus, theatre, opera and ballet performances, as well as other similar performances. The same 6% rate will now apply to admission to dance events.</p>
<p>The amended section also retains the 6% VAT rate for admission to and the exhibition of zoos, as well as the exhibition of nature areas located outside urban areas.</p>
<p>Guided tours and showings of national parks, nature reserves, national urban parks and Natura 2000 areas are also covered by the reduced rate.</p>
<p>The government said the reduction for dance events is intended to align their VAT treatment with that of other comparable cultural activities, including theatre performances, concerts and opera. The measure aims to support social interaction and community life by ensuring consistent tax treatment across similar cultural events.</p>
<p>The legislation enters into force on 1 July 2026. Transitional provisions specify that older regulations will continue to apply to value-added tax on taxable transactions where the taxable event occurred before the commencement date.</p>
<p>The act was signed on behalf of the government by Minister for Finance Elisabeth Svantesson and Anna Sundblad Stahre of the Ministry of Finance.</p>

The Order grants eligible women an income tax exemption on gross employment income for a continuous period of up to 12 months. The order is effective from the year of assessment 2024 through 2028.</p>
<p><strong>Criteria for approved individuals</strong></p>
<p>To qualify for the tax exemption, a woman must meet several criteria:</p>
<ul>
<li>Citizenship &amp; residency: She must be a Malaysian citizen and a resident of Malaysia.</li>
<li>The career break: She must have ceased employment and had no employment income for at least 24 consecutive months on or after 28 October 2017.</li>
<li>Prior experience: She must have had at least three years of full-time work experience before her career break.</li>
<li>Age: She must not be older than 58 years at the time of her application.</li>
<li>New employment:
<ul>
<li>She must sign a full-time employment contract in Malaysia for at least 24 months between 1 January 2023 and 31 December 2028.</li>
<li>She must have already worked for at least 12 consecutive months under this new contract.</li>
<li>The gross monthly income from this new contract must be at least MYR 5,000.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>The exemption details</strong></p>
<p>The tax exemption applies to gross employment income for a period not exceeding 12 consecutive months.</p>
<p>Eligible women must apply through Talent Corporation Malaysia Berhad between 1 January 2024 and 31 December 2027. TalentCorp is responsible for verifying that all conditions are met.</p>
<p>The exemption period begins in the year of assessment when the individual makes the &#8220;option&#8221; for it, which must be the year the application is received or the following year. Even if exempt from paying the tax, the individual is still required to submit all necessary tax returns or account statements as required by the Income Tax Act 1967.</p>
<p><strong>Restrictions and exclusions</strong></p>
<p>The exemption excludes women employed by companies they control, sole proprietorships, or close family members, and cannot be claimed by those who already benefited from the 2019 equivalent order.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UAE has ratified the Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement on Automatic Exchange of Information Pursuant to the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF MCAA).</p>
<p>The UAE is among the <a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-issues/tax-transparency-and-international-co-operation/carf-mcaa-signatories.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">signatories</a> to the CARF MCAA, which was opened for signature on 21 July 2025. The <a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-issues/tax-transparency-and-international-co-operation/text-carf-mcaa.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">agreement</a>, developed by the OECD, establishes a framework for the annual automatic exchange of tax-relevant information on crypto-assets between competent authorities in participating jurisdictions.</p>
<p>Under the agreement, participating jurisdictions will exchange information on reportable users, including tax residency details, taxpayer identification numbers and aggregated information on crypto-asset transactions. The reporting requirements cover purchases, sales, exchanges and transfers of crypto-assets, as well as certain wallet-related transactions.</p>
<p>The CARF MCAA is intended to support the implementation of the OECD&#8217;s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), which was developed to address tax compliance risks arising from the growing use of digital assets and cross-border crypto-asset activities.</p>
<p>Information exchanged under the agreement will be transmitted through a secure international system incorporating encryption and other safeguards. The framework also establishes procedures for cooperation between authorities in cases involving reporting errors, compliance concerns and confidentiality breaches.</p>
<p>In addition, the agreement contains provisions on confidentiality and data protection, requiring exchanged information to be used solely for tax administration purposes. It also allows for the temporary suspension of information exchanges where a participating authority fails to meet the agreement&#8217;s compliance standards.</p>
<p>The ratification confirms the UAE&#8217;s participation in the expanding international network of jurisdictions adopting common reporting standards for crypto-assets, with the aim of improving transparency and enhancing the enforcement of tax compliance obligations related to digital asset transactions.</p>

		<item>
		<title>Australia: ATO issues guidance on how to evidence DTA residency in arrangements involving FTEs</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/australia-ato-issues-guidance-on-how-to-evidence-dta-residency-in-arrangements-involving-ftes/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=australia-ato-issues-guidance-on-how-to-evidence-dta-residency-in-arrangements-involving-ftes</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 16 Jun 2026 11:23:35 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Double Taxation Treaties]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Uncategorized]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Asia-Pacific]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Australia]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=83603</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has released updated guidance on 11 June 2026 clarifying how residency under double tax agreements can be demonstrated in structures involving fiscally transparent entities. Fiscally transparent entities and tax treaty residency claims How to evidence double tax agreement (DTA) residency in arrangements involving fiscally transparent entities (FTEs). What are fiscally...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has released updated <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/private-capital-program/fiscally-transparent-entities-and-tax-treaty-residency-claims" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance</a> on 11 June 2026 clarifying how residency under double tax agreements can be demonstrated in structures involving fiscally transparent entities.</p>
<p><strong>Fiscally transparent entities and tax treaty residency claims</strong></p>
<p>How to evidence double tax agreement (DTA) residency in arrangements involving fiscally transparent entities (FTEs).</p>
<p><strong>What are fiscally transparent entities</strong></p>
<p>An entity is a fiscally transparent entity (FTE) where, under the domestic law of a contracting state, the profits (or part of them) of the entity or arrangement isn&#8217;t taxed at the level of the entity or the arrangement, and it&#8217;s instead taxed at the level of the persons who have an interest in that entity or arrangement (ultimate investors).</p>
<p>In private equity investments, common entities that may be treated as FTEs for tax purposes in some contracting states include limited partnerships, as well as US-incorporated limited liability companies.</p>
<p><strong>Private capital programme&#8217;s approach to private equity</strong></p>
<p>The <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/private-capital-program/about-the-private-capital-program" target="_blank" rel="noopener">private capital programme</a> (PCP) is funded by the <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/about-ato/tax-avoidance/tax-avoidance-taskforce" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Tax Avoidance Taskforce</a>. The PCP&#8217;s work seeks to give the community confidence that the largest public and multinational groups involved in Australian private capital investments are paying the right amount of tax.</p>
<p>The establishment of a dedicated programme recognises the scale of private capital investment in Australia, as well as the unique features and the tax issues related to the entities and structures that are often used.</p>
<p>The PCP&#8217;s approach to private equity investment focuses on global private equity firms and their associated participants, including the funds and their investors, as well as the Australian targets.</p>
<p>For more information, see <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/corporate-tax-measures-and-assurance/private-equity" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Private equity</a>.</p>
<p><strong>Substantiating DTA residency for FTEs</strong></p>
<p>Ultimate investors in an FTE or an arrangement may be eligible for treaty benefits under some of Australia&#8217;s double tax agreements (DTAs).</p>
<p>Where a DTA facilitates this, ATO requires evidence that ultimate investors in the arrangement are residents of the country with which Australia has the relevant DTA.</p>
<p>The ultimate investors of an FTE are the entities to which the income derived by or through the FTE is allocated as their income for income tax purposes in their country of residence and they are liable to tax as a resident on that income.</p>
<p><strong>Primary evidence requirement</strong></p>
<p>The ATO expects the evidence regarding the residency of interest holders of FTEs in private equity arrangements to largely be primary evidence.</p>
<p>In this regard, it considers that statutory declarations, statements under penalty of perjury or their equivalents are insufficient to substantiate residency.</p>
<p>At a minimum, ATO expects the following primary evidence to be kept and produced on request for each ultimate investor for which a DTA claim is being made:</p>
<p>1. Tax identification forms which show the:</p>
<ul>
<li>name of the entity</li>
<li>type of entity</li>
<li>treatment of each entity involved in the structure under the jurisdiction of the ultimate investors&#8217; domestic tax law.</li>
</ul>
<p>2. Certification of residency issued by the tax authorities of the relevant country which demonstrates residency of an entity for domestic tax law purposes.</p>
<p>Where the above are not sufficient to substantiate residency of an interest holder for DTA purposes, ATO may also request the following, among other documents:</p>
<p>3. Incorporation documents.</p>
<p>4. Tax returns (whether foreign or domestic).</p>
<p>The above evidence is applicable to each ultimate investor. There is no de minimis for ultimate investors by reason of their holding percentage in an Australian target.</p>
<p><strong>FTE keeping records of the ultimate investors</strong></p>
<p>Where an FTE deriving Australian-sourced income is keeping records of its ultimate investors, ATO expects a spreadsheet setting out the information listed below to be produced by or on behalf of this FTE. This is an initial step to demonstrate satisfaction of the DTA residency requirement.</p>
<p>Provide a list, links or copies of the primary evidence for each of the following items:</p>
<ul>
<li>name of the investor(s) holding an interest in the FTE</li>
<li>investor(s) entity type (for example, limited partnership, limited liability corporation)</li>
<li>investor(s) entity, or entities&#8217;, country of establishment or incorporation</li>
<li>investor(s) share (%) of the FTEs income</li>
<li>name(s) of the ultimate investor(s)</li>
<li>ultimate investor(s) country, or countries, of tax residence</li>
<li>ultimate investor(s) country of DTA residence</li>
<li>treatment of the income derived by or through the FTE under the jurisdiction of the ultimate investors&#8217; domestic tax law.</li>
</ul>
<p>Where only a portion of the income for which DTA benefits are being claimed demonstrably satisfies the DTA residency requirement under the applicable DTA or DTAs, DTA benefits will only be granted on this portion of the income if the ultimate investor also satisfies the other requirements under the relevant DTA.</p>

<li>proposed amendments to the thresholds for excluding sellers engaged in low-value goods transactions;</li>
<li>proposals to clarify the definitions of “Platform” and “Platform Operator”, as well as the related Commentary, with a view to addressing divergent interpretations;</li>
<li>a proposed limitation of transactional reporting where a seller is itself a Reporting Platform Operator; and</li>
<li>the introduction of a “Related Entity” concept to exclude certain intra-group platform arrangements from the scope of reporting.</li>
</ul>
<p>Separately, delegates are still considering possible approaches to improve reporting outcomes in relation to intermediary sellers.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Italian Revenue Agency has issued <a href="https://www.agenziaentrate.gov.it/portale/documents/20143/10065067/Provvedimento+prot.+171016_2026.pdf/571e285d-057b-fbe7-5580-0eb0d627a1e5?t=1781181588517" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Provision of 8 June 2026 (Prot. n. 171016/2026)</a>, which establishes the operational rules for requesting legal advice under Article 10-octies of the Statute of Taxpayer&#8217;s Rights. This procedure is specifically designed to provide a general or abstract interpretation of tax provisions managed by the Agency, particularly when there is high complexity or uncertainty.</p>
<p><strong>Eligible subjects </strong></p>
<p>The right to request legal advice is strictly limited to three main categories of subjects:</p>
<ul>
<li>Associations and professional orders: This includes regional or national trade unions, category associations, and professional orders that represent widespread collective interests.</li>
<li>Public bodies: This category encompasses central state administrations, national public entities, and local or territorial public authorities.</li>
<li>Non-residents: This includes foreign companies, multinational entities, and foreign collective entities that do not meet the residency criteria defined in Italian tax law.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Submission and competent offices</strong></p>
<p>The entity to which the request must be sent depends on the nature of the applicant:</p>
<ul>
<li>Regional directorates: Competent for local associations, professional orders, and local public bodies operating within the region.</li>
<li>Taxpayer division: Competent for national associations, central state administrations, national public entities, and all non-resident subjects.</li>
</ul>
<p>If a request is sent to the wrong office, that office will forward it to the competent one, though the response deadline will only begin once the correct office receives it.</p>
<p><strong>Procedural requirements</strong></p>
<p>The provision outlines specific formal and administrative rules for these requests:</p>
<ul>
<li>Format and cost: Requests are exempt from stamp duty and can be written in free form. They must be signed by a legal representative or an authorised proxy.</li>
<li>Submission methods: Generally, requests must be submitted electronically via Certified Email (PEC) or the Agency’s specific telemetric service. For non-residents who do not have a local domicile in Italy, submission via ordinary email to a designated address is permitted.</li>
<li>Mandatory declaration: The applicant must declare that they are not aware of any ongoing tax audits or unresolved control activities regarding the specific interpretive issue raised in the request.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Procedural timeline</strong></p>
<p>If requests lack formal requirements, the Agency grants applicants 30 days to regularise them. The Agency may request supplementary documentation once, allowing the applicant 60 days to comply or provide justification for non-compliance.</p>
<p>The Agency issues written, reasoned responses published on the Revenue Agency&#8217;s website to ensure legal consistency and public transparency.</p>
<p>All procedural deadlines for both parties are suspended annually from 1 August to 31 August 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Tunisia&#8217;s 2026 Finance Law introduces a sweeping framework allowing taxpayers to clear outstanding obligations with substantial penalty forgiveness, while simultaneously opening an amnesty window for previously unfiled tax documents, according to a <a href="https://jibaya.tn/blog/art-69-lf-2026/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">notice</a> on 11 June 2026.</p>
<p>The scheme targets both historical debt resolution and compliance gaps.</p>
<p><strong>Complete penalty waiver for historical debts</strong></p>
<p>The law eliminates all penalties—audit charges, late payment fees, and collection costs—on tax debts recorded in the Public Treasury Collector&#8217;s accounts before 1 January 2026. Taxpayers who underwent audits resulting in settlement agreements or mandatory assessments issued by 20 June 2026 also qualify, provided the original declaration deadlines had expired before 31 October 2025.</p>
<p>Court-ordered tax assessments relating to valuation disputes, recorded by 20 June 2026, equally benefit from full penalty cancellation.</p>
<p>To activate relief, debtors must settle arrears in a lump sum or commit to a payment schedule, with the first instalment due no later than 30 June 2026. Industrial, commercial, and professional activity taxes, along with hotel tax and licence fees, enjoy identical treatment.</p>
<p>Notably, taxpayers already enrolled in previous settlement schemes are excluded.</p>
<p><strong>50% reduction on administrative violations</strong></p>
<p>Penalties for administrative tax breaches recorded before 20 June 2026 will be halved, alongside related collection expenses. The same payment and timing requirements apply. Prior settlement beneficiaries remain ineligible.</p>
<p><strong>Flexible payment terms with built-in safeguards</strong></p>
<p>Payment schedules extend up to five years, with quarterly instalments determined by the Finance Minister according to debtor classification and collection capacity. Extensions are permitted if the total period remains within five years.</p>
<p>Missed payments restart collection proceedings and trigger a 1.25% monthly penalty on overdue instalments. Taxpayers forfeit relief benefits if final payments remain outstanding 120 days beyond the scheduled deadline.</p>
<p><strong>Filing amnesty for missing declarations</strong></p>
<p>Tax declarations—including contracts, deeds, and registration documents—with original deadlines before 31 October 2025 can be filed penalty-free between 1 January 2026 and 30 September 2026. Principal tax must accompany submission or registration.</p>
<p>This applies to omitted and corrective filings, even those prompted by tax authority intervention or audit notice. The amnesty covers penalties under Articles 81, 82, and 85 of the Code of Tax Rights and Procedures.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Australia&#8217;s largest accounting body, CPA Australia, has sounded a warning over the government&#8217;s newly introduced <a href="https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/ems/r7493_ems_a90ad43e-17d7-4cd3-859b-84ac4e6f3dea/upload_pdf/JC018386.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Treasury Laws Amendment Bill 2026</a>, cautioning that the legislation risks making the tax system more complex rather than simpler.</p>
<p>The Bill delivers the core elements of the Federal Budget&#8217;s tax package — including changes to capital gains tax (CGT), negative gearing, the Working Australians Tax Offset, and a standard deduction — but leaves critical components unresolved.</p>
<p>CPA Australia Tax Lead Jenny Wong flagged a key structural concern: the proposed minimum tax on discretionary trusts, considered the most consequential reform for private business owners, has been split into a separate Bill, leaving what she described as a major gap in the system.</p>
<p>Beyond the gaps. Wong criticised the Government&#8217;s decision to introduce sweeping reforms before completing consultation, calling it deeply concerning and urging a &#8220;consult first, legislate later&#8221; approach.</p>
<p>CPA Australia also warned that implementing the changes in stages creates a two-tier system where some Australians know where they stand and others do not — with real consequences for investment decisions being made right now.</p>
<p><strong>Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 </strong></p>
<p>The Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026 introduces a comprehensive package of tax reforms designed to improve the fairness and sustainability of the Australian tax system.</p>
<p>The bill is divided into four primary schedules, each targeting specific areas of tax law.</p>
<p>The key measures are as follows:</p>
<p><strong>Capital gains and housing </strong></p>
<p>From 1 July 2027, the 50% capital gains tax discount for individuals and trusts will be retired in favour of cost base indexation, ensuring only inflation-adjusted gains face taxation. However, a new 30%  minimum tax on capital gains will prevent high-value investors from reducing their tax burden by timing asset sales during low-income years. Low-income individuals receiving Age Pension or JobSeeker payments are protected from this floor.</p>
<p>Legacy assets acquired before 20 September 1985—previously untouched by CGT—will be brought into the tax net for gains accruing after 1 July 2027. To preserve housing investment incentives, developers and affordable housing investors retain the option to apply the existing 50% discount (or up to 60% for affordable housing projects).</p>
<p><strong>Rental losses contained </strong></p>
<p>Negative gearing restrictions take effect for established residential properties purchased on or after 12 May 2026. Investors can no longer offset net rental losses against unrelated income such as wages; losses become &#8220;quarantined&#8221; and may only reduce future property-related income or gains. New residential dwellings remain exempt from quarantining, and properties acquired before the cutoff date retain grandfathered treatment under existing rules.</p>
<p><strong>Relief for wage earners and simplified deductions</strong></p>
<p>The Working Australians Tax Offset (WATO), rolling out from the 2027–28 income year, delivers a maximum AUD 250 non-refundable tax offset to workers with net labour income above the tax-free threshold. In parallel, a new AUD 1,000 standard deduction for work-related expenses simplifies claims from 2026–27 onwards, allowing workers to claim without receipts. Those with genuine expenses exceeding AUD 1,000 may still itemise and substantiate their claims, though this forfeits the standard deduction. The change eliminates the former AUD 300 substantiation exemption and $150 laundry expense concession.</p>

		<title>Denmark: Supreme Court clarifies limitation period for tax refund claims</title>

					<description><![CDATA[The Danish Supreme Court (Højesteret) issued a ruling in Cases BS-36976/2025-HJR and BS-36974/2025-HJR on 11 June 2026, concerning the limitation period (statute of limitations) for claims seeking refunds of withheld dividend and royalty taxes. The cases involved the Ministry of Taxation and three taxpayers (A, B, and C), who sought refunds on the grounds that...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Danish Supreme Court (Højesteret) issued a <a href="https://www.domstol.dk/hoejesteret/aktuelt/2026/6/foraeldelsesfrist-for-tilbagebetaling-af-indeholdt-udbytte-og-royaltyskat/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ruling</a> in Cases BS-36976/2025-HJR and BS-36974/2025-HJR on 11 June 2026, concerning the limitation period (statute of limitations) for claims seeking refunds of withheld dividend and royalty taxes. The cases involved the Ministry of Taxation and three taxpayers (A, B, and C), who sought refunds on the grounds that Danish companies had withheld tax in excess of the amounts payable under applicable double taxation agreements.</p>
<p><strong>Core dispute</strong></p>
<p>The central legal question was whether these refund claims were subject to the standard three-year limitation period found in the Limitation Act or the extended five-year limitation period specified in Section 67 A of the Withholding Tax Act (Kildeskatteloven).</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>The Ministry of taxation&#8217;s position:</strong> The Ministry argued that the five-year period in Section 67 A only applied to the tax authorities&#8217; claims against the companies responsible for withholding the tax, not to the refund claims made by the taxpayers themselves.</li>
<li><strong>The taxpayers&#8217; position: </strong>The taxpayers argued that their refund claims were &#8220;claims covered by Sections 65-65 D&#8221; as stated in Section 67 A, and that the legislative history supported a five-year window.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Historical context</strong></p>
<p>From the introduction of Section 67 A in 2010 until 2016, the Danish tax authority (SKAT) had officially practiced a five-year limitation period for such refunds. However, in June 2016, SKAT issued a &#8220;steering signal&#8221; (SKM2016.263.SKAT) changing this practice to a three-year period, claiming the previous interpretation was incorrect.</p>
<p><strong>The Supreme Court’s reasoning</strong></p>
<p>The Supreme Court reached its decision based on several factors:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Ambiguity of wording: </strong>The Court found that the text of Section 67 A was not entirely clear on whether it specifically included or excluded taxpayer refund claims.</li>
<li><strong>Legislative intent:</strong> The legislative history (preparatory works) for Section 67 A explicitly stated that &#8220;claims for recovery of too much withheld tax&#8221; should be able to occur within the five-year period. The Court interpreted this as referring primarily to the claims raised by taxpayers, as these are the most common.</li>
<li><strong>Systemic consistency:</strong> The Court noted that the five-year period was intended to align these cases with other complex tax matters, such as transfer pricing and corporate restructurings, which also carry a five-year limitation period for both the authorities and the taxpayers.</li>
<li><strong>Previous administrative practice:</strong> The Court emphasised that the tax authorities themselves had understood and administered the law using the five-year period for several years after its enactment.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>The final result</strong></p>
<p>The Supreme Court ruled that the five-year limitation period applies to claims for the refund of withheld dividend and royalty taxes. Consequently, the Court found that the tax authorities lacked the legal basis for the 2016 practice change that had shortened the period to three years.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

<p>The notification portal will launch on 1 July 2026, with submissions required by 30 September 2026 for the 2024 and 2025 assessment years.</p>
<p><strong>New filing portal opens mid-2026</strong></p>
<p>Under the <a href="https://www.ejustice.just.fgov.be/eli/wet/2023/12/19/2023048529/staatsblad" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Law of 19 December 2023</a>, which introduced minimum tax requirements for in-scope groups, taxpayers must designate a single entity to file the GIR on behalf of the entire group (Articles 53(3) and 54(2)). <p><strong>Key dates and requirements</strong></p>
<p>Groups have until 30 September 2026 to notify their designated GIR filing entity for both 2024 and 2025.</p>
<p>This extended timeline provides additional time for multinational enterprises and large domestic groups to ensure compliance with the global minimum tax framework before submission commences.</p>
<p>Law of 19 December 2023, or the Belgian Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax Act, enacted on 19 December 2023, establishes a minimum tax rate for multinational enterprises (MNEs) and large-scale domestic groups. This law transposes EU Directive (EU) 2022/2523, which aims to ensure a global minimum tax rate of 15%. The legislation applies to group entities established in Belgium that are part of a group with annual revenues of at least EUR 750 million.</p>
<p>To ensure tax compliance, the law introduces three distinct mechanisms: a domestic top-up tax, an Income Inclusion Rule (IIR), and an Undertaxed Profit Rule (UTPR). Detailed definitions are provided for various organisational structures, including pension funds, non-profit organisations, and investment entities, many of which are specifically excluded from the scope of the tax.</p>
<p>Additionally, the text specifies rigorous accounting standards and adjustment methods required to calculate qualifying income and adjusted covered taxes. Ultimately, these measures aim to prevent base erosion and ensure that large entities contribute a fair share of tax across all jurisdictions where they operate.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Brazilian Federal Revenue Service (RFB) <a href="https://www.gov.br/receitafederal/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/2026/junho/receita-federal-oficializa-identidade-do-programa-confia-e-reforca-regras-para-uso-da-marca-e-do-selo-de-conformidade-confia" target="_blank" rel="noopener">clarified</a>, on 12 June 2026, how companies in its cooperative tax programme should display their credentials.</p>
<p>Ordinance RFB No. 695, issued on 10 June 2026, establishes the official identity of the Cooperative Tax Compliance Programme (Confia), setting out standardised rules for the brand and compliance seal.</p>
<p>The measure aims to improve transparency and give legal certainty to how the programme is communicated.</p>
<p><strong>What Confia represents</strong></p>
<p>Confia, made permanent under Complementary Law No. 225 of 8 January 2026, encourages closer collaboration between tax authorities and taxpayers. The new ordinance introduces three components: the Confia Brand (representing the programme itself), the Confia Seal (awarded to participating companies), and a formal Brand Usage Manual. The Federal Revenue Service controls the brand; the seal is granted only to companies that meet compliance standards and maintain good standing in the programme.</p>
<p><strong>Conditions and consequences</strong></p>
<p>The Confia Seal is neither permanent nor automatic. Companies must continue to satisfy requirements set out in Normative Instruction RFB No. 2,295 of 3 December 2025. Non-compliance can result in withdrawal of the seal and removal from the programme. Misuse of the seal carries additional penalties, though the regulation guarantees due process and the right to a full defence.</p>
<p>Companies may display the seal in institutional materials, provided they follow the Brand Usage Manual guidelines for both physical and digital applications. The manual is published on the Federal Revenue Service and Confia websites.</p>
<p>The ordinance takes effect from 11 June 2026 and supersedes RFB Ordinance No. 445 of 2 August 2024.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bangladesh has proposed a 15% capital gains tax on profits from the sale or transfer of gold, silver, jewellery, precious stones, diamonds, coins, digital currencies, artworks, antiques and club memberships under the Finance Bill 2026 presented with the national budget for fiscal year 2026-27.</p>
<p>Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury announced the proposal in parliament, under which gains from assets declared in a taxpayer&#8217;s return would be treated as capital gains and taxed at 15%. The same rate will apply to gains from securities, including treasury bills, bonds, savings instruments, debentures, sukuk and other shariah-based securities, as well as shares and stocks.</p>
<p>The proposal comes as domestic gold prices remain elevated. The price of 22-carat gold rose by BDT 6,590 per bhori on June 13 to BDT 224,940 per bhori, after reaching a record BDT 286,000 per bhori earlier this year.</p>
<p>National Board of Revenue (NBR) officials defended the measure at a seminar on the Finance Bill, saying personally owned gold jewellery has been classified as a capital asset rather than a personal asset. Revenue officials said the provision is intended to reduce opportunities for tax evasion and is based on practices used in several European countries.</p>
<p>The budget also includes incentives for the jewellery sector. The government has proposed replacing the existing 5% VAT on gold with a fixed VAT of BDT 2,500 per bhori and reducing the tax deducted at source on purchases of gold, silver, jewellery, precious stones, diamonds and platinum from 5% to 0.5%.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Austria&#8217;s Federal Ministry of Finance has updated the list of jurisdictions participating in the automatic exchange of information (AEOI) for Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) Information Returns (GIRs), providing further guidance on reporting obligations under the Pillar Two global minimum tax regime.</p>
<p>In <a href="https://findok.bmf.gv.at/findok/resources/pdf/3c4915b9-382f-4b29-aeb6-d5f211eb74c4/84432.1.1.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">BMF Letter No. 2026-0.475.107</a>, published on 9 June, the ministry outlined exchange relationships in force under Council Directive (EU) 2025/872 (DAC9), the Multilateral Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters and the GIR Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement (GIR-MCAA).</p>
<p>The guidance applies to Austrian constituent entities of multinational enterprise (MNE) groups and large domestic groups with consolidated annual revenue of at least EUR 750 million. These entities are required to submit a GIR electronically to the Tax Office for Large Businesses (Finanzamt für Großbetriebe) using the prescribed template.</p>
<p>GIRs must generally be filed within 15 months after the end of the fiscal year, while a transitional period allows an extended deadline of 18 months. The ministry noted that the first GIR filing deadline will not expire before 30 June 2026.</p>
<p>Where a group files a GIR centrally in a jurisdiction that has an active exchange relationship with Austria, local Austrian entities are exempt from filing a separate GIR. Instead, they must submit a &#8220;Notification 2&#8221; identifying the reporting entity and the jurisdiction in which the report was filed.</p>
<p>As of 1 June 2026, Austria recognised 34 jurisdictions with exchange relationships for fiscal years beginning on or after 31 December 2023.</p>

		<title>EU: FASTER directive signals need for Swiss withholding tax reform</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/eu-faster-directive-signals-need-for-swiss-withholding-tax-reform/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=eu-faster-directive-signals-need-for-swiss-withholding-tax-reform</link>

					<description><![CDATA[The European Union&#8217;s Faster and Safer Tax Relief of Excess Withholding Taxes (FASTER) directive establishes streamlined withholding tax relief procedures that expose significant gaps in Switzerland&#8217;s current system. While EU member states prepare to implement rapid electronic refunds by 1 January 2030, Swiss authorities continue to rely on largely paper-based mechanisms, creating a competitive disadvantage...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The European Union&#8217;s Faster and Safer Tax Relief of Excess Withholding Taxes (FASTER) directive establishes streamlined withholding tax relief procedures that expose significant gaps in Switzerland&#8217;s current system.</p>
<p>While EU member states prepare to implement rapid electronic refunds by 1 January 2030, Swiss authorities continue to rely on largely paper-based mechanisms, creating a competitive disadvantage for cross-border investors.</p>
<p><strong>The current Swiss framework</strong></p>
<p>Switzerland imposes a withholding tax of 35% on dividend payments from Swiss resident corporations and interest on bonds issued by Swiss resident debtors. This rate ranks among the world&#8217;s highest. Excess withholding tax cannot be recovered through mechanisms other than a formal refund process, and refund claims are restricted to the calendar year following payment, creating substantial delays for investors seeking cash recovery. For all jurisdictions except Germany, the process remains exclusively paper-based as of June 2026.</p>
<p><strong>FASTER&#8217;s acceleration mechanisms</strong></p>
<p>The FASTER directive, which EU member states must transpose into national law by 31 December 2028, introduces three interconnected innovations. Tax residency certificates will be issued electronically within 14 days, eliminating the postal delays that characterise the Swiss system. Member states must then adopt either relief-at-source treatment (where reduced rates apply at payment) or a quick refund procedure guaranteeing reimbursement within 60 days, with statutory interest payable if deadlines are missed.</p>
<p>Standardised XML-based reporting will occur in near-real-time, requiring financial intermediaries to file detailed payment information by the end of the second month following each transaction.</p>
<p><strong>Implications for Switzerland</strong></p>
<p>Swiss authorities recognise the need for digitisation and have expanded online filing, but only for German-resident investors to date. Extending digital access to other jurisdictions remains stalled pending bilateral agreements for secure transmission channels. The gap between the current Swiss practice—permitting refund claims only after each calendar year ends—and FASTER&#8217;s two-month window is substantial.</p>
<p>The EU standard may catalyse change at the cantonal level. Introducing electronic tax residency certificates modelled on FASTER&#8217;s standards would streamline relief processing for both foreign investors and Swiss banks managing refunds for Swiss resident clients participating in cross-border transactions.</p>
<p>Without such alignment, Switzerland risks reduced competitiveness as EU-based withholding regimes become faster and more accessible.</p>
<p>On 14 May 2024, the Council <a href="https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/taxation/business-taxation/faster-directive_en" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reached</a> an agreement on the Faster and Safer Tax Relief of Excess Withholding Taxes (FASTER) Directive. The new rules make withholding tax procedures in the EU more efficient and secure for investors, financial intermediaries and national tax administrations.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Hong Kong government has <a href="https://www.ird.gov.hk/eng/ppr/archives/26061202.htm" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> the Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Preferential Tax Regimes for Funds, Family-owned Investment Holding Vehicles and Carried Interest) Bill 2026 in the Gazette on 12 June 2026.</p>
<p>The bill aims to enhance the preferential tax regimes for privately offered funds, family-owned investment holding vehicles (FIHVs) managed by eligible single family offices and carried interest, with a view to attracting more funds and family offices to establish a presence in Hong Kong.</p>
<p>The bill covers amendments to the Inland Revenue Ordinance in areas such as: (i) expanding the definition of &#8220;fund&#8221;; (ii) expanding the scope of qualifying investments; (iii) removing the 5 per cent threshold requirement for incidental transactions; (iv) relaxing the tax exemption treatment for special purpose entities (SPEs) and family-owned SPEs; and (v) introducing a series of enhancement measures to the tax regime for carried interest.</p>
<p>The Bill will also introduce, under the unified tax regime for funds, a tax reporting mechanism as well as economic substance requirements similar to those under the tax concession regime for FIHVs.</p>
<p>&#8220;Hong Kong is now the world&#8217;s largest cross-boundary wealth management centre. The National 15th Five-Year Plan clearly supports Hong Kong in continuing to strengthen its functions as an international asset and wealth management (WAM) centre. In this connection, the Government has long been committed to reinforcing our leading position in this area through providing a competitive tax environment. The relevant amendments under the Bill will attract more funds and family offices to set up and operate in Hong Kong, and in turn create new opportunities for Hong Kong&#8217;s WAM industry. In particular, this would help further attract private credit investment activities in the region, while complementing Hong Kong&#8217;s development in areas such as digital assets and trading of precious metals and commodities,&#8221; a spokesperson for the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau said.</p>
<p>The bill will be introduced into the Legislative Council for first reading on 24 June 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US House Ways and Means Committee held a <a href="https://waysandmeans.house.gov/event/full-committee-legislative-hearing-on-digital-asset-taxation/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">hearing</a> on 9 June 2026 to explore new tax rules for digital assets, advancing eight bills and discussion drafts that aim to simplify compliance and establish clearer rules for activities like cryptocurrency mining and staking.</p>
<p>The proposals address longstanding gaps in how the tax code treats digital assets compared to traditional investments.</p>
<p>Committee Chairman Jason Smith (R-Mo.) emphasised the importance of creating workable rules, noting that roughly 25% of Americans now own cryptocurrency. He identified three core problems: transactions like mining and staking that don&#8217;t fit existing tax frameworks; digital assets lacking comparable tax benefits; and burdensome compliance requirements for owners. Ranking Member Richard Neal (D-Mass.) acknowledged the topic&#8217;s complexity and expressed support for certain provisions, but cautioned against tilting the tax code in favour of digital assets, warning that &#8220;it&#8217;s much easier to put something in the tax code than it is to take it out.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Key proposals under review</strong></p>
<p>The hearing examined multiple legislative proposals, including H.R. 9176 addressing digital asset trading, H.R. 9172 covering wash sale and constructive sale rules, and a discussion draft on US-sourced gains. The committee also discussed a de minimis exception for small gains, revised mining and staking rules, charitable contribution treatment, and voluntary disclosure mechanisms. No formal markup has yet been scheduled.</p>
<p><strong>Wider congressional context</strong></p>
<p>The hearing follows the Senate Banking Committee&#8217;s May 2026 passage of the CLARITY Act (H.R. 3633), which establishes market structure rules for digital assets. Lawmakers from both parties stressed the need for tax rules that provide clarity and certainty whilst recognising that digital assets will remain integral to the economy.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UK&#8217;s His Majesty&#8217;s Revenue and Customs (HMRC) has published <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/get-access-to-pillar-2-top-up-taxes-as-an-agent" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance</a> outlining how agents can access and amend a client&#8217;s domestic top-up taxes and multinational top-up taxes (Pillar Two top-up taxes) information through its online service.</p>
<p>The guidance, issued on 10 June 2026, explains the steps agents must complete before they can manage Pillar Two top-up tax matters on behalf of clients.</p>
<p>HMRC said agents should first determine whether a client is required to report Pillar Two top-up taxes. To use the service, agents must have an agent services account. Those without an account can create one before proceeding.</p>
<p>The guidance also states that agents must obtain authorisation through HMRC&#8217;s digital handshake process. Each client must accept a digital handshake request before an agent can access the client&#8217;s Pillar Two top-up taxes information.</p>
<p>Once authorised, agents can sign in to their agent services account to access the Pillar Two top-up taxes service. HMRC noted that online services may operate more slowly during busy periods and advised users to check for any service issues.</p>
<p>After signing in, agents are able to act on behalf of clients in relation to Pillar Two top-up taxes. The service allows agents to view, amend and submit Pillar Two top-up taxes returns, contact HMRC regarding current and previous returns, and view or update details including contact information, accounting periods and organisation type.</p>
<p>Agents can also provide repayment bank details to HMRC when a repayment is due and view amounts owed and paid under the Pillar Two top-up taxes regime.</p>
<p>The guidance forms part of HMRC&#8217;s support for agents managing compliance obligations associated with domestic top-up taxes and multinational top-up taxes under the Pillar Two framework.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>In the landmark decision of<a href="https://www.hcourt.gov.au/sites/default/files/eresources/2026-06-10/HCA/Commissioner%20of%20Taxation%20v%20Bendel%20%28M47-2025%29%20%5B2026%5D%20HCA%2018.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Commissioner of Taxation v Bendel HCA 18</a>, the High Court of Australia dismissed the Commissioner’s appeal by a 5–2 majority, providing critical judicial clarification on the intersection of trust law and anti-avoidance tax rules.</p>
<p>The Court held that unpaid present entitlements (UPEs) belonging to a corporate beneficiary are not treated as &#8220;loans&#8221; under Division 7A of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth) simply because they remain unpaid.</p>
<p>The ruling confirms the Full Federal Court&#8217;s earlier decision in <a href="https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/cases/cth/FCAFC/2025/15.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Bendel [2025] FCAFC 15</a> and settles a question that has shaped trust distribution practices for over a decade.</p>
<p><strong>The core dispute and Division 7A</strong></p>
<p>The dispute centred on whether a private company, Gleewin Investments, made &#8220;loans&#8221; to Gleewin Pty Ltd (the trustee of the Steven Bendel 2005 Discretionary Trust) by failing to call for the payment of trust income set aside for its benefit between 2014 and 2017.</p>
<p>Division 7A is intended to prevent private companies from making tax-free distributions of profits to shareholders or their associates through payments, loans, or forgiven debts. The Commissioner argued that by remaining &#8220;passive&#8221; and not demanding payment, the corporate beneficiary provided &#8220;financial accommodation&#8221; to the trustee, which falls under the expanded definition of a &#8220;loan&#8221; in section 109D(3).</p>
<p><strong>The majority’s rejection of &#8220;financial accommodation&#8221;</strong></p>
<p>The majority (Gageler CJ, Gordon, Edelman, Steward, and Gleeson JJ) rejected the Commissioner&#8217;s broad interpretation for several key reasons:</p>
<ul>
<li>Inactivity vs. action: The Court ruled that a &#8220;provision&#8221; of financial accommodation requires some form of active transfer of value or bilateral interaction. Mere inactivity or the failure of a beneficiary to insist on its rights does not constitute a &#8220;transaction&#8221; or a &#8220;provision&#8221; of accommodation.</li>
<li>Trustee-beneficiary relationship: The Court found that the resolutions to set aside income did not create a standard debtor-creditor relationship. Instead, the amounts were held on separate trusts for the corporate beneficiary. This meant the trustee had a continuing duty to invest and manage those funds for the beneficiary, rather than a simple &#8220;unconditional duty to pay&#8221; a debt.</li>
<li>Double taxation concerns: The Court noted that the Commissioner&#8217;s construction would lead to &#8220;problematic&#8221; double taxation. The same amount of income would be taxed first in the hands of the corporate beneficiary (under trust distribution rules) and then taxed again in the following year as a &#8220;deemed dividend&#8221;.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Statutory context and Subdivision EA</strong></p>
<p>A significant factor in the ruling was the existence of Subdivision EA, which was enacted specifically to address UPEs in trust structures. The Court observed that when Parliament addressed the issue of value being &#8220;shifted&#8221; from a trust to a shareholder through unpaid entitlements, it chose to tax the shareholder receiving the benefit, not the trustee.</p>
<p>The majority concluded that the Commissioner was essentially attempting to use the general &#8220;loan&#8221; provisions in section 109D to achieve an outcome that Parliament had already specifically addressed—and limited—elsewhere in the law.</p>
<p><strong>Judicial clarification and impact</strong></p>
<p>This decision upholds the earlier ruling of the Full Federal Court and brings an end to over a decade of uncertainty regarding the tax treatment of UPEs.</p>
<p>For private groups, the ruling is highly significant for Australian business structures that commonly utilise discretionary trusts with corporate beneficiaries to manage wealth and business income.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[The European Commission released a country-by-country compliance guide for multinationals navigating the EU&#8217;s new global minimum tax framework on 10 June 2026. The “Manual for MNE Groups on Global Minimum Tax (Pillar Two) Compliance Obligations” covers Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Poland, Romania, Slovenia and Sweden, and stems from...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The European Commission released a country-by-country <a href="https://reforms-investments.ec.europa.eu/document/download/57c18ae7-346c-447e-baaf-4aeb4744bd49_en?filename=2026-06-10%20-%20D6%20Manual%20Final%20for%20SG%20Ref-1.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">compliance guide</a> for multinationals navigating the EU&#8217;s new global minimum tax framework on 10 June 2026.</p>
<p>The “Manual for MNE Groups on Global Minimum Tax (Pillar Two) Compliance Obligations” covers Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Poland, Romania, Slovenia and Sweden, and stems from the SG REFORM Technical Support Instrument project aimed at building Member State capacity to implement Directive (EU) 2022/2523.</p>
<p>The manual is based on information available to 1 May 2026 and is not official EU guidance; domestic updates remain critical for compliance.</p>
<p>All 14 jurisdictions have transposed the Pillar Two Directive into domestic law, but implementation varies significantly. The manual highlights that groups with multiple entities in a single Member State face divergent compliance routes: some jurisdictions enforce a designated or liable entity model, whilst others permit optional appointments, apply local allocation rules, or require entity-by-entity filing. These structural differences mean groups cannot adopt a one-size-fits-all approach across borders.</p>
<p><strong>Central filing does not eliminate local obligations</strong></p>
<p>The EU&#8217;s DAC9 framework allows groups to submit a single Pillar Two information return centrally and route it between tax administrations. Member States were required to implement DAC9 by 31 December 2025; tax authorities must exchange the information by 31 December 2026, and the first Pillar Two top-up tax information returns are expected by 30 June 2026.</p>
<p>However, DAC9 addresses only the information return—analogous to the OECD&#8217;s GloBE Information Return—not every domestic compliance requirement. Groups filing centrally must still manage local registration, notifications to appointing a designated entity, payment obligations, XML schema validation, and reasonable care documentation. For groups filing outside the EU, verification of active GIR MCAA bilateral exchange relationships for the relevant year remains essential; the OECD publishes an updated registry of operational GloBE exchanges.</p>

		<title>Pakistan reduces exemptions, accelerates tax administration digitalisation in FY2026-27 budget</title>

					<description><![CDATA[Pakistan&#8217;s government presented its Federal Budget for FY2026-27 on 12 June 2026, targeting PKR 20.6 trillion in revenue through higher tax collections, tax administration reforms and broader economic documentation as it seeks to maintain macroeconomic stability and remain on track with its IMF-supported programme. The budget projects PKR 15.26 trillion in Federal Board of Revenue...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Pakistan&#8217;s government presented its <a href="https://www.finance.gov.pk/budget/budget_2026_27/Annual_Budget_Statement.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Federal Budget for FY2026-27</a> on 12 June 2026, targeting PKR 20.6 trillion in revenue through higher tax collections, tax administration reforms and broader economic documentation as it seeks to maintain macroeconomic stability and remain on track with its IMF-supported programme.</p>
<p>The budget projects PKR 15.26 trillion in Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) tax collections, comprising PKR 7.61 trillion in direct taxes and PKR 7.65 trillion in indirect taxes. Non-tax revenue is estimated at PKR 5.34 trillion, including PKR 1.68 trillion from the Petroleum Levy and PKR 50 billion from the newly introduced Climate Support Levy.</p>
<p><strong>Tax reforms and revenue measures</strong></p>
<p>The government&#8217;s tax strategy focuses on broadening the tax base, reducing exemptions and accelerating digitalisation of tax administration. Tax expenditures arising from exemptions and concessions were estimated at PKR 2.35 trillion in the previous year, prompting efforts to rationalise relief measures and improve compliance.</p>
<p>Among relief measures, salaried individuals will benefit from revised income tax slabs, with the threshold for the highest 35% tax rate raised from PKR 4.1 million to PKR 7 million.</p>
<p>The budget also abolishes tax on deemed income from immovable property under Section 7E, reduces advance tax on property purchases to 1.25% and lowers tax on property sales or transfers to 2.75%.</p>
<p>The government has abolished Super Tax for taxpayers with income up to PKR 500 million and reduced the rate from 10% to 8% for higher-income taxpayers, excluding the banking, exploration and production, and fertiliser sectors.</p>
<p>Export-related taxes have also been eased. Tax collection on export proceeds has been reduced from 2% to 1.25%, while the preferential 0.25% tax rate for IT and IT-enabled services exports has been extended until tax year 2029.</p>
<p>Withholding tax on international debit, credit and prepaid card transactions has been cut from 5% to 0.5%.</p>
<p>New measures include a 5% withholding tax on social media earnings from platforms such as YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, to be collected by banks and financial institutions.</p>
<p>A tax credit equal to 10% of investment in electronic systems linked to the FBR&#8217;s digital platform has also been introduced.</p>
<p><strong>GST and excise duty changes</strong></p>
<p>Several consumer goods will move to retail-price-based sales tax collection, with GST charged at the manufacturer or import stage on the printed retail price. Products affected include milk products, edible oils, jams, ketchup, footwear, crockery, sanitaryware, hair products and plastic household goods.</p>
<p>The budget removes Federal Excise Duty on tampons, while increasing the duty on e-cigarette liquids from PKR 10,000 to PKR 16,500 per kg.</p>
<p>Imported vehicles above 2,000cc engine displacement, luxury imported vehicles and luxury electric vehicles will face Federal Excise Duty rates ranging from 40% to 41%. Token tax on motor vehicles in Islamabad Capital Territory has also been increased.</p>
<p><strong>Social spending and development priorities</strong></p>
<p>The government has increased funding for the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) to PKR 844.8 billion. An additional PKR 1 billion has been allocated for free medicines in federal government hospitals, while grants to the Higher Education Commission have been enhanced to support higher education and research.</p>
<p>The federal Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP) has been set at PKR 1 trillion, up 22% from the previous year, while combined federal and provincial development spending is projected at PKR 3.7 trillion.</p>
<p>Climate-related initiatives feature prominently in the budget. The government expects to raise PKR 50 billion through the Climate Support Levy and has allocated nearly PKR 5 billion to the Ministry of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination, including PKR 2.48 billion for development projects. Around 94% of the ministry&#8217;s development budget is earmarked for the Green Pakistan Programme.</p>
<p><strong>Defence and fiscal management</strong></p>
<p>Defence Affairs and Services spending has been allocated PKR 3.01 trillion, up from the revised estimate of PKR 2.60 trillion for FY2025-26. The allocation includes spending on personnel, operations, physical assets and civil works, while defence-related non-tax revenue is projected at PKR 31.47 billion.</p>
<p>The budget also outlines fiscal risk management measures, including protection of the primary surplus, reforms of state-owned enterprises through performance-based contracts, accelerated privatisation and debt management initiatives aimed at extending maturities and reducing debt-servicing costs.</p>
<p>Additional initiatives include the introduction of AI-enabled climate budgeting, new Sarwa Islamic Saving and Term Accounts under National Savings Schemes, and the establishment of the Prime Minister&#8217;s Austerity Fund 2026 to support expenditure rationalisation. Climate-responsive allocations account for 11% of development spending, while gender-responsive allocations represent 9% of current expenditure.</p>

		<title>Norway: Parliament mandates mandatory e-invoicing, digital bookkeeping</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/norway-parliament-mandates-mandatory-e-invoicing-digital-bookkeeping/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=norway-parliament-mandates-mandatory-e-invoicing-digital-bookkeeping</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Fri, 12 Jun 2026 13:12:59 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Policy announcements by government]]></category>
